docs.title: Apogee Engine
docs.text:
A free, open-source C# 3D engine made for crunching numbers: big worlds in double precision, a data-oriented ECS, SIMD, and the best libraries that exist for everything else.

Apogee is a set of small Apogee.* libraries, each with its own interop, on top of SDL3, Vulkan, Flecs, Luau, Jolt, OpenAL Soft, GameNetworkingSockets, Steamworks, Dear ImGui and RmlUi. The editor and dev builds run on CoreCLR; shipped games are NativeAOT, so engine code never uses runtime reflection. The engine is C#; games and mods are written in Luau and data. It is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

Pre-alpha

APIs change without notice. The engine is developed on Linux with Vulkan; Windows is built and tested by CI, and the Metal backend for macOS has never run on a GPU. See Help wanted.

The editor is very bare-bones for now: it cannot import 3D models or other assets (it only places and re-imports files already in the game folder), and it has no materials, no animations and no game export.

The source is at github.com/apogeeengine/Apogee.Engine.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Is Apogee ready to make a game with? Not yet in the sense of a stable engine: it is pre-alpha and APIs change. It is complete enough to build on if you read the code, and every library has tests and a Manual page.

Why not Unity, Unreal or Godot? Use them if they fit: for many games they are the right choice. Apogee is for games where the engine's assumptions get in the way of numbers: very large worlds, heavy simulation, custom data layouts. There you want to own the stack and have a foundation instead of a framework.

Why C#? Modern C# (unsafe code, spans, function pointers, SIMD, NativeAOT) is fast enough for the hot paths and much faster to work in than C++. Shipped games are NativeAOT, so there is no JIT and no runtime reflection.

Why Luau and not C# for games and mods? Scripts must be sandboxed, limited in time and memory, and reloadable while the game runs, and a mod must not be able to run native code. Luau was built for that. The engine is C#; the games made with it and their mods are Luau and data.

Which platforms? Windows, Linux and macOS, on x64 and Arm64 where the libraries allow. Vulkan 1.3 is the graphics API on Windows and Linux; macOS uses Metal 3, which is written but untested (help wanted). There is no console, mobile or web target.

Is there a Direct3D 12 backend? No, and it is not planned: Vulkan covers Windows. The graphics page says what it would take.

Do I have to use Steam? No. Apogee.Steam is a separate library, and a game that does not start it never touches Steam.

Can I use FMOD or Wwise? Not out of the box: the repository only ships libraries it may redistribute, so audio is OpenAL Soft. If your game needs one of them, replace Apogee.Audio in your project.

Do I have to credit Apogee in my game? The Apache License asks you to keep the license and NOTICE with copies of the engine you redistribute. The third-party libraries ask for their notices in your credits or documentation: Third-party notices lists what each one needs. We do not ask for royalties or a logo.

Is the engine written with AI? Parts of it are written with an AI assistant, under the maintainer's review and with tests. CONTRIBUTING.md says what we expect when you do the same.

docs.title: What Apogee is
docs.text:
Apogee is an engine for games that crunch numbers: simulations with big worlds, many entities and a lot of arithmetic per frame. Its choices follow from that.

  • Numbers first. Positions are double so a world can be thousands of kilometers wide without jitter; everything the GPU sees is float. The ECS is Flecs. Hot paths use unmanaged memory, unsafe code and SIMD, and do not allocate.
  • The best library for each job. SDL3 for windows and input, Vulkan 1.3 with VMA and the Slang shader compiler for graphics, Jolt for physics, Luau for scripting, OpenAL Soft for audio, GameNetworkingSockets for networking, Dear ImGui for tools, RmlUi for game UI. Our work is the thin, fast layer between them and the game.
  • Small libraries. One Apogee.* project per concern, each with its own interop. Take what you need; nothing forces the rest on you.
  • Our own bindings. The raw bindings (Apogee.Native.*) come from our own generator, checked by tests that every entry point resolves and every struct has clang's size. They are committed; nothing is hand-edited.
  • AOT by default. Shipped games are NativeAOT. No runtime reflection, no Reflection.Emit, no loading managed code: a source generator writes the registry that gives scripts, serialization and the editor's inspectors their view of the engine's classes.
  • Luau for games and mods. The engine core is C#. Game developers and modders both write Luau and data, so scripts can be sandboxed, limited per owner and hot-reloaded.
  • Everything redistributable. The repository ships only libraries whose headers and binaries we may redistribute, so a clone builds and runs with nothing to download.
  • You own your stack. Apache-2.0, no royalties, no logo screen. If the project goes somewhere you do not want to follow, fork it.

docs.title: What Apogee is not
docs.text:
• It is not a general-purpose engine for every kind of game, and it is not a drop-in replacement for Unity, Unreal or Godot. Pull requests that drift from the purpose above are declined, because adding everything is how engines end up doing nothing well.
  • It targets desktop platforms: Windows, Linux and macOS. No consoles, no mobile, no web.
  • Games and mods are written in Luau, not C#. There is no visual scripting.
  • It has no feature toggles: everything is always compiled. Options are build modes and dev tools only.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Pre-alpha. The libraries below are all there and tested, but APIs will change and some corners are thin. The maintainers develop on Linux with Vulkan. Windows is built and tested by CI; Metal (macOS) is written, its shaders pass Apple's compiler, but it has never run on a GPU. Direct3D 12 is not planned. The editor is very bare-bones for now: it cannot import 3D models or other assets (it only places and re-imports files already in the game folder), and it has no materials, no animations and no game export. Help wanted lists what we need.

docs.title: License
docs.text: Apogee's own code, tools and documentation are under the Apache License, Version 2.0: you may use, modify and distribute them, in open or closed source, for free games and commercial ones, with no royalties. The license text is LICENSE in the repository, and NOTICE is the notice to keep with it when you redistribute the engine. Contributions are accepted under the same license (see Contributing).

docs.title: Third-party libraries
docs.text:
The engine links, loads or vendors third-party libraries, each under its own license (MIT, BSD, Zlib, Apache-2.0, the FreeType License, LGPL for OpenAL Soft). ThirdParty/README.md says where each came from, at what version and how its binaries were built. Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md lists what a game that ships a library has to include with it (most ask for their copyright notice in the credits or documentation).

Two things worth knowing:

  • OpenAL Soft is LGPL, so it is its own shared library beside the program, loaded at run time and replaceable, never linked statically.
  • Steamworks is Valve's. Only its redistributable_bin libraries are in the repository, as the SDK Access Agreement allows. The C# bindings generated from its headers carry Valve's terms, not the Apache License, and using Steamworks needs a partner account and an agreement with Valve.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Two references, both generated from the code so they cannot drift from it:

  • C# API: every public type of the engine's libraries, from the XML documentation comments (DocFX).
  • Luau API: what scripts and mods can use: classes, libraries, enums and the globals a game sets, from the same registry that gives luau-lsp its type definitions.

The raw native bindings (Apogee.Native.*) are not listed: they mirror the C headers of their libraries, which document them.

docs.title: Class AudioSystem
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Audio Assembly: Apogee.Audio.dll

The game's audio, on OpenAL Soft: sounds (WAV, FLAC, MP3, Ogg Vorbis) played in 3D around the entity that has an , on buses, with reverb zones and occlusion. OpenAL Soft is a separate shared library that ships beside the program (see Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md): without it is false, every call does nothing and returns something inert, and the game runs in silence.

public sealed class AudioSystem : EngineObject, IDisposable

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: Call once a frame, after the world has progressed (it reads the entities' world transforms). Files are read through , so sounds live in res://, mods and packs. One audio system per process: OpenAL's current context is process-wide. The OpenAL listener stays at the origin; every voice is placed relative to the nearest , in double precision, so sound stays exact far from the world's origin. To use another audio middleware, replace this library (the engine has no backend layer).

docs.title: Class VfsWatcher
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.FileSystem Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Notices when files of a change, for hot reload. It watches every folder that backs a mount (zips and packs do not change under a running game) and gives the changes as virtual paths: the one the file has through the mount it was found in, and every other path that is a view of it (a package at res://packages/core is also mod://core). Saving a file usually makes several events (a temporary file, a rename, a write): a path is reported once, after it has been quiet for debounce. Files and folders whose name starts with a dot, and editors' temporary files, are ignored. Create it after the mounts; call from the thread that owns what is reloaded.

public sealed class VfsWatcher : IDisposable

docs.title: Class VirtualFileSystem

Namespace: Apogee.Content.FileSystem Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

The engine's view of its files: res:// (the game's content, from folders and packs), user:// (what the player's machine keeps: saves, settings, mods) and mod://<id>/ (a mod's own files), each made of mounted s. A path is looked up in every source mounted at a prefix of it, the one mounted last first, so that a patch pack or a mod's folder overrides what is under it; a source can also a file. Listings are the union of the sources, sorted ordinally. Only a writable source takes writes, and a path that is not valid (see ) is refused, so a script cannot name anything outside its mounts. Paths are case-sensitive, even on a file system that is not: write them as they are on disk.

docs.title: Class AssetImporter
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.Import Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Turns the assets of a game into the engine's own formats. It is a small registry: each takes some extensions (models, images, shaders…) and writes an artifact for each asset, in res://imported/ beside an index.xml that says which source each came from ( reads it). Artifacts are kept: an asset is imported again only when its key changes, the SHA-256 of the importer's name and fingerprint, the asset's .import.xml settings, the asset, and every file the import read for it (a model's buffers and textures, the modules a shader imports). Artifacts whose source is gone are deleted. Importers run in the order of the list, and a file that an earlier import read (a model's image) is not imported on its own. res:// has to be writable.

public sealed class AssetImporter

docs.title: Class BasisEncoder
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.Import Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Encodes an RGBA8 texture and its mip chain as UASTC in a KTX 2 file, with libktx's Basis Universal encoder: the blocks go through RDO (rate-distortion optimization, which makes them compress better) and the levels are supercompressed with zstd. A color or data texture and a normal map get different settings: normal maps skip RDO and take a slower, more accurate encoder level, because errors in a normal are visible as lighting noise. Normal maps stay RGB (libktx's own "normal map" mode would keep two channels as RRRG, which the shaders do not read). The encoder is slow, which is what the import cache is for; it is deterministic.

public static class BasisEncoder

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
AssetImporter

Turns the assets of a game into the engine's own formats. It is a small registry: each takes some extensions (models, images, shaders…) and writes an artifact for each asset, in res://imported/ beside an index.xml that says which source each came from ( reads it). Artifacts are kept: an asset is imported again only when its key changes, the SHA-256 of the importer's name and fingerprint, the asset's .import.xml settings, the asset, and every file the import read for it (a model's buffers and textures, the modules a shader imports). Artifacts whose source is gone are deleted. Importers run in the order of the list, and a file that an earlier import read (a model's image) is not imported on its own. res:// has to be writable.

BasisEncoder

Encodes an RGBA8 texture and its mip chain as UASTC in a KTX 2 file, with libktx's Basis Universal encoder: the blocks go through RDO (rate-distortion optimization, which makes them compress better) and the levels are supercompressed with zstd. A color or data texture and a normal map get different settings: normal maps skip RDO and take a slower, more accurate encoder level, because errors in a normal are visible as lighting noise. Normal maps stay RGB (libktx's own "normal map" mode would keep two channels as RRRG, which the shaders do not read). The encoder is slow, which is what the import cache is for; it is deterministic.

ContentLoader

Loads models and textures the way a game wants them: the imported artifact when there is one (), the source file otherwise. A game that was never imported loads from its sources, so the same call works everywhere. A package's files have artifacts when the package shipped them (it was imported as a folder of its own, its imported/ is at mod://id/imported). It does not check that the artifact is current: importing is the step that does.

ImageImporter

PNG and JPEG images into KTX 2 files with their mip chains, GPU-compressed () unless the settings say otherwise.

ImportContext

An asset being imported: its bytes, its settings, and the files it reads, which become the artifact's dependencies.

Ktx2Writer

With zstdLevel each level is compressed with zstd (supercompressionScheme 2, which libktx inflates when it loads): the file is smaller, the texture the same. This is not GPU texture compression: the texture is RGBA8 in memory and on the GPU. That is ; this writer is for compression="none" and for textures too small to compress.

ModelFile

The engine's own model file (.amodel): a as it is after import, ready to load without a glTF parser, its files, or any decoding of images. Vertex and index buffers are compressed with meshoptimizer's codecs (lossless: the model comes back bit for bit), textures are embedded KTX 2 files (), the rest is plain little-endian fields. Loading is far faster than reading the glTF, and the file is smaller than the sources it replaces.

Namespace: Apogee.Content.Packages Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

The packages of a game: the base game's and the mods. finds them (), reads their manifests, decides which load and in which order (), and mounts each one that loads at mod://<id>/, whatever it is (a folder, a zip), so that a package's files have one address everywhere. What is wrong with a package that does not load is in its ; what is wrong with the search itself (a manifest that does not parse, an id that is not its folder's name) is in . Dispose it to take the mounts away.

docs.title: Class PackageSolver
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.Packages Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Decides which packages load and in what order. There is one version of each id: the first candidate with an id wins and later ones are ignored with a problem. A package is disabled, with a reason, when it needs a newer API or another game version, the player switched it off, a dependency is missing, disabled, or out of its version range, it is in a dependency cycle, or it is a base package that needs a mod; disabling cascades to what depends on it. What loads is ordered so that dependencies come first, base packages before mods and otherwise by id, so that the order is the same on every machine.

public static class PackageSolver

docs.title: Merge(XmlNode, XmlNode)
docs.text:
patch merged into original (neither changes): an attribute of the patch replaces the original's (and adds it when it has none), its text replaces the text, and its children are matched with the original's children by name and id or, without an id, by name and place (the second <Unit/> of a patch is the second of the original). A matched child is merged the same way, one with remove="true" removes its match, and one that matches nothing is added at the end. A child with append="true" is never matched: it is always added at the end (how to add a third <Tag> to a definition that has two). The patch, remove and append attributes are not kept.

Namespace: Apogee.Content.Xml Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

XSD, the parts content definitions need: checking XML against a schema and turning it into data (). A set is every .xsd file loaded into it (and the ones they include), so that a package can bring the schema of the definitions it adds, and the children it adds to an open element of another's.

Supported: element and attribute declarations (type, ref for elements, default, fixed, use, minOccurs, maxOccurs), complexType with sequence, choice and all (the order of children is not checked; a choice's members each repeat as they say, so a choice repeated stands for any order), group and attributeGroup, complexContent and simpleContent extensions, any and anyAttribute, simpleType restrictions (enumeration, minInclusive, maxInclusive, minExclusive, maxExclusive, pattern, minLength, maxLength, length) and lists, the built-in types, annotation, and include/import of a file by its location (no namespaces: names are plain). Anything else is a that names it, so a schema never means less than it says.

docs.title: Decode(XmlNode, string?, string?)
docs.text:
Checks node against the schemas and turns it into data. An element with a complex type is a record: its attributes (numbers, booleans and text by their types, a list type as a list), the defaults of the attributes it leaves out, and its child elements by name; a child that may repeat is a list; an element that holds nothing but one repeatable element (<units><unit/><unit/></units>) is that list; an element with a simple type is its value. Two conventions are read from an element's xs:appinfo: map (a container of <entry key="…"> items is a record by the keys; an item that has nothing but a key and a value gives the value) and defaults (the element left out is decoded as an empty one, so that the defaults of its attributes apply; a list left out is empty). An open element (xs:any) gives each child the global element <its name>.<child name> when the schemas have one, and keeps the others as they are.

public DecodeResult Decode(XmlNode node, string? origin = null, string? asElement = null)

ContentOptions

GltfLoader

Reads glTF 2.0 (.gltf with its files, or .glb) into a : the default scene's meshes placed in the world, metallic-roughness materials with their textures decoded, and punctual lights. Supported extensions: KHR_texture_transform, KHR_texture_basisu, KHR_materials_emissive_strength, KHR_materials_unlit, KHR_lights_punctual. Draco and meshopt compression are refused with a clear error.

ImageDecoder

Decodes PNG, JPEG, BMP, TGA and the other formats stb_image reads into RGBA8 textures with a full mip chain.

Ktx2Loader

Loads KTX 2 files. Basis Universal data (ETC1S and UASTC) is transcoded to the best format the GPU samples: BC7, ASTC 4x4, or RGBA8.

LightData

A KHR_lights_punctual light in world space. Intensity is in lux (directional) or candela (point and spot), as glTF defines it.

MaterialData

glTF's metallic-roughness material.

MeshData

One glTF primitive: triangles with one material.

MeshProcessing

Mesh clean-up and the vertex attributes glTF lets a file leave out.

ModelData

A glTF file, flattened: the meshes the default scene uses, where they are, their materials and textures, and its lights.

ModelMerge

Combines models into one scene: the way a sample or a level puts several glTF files and generated shapes together.

Png

A minimal PNG writer for 8-bit RGBA images: screenshots and test files. Reading goes through stb_image.

ProceduralMeshes

Simple shapes built in code: for sample scenes, tools and tests. Every mesh has normals, UVs and tangents, and counter-clockwise front faces.

TextureData

A decoded texture ready to upload: the GPU format, the size, and the bytes of every mip level (largest first, each tightly packed).

docs.title: Class DebugDraw
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Graphics Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

Immediate-mode debug drawing: lines and triangles in world positions that live for one frame. Anything may add to it (gameplay, physics, tools) with no knowledge of rendering; the renderer draws what is in it when a frame is rendered and the owner then s it for the next. Positions are double precision, like the world's, and are turned into offsets from the camera only when drawn. The number of lines and triangles is capped (); what does not fit is counted in and left out, so a loop that draws too much costs a frame's detail and not the program's memory.

public sealed class DebugDraw

docs.title: Struct Double3
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Numerics Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

A position in the double-precision world: three doubles (24 bytes). Float has 24 bits of precision, so at 5 km from the origin a float position moves in 0.5 mm steps; a double keeps sub-micrometre steps for thousands of kilometres. Only positions are double. Directions, rotations, scales and everything the GPU sees stay float: positions are turned into float offsets from a nearby origin (the camera) with before they are used. Plain scalar code on purpose: positions are added and subtracted, not crunched in bulk.

docs.title: Struct Frustum
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Numerics Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

The view volume of a perspective camera with an infinite far plane, as five planes (left, right, bottom, top, near) in the camera-relative space the renderer works in. A plane is (nx, ny, nz, d) and a point is inside when n·p + d >= 0 for all five. The four side planes pass through the camera, which is the origin, so their d is zero; moves the origin for a scene whose coordinates are relative to something else. The normals are not unit length (the side ones are forward * tan + right); the culling kernel takes that into account.

docs.title: Struct Trs
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Numerics Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

A placement in the double-precision world: a position, a rotation and a scale (not a matrix, so a position far from the origin keeps its precision). A point is scaled, then rotated, then moved. Non-uniform scale is allowed, but there is no shear: the scale of a child under a rotated, non-uniformly scaled parent is the product of the two scales, which is exact only when the parent's scale is uniform or its rotation lines up with the child's axes (the usual rule of game engines).

docs.title: Class ImGuiLibrary
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.DevTools Assembly: Apogee.DevTools.dll

Dear ImGui for Luau scripts, as the global table imgui: snake_case functions over the same calls the dev tools use. A widget returns changed, value; a window or tree that can be open returns whether it is; every begin has its end (ImGui recovers from a script that forgets, at the end of the frame). With no frame open every call does nothing and returns what it was given, so tool code can stay in a shipped game. Ids are the labels, with ImGui's ## and ### conventions.

[ScriptLibrary("imgui")]
public static class ImGuiLibrary

docs.title: Class WorldSnapshot
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Ecs Assembly: Apogee.Ecs.dll

The user entities of a world as they were (Snapshot), or a part of them (SnapshotTree): ids, names, parents and component bytes. Restoring it brings the entities back under the same ids, so a selection, an undo history or a reference between entities stays valid. A snapshot names its components by their description, not by their id in the world it was taken from, so it can be restored into another world (a new session after a play run): the entities come back under the same ids there too.

public sealed class WorldSnapshot

Namespace: Apogee.Graphics.Metal Assembly: Apogee.Graphics.dll

A Metal command buffer being recorded. Metal has encoders where Vulkan has one command buffer: this opens the one the next command needs (render, compute or blit) and ends the one that is open. docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
BindlessHeap

The one set of resources every pipeline sees: arrays of sampled images, samplers and storage images that shaders index with integers, plus the push constants. Slot 0 of the images and samplers is a white texel and a linear repeat sampler, so an unset index still reads something sane.

CommandRecorder

A command buffer being recorded, with the operations the engine needs on it. Everything here is on the one queue family the device uses.

Frame

One frame in flight: its command buffer, the window's image, per-frame upload memory, and deferred destruction.

FrameLoop

Keeps frames in flight (two by default): each has its own command buffer, upload arena and timer queries, and waits only for the frame that used its slot two frames ago. Without a swapchain it runs headless: the same frames with no window image, for screenshots, tests and servers. Made by .

GpuBuffer

A buffer in GPU memory. Every buffer has a device address, so shaders reach it through a pointer in push constants.

GpuImage

An image with a view of the whole of it (the aspect a shader samples).

GpuInfo

A GPU a backend found, and whether the engine can use it.

GpuSampler

GraphicsDevice

The logical device of one graphics API and everything created with it. The renderer talks to this class and the abstract classes it hands out (buffers, images, pipelines, a command recorder, a swapchain and frame loop); Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan has the Vulkan implementation, and a Metal one follows. The engine's baseline is the same on every API: dynamic rendering, explicit barriers, buffer device addresses and bindless textures; a GPU without them is rejected with the reason.

GraphicsDeviceOptions

GraphicsException

A graphics call failed or the machine cannot do what the engine needs (no usable GPU, a missing feature); the message says which. Each backend has its own subclass.

GraphicsPipelineDescription

Everything that makes a graphics pipeline (front faces are counter-clockwise by default, as in glTF). Geometry is pulled from buffers by the vertex shader (no vertex input state), depth is reverse-Z (the near plane is 1, so is greater-or-equal), and the pipelines render with dynamic rendering into attachments of these formats.

ImageView

A view of (part of) an image, as the API of a backend sees it. Opaque: the backend that made it knows what is in it.

ImmediateContext

Records a command buffer, submits it and waits for it: for loading and tools, where stalling is fine. A frame never uses this. Safe to call from several threads (the calls are serialized).

Pipeline

A compiled pipeline; bind it with .

ResourceStates

Which states write a resource.

Swapchain

The images of a window, which the frame loop acquires, renders to and presents. Made by .

DepthTarget

The depth attachment. The engine uses reverse-Z, so the usual clear value is 0 (the far plane).

FrameAllocation

Space in a frame's upload arena: an address for shaders and memory for the CPU to fill.

FrameScope

A debug label with a GPU timer; dispose it to end the section.

GpuTiming

How long a named part of a frame took on the GPU.

ImageBarrier

One image transition: from the state it was last used in to the state the next use needs.

ImageDescription

What an image is: format, size, mip chain, layers and what it will be used for.

ImageRegion

Where in a staging buffer the bytes of one image subresource are.

SamplerDescription

ShaderCode

One shader stage: the compiled code for the device's (SPIR-V for Vulkan, Metal shading language source for Metal) and the entry point in it to run. A compute shader also says its size.

ThreadGroupSize

The size of a compute shader's thread group, [numthreads(x, y, z)]. Vulkan pipelines have it inside; a Metal dispatch has to be told.

docs.title: Class InputActionRouter
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Input Assembly: Apogee.Input.dll

Turns the player's input into the actions of an that fire in the active contexts, and says how far analog actions are pushed. Of the bindings on an input whose modifiers are all held, the one with the most modifiers wins, so Shift+Tab isn't also Tab, and a key still fires while running with Shift. A key with a hold binding fires its press on a quick release instead; a key with a double tap waits a moment for the second tap before firing its press. feeds it from SDL; , , and feed it by hand, with explicit times (seconds, any origin), for tests and replays. Call once a frame to raise , and after the frame's logic ran.

InputAction

One action the player can bind: where it works (its contexts) and what it is bound to (its defaults until the player rebinds it).

InputActionMap

Every action the player can bind, where each works (its contexts) and what it is bound to. Contexts are names the game chooses (world, on_foot, vehicle, menu); situations say which are active together, so two actions that can never be active at once may share an input. A turns the player's input into these actions.

InputActionRouter

Turns the player's input into the actions of an that fire in the active contexts, and says how far analog actions are pushed. Of the bindings on an input whose modifiers are all held, the one with the most modifiers wins, so Shift+Tab isn't also Tab, and a key still fires while running with Shift. A key with a hold binding fires its press on a quick release instead; a key with a double tap waits a moment for the second tap before firing its press. feeds it from SDL; , , and feed it by hand, with explicit times (seconds, any origin), for tests and replays. Call once a frame to raise , and after the frame's logic ran.

What an action is bound to, in the text form players edit: [Hold |Double ][Ctrl+][Shift+][Alt+]input. Keys go by their position on a US QWERTY keyboard (W, Tab, F1, BracketLeft…: ), so AZERTY players get ZQSD for WASD; mouse inputs are Mouse Left, Mouse Right, Mouse Middle, Mouse Wheel Up, Mouse Wheel Down, Mouse Back, Mouse Forward and the motion Mouse X- … Mouse Y+; gamepad inputs are Joy A … Joy Right (Xbox names), the sticks Joy LX- … Joy RY+ (Y+ is down) and the triggers Joy LT, Joy RT. Attaches the body of attachment so that its point point (turned by pointRotation), in the attachment's own space, meets the hitch. False if the hitch holds something already. A mounted attachment must be a dynamic or kinematic body without a vehicle; a trailer may be a vehicle.

docs.title: Detach()
docs.text:
Lets the attachment go. A mounted one gets a body of its own again where it is (it keeps moving as the point of the vehicle it was at, and its mass leaves the vehicle); a trailer's joint goes. A mounted entity is put back under the hitch's parent... in the world, in its place: it is a root again.

public void Detach()

How a hitch holds what it carries.

public enum HitchKind

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Mount = 0

A rigid mount (a loader, a crane, a blade): the attachment becomes part of the truck (its shape and mass), carried rigidly where the hitch entity is. Lifting is moving the hitch entity.

Trailer = 1

A drawbar or fifth wheel: the trailer stays a body of its own, held to the truck by a joint that lets it swing within angle limits.

docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Physics Assembly: Apogee.Physics.dll

How a body moves.

public enum MotionKind

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Dynamic = 2

The simulation moves it, and its entity's transform follows.

Kinematic = 1

The game moves it: it follows its entity's transform and pushes dynamic bodies (doors, lifts, animated machines).

Static = 0

It never moves (ground, walls); teleporting it is allowed but slow, and it does not push anything.

docs.title: Class PhysicsLayers
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Physics Assembly: Apogee.Physics.dll

Which bodies collide with which. A body has , the collision layers it belongs to (a bit each), and , the layers it collides with; two bodies collide when each is in a layer the other's mask holds. There are 14 layers for the game (bits 0 to 13). The native layer keeps two more bits of its own to sort bodies into the broad phase (static, sensor, moving); static bodies never collide with each other. See Native/jolt/apogee_jolt.h.

A vehicle on a dynamic body: wheels with suspension and tires, or tracks, an engine and a clutch (Jolt's VehicleConstraint). The game owns the gearbox: it sets (the signed overall ratio it wants, 0 for neutral) and in the signal, which runs before each physics step, together with the driver's inputs, and the vehicle gives them to Jolt. Make one with .

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: A road or tracked vehicle on Jolt's wheeled and tracked VehicleConstraint, tuned for heavy vehicles. Differences from Jolt's own: its transmission stays in manual mode with one forward and one reverse gear whose ratio is rewritten each step; wheels at one axle share a differential whose ratio goes with the wheel size; the wheels of a vehicle with no powered wheel (a trailer) stay in neutral; and the steered wheels turn about one center (Ackermann).

docs.text:
BodyDesc

What a body is made of and how it behaves: the shape, how it moves, its mass, surface and layers. Fill one in and give it to ; the same description can make any number of bodies. Where the body is comes from its entity's transform (its scale is applied to the shape).

CharacterController

A walking character: a capsule that slides along walls, climbs stairs and slopes, sticks to the ground going down and stands on moving platforms, without being a rigid body (Jolt's CharacterVirtual). Make one with ; it moves in every fixed step toward , and its entity's transform (the feet) follows, blended between steps like a dynamic body's. Dynamic bodies are pushed by it and do not push it.

Hitch

A hitch on a vehicle: a point on its body where an attachment or a trailer is attached. The hitch is an entity under the vehicle's, whose transform is the hitch's frame in the vehicle's space; takes the attachment's entity and the attach point in the attachment's space, which meets the hitch's frame. Make one with . A hitch holds one body at a time; the pair do not collide while hitched.

PhysicsDebugOptions

What puts in a .

PhysicsException

The physics library could not do what was asked (it did not load, or Jolt refused a shape).

PhysicsLayers

Which bodies collide with which. A body has , the collision layers it belongs to (a bit each), and , the layers it collides with; two bodies collide when each is in a layer the other's mask holds. There are 14 layers for the game (bits 0 to 13). The native layer keeps two more bits of its own to sort bodies into the broad phase (static, sensor, moving); static bodies never collide with each other. See Native/jolt/apogee_jolt.h.

PhysicsOptions

How a is made. The defaults suit heavy vehicles on a large map.

PhysicsShape

A collision shape: an immutable thing a body (or another shape) is made of, in the body's local space. Made with the static functions, given to , and shared freely: many bodies can use one. Jolt counts references, so a shape that a script lets go of lives on in the bodies that use it.

PhysicsWorld

The physics simulation of one ECS : Jolt Physics with double-precision positions, stepped at a fixed rate. Entities get a with ; a dynamic body's entity follows the simulation (its is written, local to its parent, so the world's transform system then fills in the ), and a kinematic body follows its entity.

Vehicle

A vehicle on a dynamic body: wheels with suspension and tires, or tracks, an engine and a clutch (Jolt's VehicleConstraint). The game owns the gearbox: it sets (the signed overall ratio it wants, 0 for neutral) and in the signal, which runs before each physics step, together with the driver's inputs, and the vehicle gives them to Jolt. Make one with .

VehicleDesc

A vehicle: its engine, drivetrain and wheels. Give it to with the entity of a dynamic body.

WheelDesc

One wheel of a vehicle. The vehicle's space has +Z forward, +Y up and +X to its left (glTF's). Its is where the wheel's center sits with its suspension fully extended: the suspension reaches above that, and the wheel rests somewhere in that travel under the load.

docs.title: Class Camera
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Rendering Assembly: Apogee.Rendering.dll

A perspective camera in a right-handed world (+Y up, looking down -Z at yaw 0). The projection is reverse-Z with an infinite far plane: the near plane maps to depth 1 and infinity to 0, which spreads float precision evenly over the whole depth range. Normalized device y points down, as in Vulkan, so no viewport flip is needed; the image, and so the winding of triangles (counter-clockwise for front faces, as in glTF), is unchanged. The position is a (the world is double precision) and the renderer works relative to it: has the camera at the origin, and everything else is turned into an offset from the camera before it reaches the GPU.

public sealed class Camera

docs.text:
GraphPlan

The graph, compiled: which passes run, in what order, what is allocated, and the barriers in front of each pass.

PassBuilder

What a pass declares while the graph is built: how it uses each image and buffer. The graph derives culling, lifetimes and barriers from this.

PassPlan

What the planner decided about one pass.

RenderGraph

One frame's rendering as a graph. Passes declare how they use images and buffers; culls the passes nothing depends on, shares memory between transients whose lifetimes do not overlap, and works out the barriers; runs the rest in the order they were added, each in a labelled, timed section. Build a new graph every frame: it is cheap, and the transients come from a that lives across frames.

docs.title: Class ReloadablePipelines<T>
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Rendering.Shaders Assembly: Apogee.Rendering.dll

The pipelines a renderer builds from some shader modules, rebuilt when one of them changes (or a module it imports) without stalling the frame. A change starts a build on another thread: the shaders are compiled through the and the pipelines made, while the renderer carries on with . The renderer calls at the start of a frame; if a build has finished, the new pipelines become current there, and the old ones are destroyed through once the GPU is done with the frames that used them. A build that fails (a shader that does not compile) leaves as it was, is logged, and shows in until a later build works. Changes that arrive during a build start another one right after it.

public sealed class ReloadablePipelines<T> : IDisposable where T : class

docs.title: Class ShaderLibrary
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Rendering.Shaders Assembly: Apogee.Rendering.dll

Where renderers get their shaders. takes the compiled artifact of a shader module when its project was imported (), which is how a shipped game and a mod that ships its shaders work: the Slang compiler is never loaded. A module without an artifact is compiled, as in development, if the compiler is there, and the error says what to do when it is not. The engine's own shaders are mounted as shaders:// (); a mod's are at mod://id/…, with their artifacts in mod://id/imported. The library remembers which files each module it loaded was made from, so that when files change (, from HotReloader.ShadersChanged or a ) it can say which modules are out of date (): rebuilds on that. It is thread safe.

docs.text:
PipelineScope

The pipelines one build made. Disposing destroys them all; they go through when a rebuild replaces them.

ReloadablePipelines<T>

The pipelines a renderer builds from some shader modules, rebuilt when one of them changes (or a module it imports) without stalling the frame. A change starts a build on another thread: the shaders are compiled through the and the pipelines made, while the renderer carries on with . The renderer calls at the start of a frame; if a build has finished, the new pipelines become current there, and the old ones are destroyed through once the GPU is done with the frames that used them. A build that fails (a shader that does not compile) leaves as it was, is logged, and shows in until a later build works. Changes that arrive during a build start another one right after it.

ShaderImporter

Slang modules into s (.ashader): each module with entry points is compiled to SPIR-V (Vulkan) and to Metal shading language (Metal), with its reflection, once without defines and once for each <Variant> its .import.xml lists. The files the compiler read (import, #include) are the artifact's dependencies, so editing a library re-imports every shader that uses it, and the library is not imported on its own. A module with no [shader(…)] entry point is not an asset: it only serves the others.

ShaderLibrary

Where renderers get their shaders. takes the compiled artifact of a shader module when its project was imported (), which is how a shipped game and a mod that ships its shaders work: the Slang compiler is never loaded. A module without an artifact is compiled, as in development, if the compiler is there, and the error says what to do when it is not. The engine's own shaders are mounted as shaders:// (); a mod's are at mod://id/…, with their artifacts in mod://id/imported. The library remembers which files each module it loaded was made from, so that when files change (, from HotReloader.ShadersChanged or a ) it can say which modules are out of date (): rebuilds on that. It is thread safe.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Camera

A perspective camera in a right-handed world (+Y up, looking down -Z at yaw 0). The projection is reverse-Z with an infinite far plane: the near plane maps to depth 1 and infinity to 0, which spreads float precision evenly over the whole depth range. Normalized device y points down, as in Vulkan, so no viewport flip is needed; the image, and so the winding of triangles (counter-clockwise for front faces, as in glTF), is unchanged. The position is a (the world is double precision) and the renderer works relative to it: has the camera at the origin, and everything else is turned into an offset from the camera before it reaches the GPU.

ClusterGrid

The grid lights are culled against: 16 x 9 cells over the screen and 24 slices in depth, spaced exponentially from the camera's near plane to so that near slices are thin. This is the CPU twin of the shaders (cluster_build and common.slang), for tests and tools.

DebugDrawLibrary

Debug drawing for Luau scripts, as the global table debug_draw: lines and shapes that last one frame, drawn over the world. Call them every frame (from a system, or from the devtools.on_gui function) for as long as they should show. Colors are vectors of red, green and blue from 0 to 1; without one a line is white. Positions are the world's. With nowhere to draw (no renderer) the calls do nothing.

GpuModel

A on the GPU: its vertices, indices, materials and textures in buffers and in the bindless heap. It is placed in the world any number of times (by a , or by entities with a ); each placement costs one instance record per mesh instance, never another copy of the data.

ModelLibrary

The models that entities draw ( is an id from here; scripts see this as models). A model is loaded once per path whatever the number of entities that show it, and reloaded in place when its file changes, so entities keep their id. Ids are never reused.

OverlayChain

Several overlays as one, drawn in order over the finished image: the game's UI first, the dev tools on top of it.

RenderScene

One placed in the world, with the lights and sky it is lit with. The lights can be changed every frame. The model's own coordinates (instance transforms, light positions, bounds) are relative to the scene's , a position in the double-precision world; every frame the renderer turns them into offsets from the camera, so a scene can be anywhere in the world. For many models, or for models placed by entities, see .

RenderSettings

RenderStats

RenderWorld

An ECS as something to draw: every entity with a and a shows its model there, every lights it, and the entity with is the eye (). Nothing is copied: the world is read when a frame is rendered, so what the systems moved this frame is what is drawn.

SceneRenderer

The Forward+ renderer. Every frame it builds a render graph: a depth prepass, a light-culling compute pass over the 16 x 9 x 24 cluster grid, the PBR forward pass (opaque and alpha-masked, then blended draws far to near), and a tone-mapping pass into the target.

docs.text:
Runs a loaded module again from its file and updates it where it is: the module's table that every script that required it holds gets the new fields (and loses the ones the new code does not have), so they see the new functions without being reloaded themselves. What the module registered when it first loaded (functions that draw, signal connections, systems, defs.on_change listeners) is taken back and registered again by the new run. If the new code fails (a syntax error, a runtime error, a timeout) nothing changes: the old module and its registrations stay. A module may have a function on_reload(new, old), called before the update, to take state from the old table. A function a script copied into a local (local f = module.f) stays the old one; a module that returns something other than a table is replaced in the cache only.

docs.title: Class PackageLoader
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Scripting Assembly: Apogee.Scripting.dll

Runs the packages of a in a VM. Each package's scripts run in the order its manifest lists them, packages in load order; a package's base-game scripts run as the VM's base owner, a mod's as an owner of its own (its own memory category and limits), with:

  • @<id>/… as a require alias for each package, so that a mod can use a dependency's modules;
  • confinement: a mod may require files of its own package and of the packages it depends on (and res://), nothing else;
  • the fs library with the same rules: a mod reads res://, its own package, its dependencies', and user://moddata/<id>/, and writes only user://moddata/<id>/;
  • modules that run as the owner of the package they are in, whoever required them.

A script that fails stops its package (the error is logged and in the result), and what depends on it is not run; it never stops the game. Content the package brought stays loaded.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
DefinitionOptions

What a host adds to or takes out of the definitions.

DefinitionWriter

Writes the engine's API as Luau type definitions (apogee.d.luau) for luau-lsp, from the registry: the classes, enums and script libraries the generator described, and the hand-written natives with the declarations they were registered with. The output depends only on the registry, in a fixed order.

HostGlobal

A global that the host sets in its VMs (), which the definitions declare for the scripts that run there.

HotReloader

Reloads what changed on disk while the game runs (a development run, the editor). , called from the thread that owns the VM, takes the changes a has noticed and sorts them: a .luau file that a script has required is a module reload (: updated in place, the old one stays if the new one fails); a definition or schema in a package's content or schema folders makes the definitions be read again ( is replaced and defs.on_change listeners are called); an image or model is imported again (when the project has been imported: imported/index.xml) and says which; a .slang file raises , for the renderer to rebuild what uses it (the engine's renderers do not yet). A change that cannot be applied to a running game (a package's mod.xml, a script that only runs once) is listed in .

LuauTestRunner

Runs the *.test.luau files under a folder, each in a VM of its own (so one file's globals, modules and worlds cannot touch another's). A file's describe bodies run as it loads; its cases then run in order, one frame at a time, with @engine/test.

LuauVm

One Luau VM for the game and its mods. Every script runs in a thread of its own with its own globals over the read-only ones (luaL_sandbox), and belongs to a : the owner's memory category counts what it allocates, and its time budget limits each call. Not thread safe: use it from the thread that made it.

LuauVmOptions

ModuleReload

What did.

PackageLoader

Runs the packages of a in a VM. Each package's scripts run in the order its manifest lists them, packages in load order; a package's base-game scripts run as the VM's base owner, a mod's as an owner of its own (its own memory category and limits), with:

  • @<id>/… as a require alias for each package, so that a mod can use a dependency's modules;
  • confinement: a mod may require files of its own package and of the packages it depends on (and res://), nothing else;
  • the fs library with the same rules: a mod reads res://, its own package, its dependencies', and user://moddata/<id>/, and writes only user://moddata/<id>/;
  • modules that run as the owner of the package they are in, whoever required them.

A script that fails stops its package (the error is logged and in the result), and what depends on it is not run; it never stops the game. Content the package brought stays loaded.

PackageLoaderOptions

PackageRunResult

What happened to a package's scripts.

PhysicalScriptFileSystem

Scripts from a folder of the real file system.

ReferenceWriter

Writes the engine's Luau API as Markdown pages for the Manual (--luau-docs), from the same registry as : one page per class (classes/Name.md), one per script library (libraries/name.md), one for all enums (enums.md) and reference.md, which lists everything with the host's globals. The output depends only on the registry, in a fixed order, with \n line ends.

Draws what RmlUi hands the host onto the frame's output, as a pass of the render graph: use it as (part of) the of SceneRenderer.Render. RmlUi compiles geometry once and renders it many times; the renderer keeps the compiled vertices and indices in memory and, when a frame is built, packs the geometry that frame draws into per-frame upload buffers (as the ImGui backend does), so nothing on the GPU depends on when RmlUi releases or re-renders a piece of geometry. docs.text: Call when the window changes size, once a frame (it lays out and runs animations and delivers nothing by itself: events are delivered when input is given), and let the draw (it is the render overlay: it asks for the picture when the frame's graph is built). The table is read when RmlUi needs a value: change it and say so with (or change a top-level field with ), and the elements that show it are updated at the next frame.

An element of a document (a div, a text node, a whole document) as scripts hold it. The object is a handle: it names the element without keeping it alive, so one whose element has been destroyed (its document was closed, an ancestor was destroyed) is false and every call on it does nothing or answers "none". An element made with or belongs to the object that holds it until it is put in a tree with or ; an element nobody ever put in a tree is destroyed when the script lets go of it, and one in a tree lives as long as the tree does. Elements are made, moved and changed here.

UiEvent

An event that reached a listener (). It is only good inside the handler: afterwards its calls do nothing.

UiInput

Feeds the UI from SDL: the pointer, buttons, wheel, keys and typed text of one window, as pumps them. Every event goes to the UI, which uses what lands on its elements; and tell the game whether it should leave an event alone. Call once a frame.

UiRenderer

Draws what RmlUi hands the host onto the frame's output, as a pass of the render graph: use it as (part of) the of SceneRenderer.Render. RmlUi compiles geometry once and renders it many times; the renderer keeps the compiled vertices and indices in memory and, when a frame is built, packs the geometry that frame draws into per-frame upload buffers (as the ImGui backend does), so nothing on the GPU depends on when RmlUi releases or re-renders a piece of geometry. Textures are images in the bindless heap, and the handle RmlUi holds for one is its bindless index (0 is the white texel that untextured geometry samples).

UiSystem

The game's user interface: RmlUi with one context (the screen), its documents, fonts and input, behind the script global ui. Documents are written in RML and RCSS (HTML and CSS as RmlUi knows them) with scripts of their own in Luau, or built from Luau; both go through s. RmlUi is process-wide, so there is one system at a time.

docs.title: Luau API
docs.text:
Luau is the only scripting language, for games and for mods. This reference is written by Apogee.Runtime --luau-docs from the engine's registry (the classes the source generator described, the script libraries and the hand-written natives), the same source as the type definitions for luau-lsp (--luau-defs, see Scripting).

Open the reference: the globals a game sets, every class, every library, and the enums.
