Things the sample shows on purpose: the state is separate from the documents (the scripts of a document only call into state, and the tests exercise state without any UI); a theme is a set of custom properties and the Options button restyles every document by changing a class; values that change continuously are a data model (data-style-left on the minimap dot, {{speed}}), updated once a frame with model:dirty(); and the data models are opened before the documents that use them load.

The game says game.set_escape_quits(false): in a window the runtime ends a run on Escape, which a game with a pause menu cannot have. game.quit() is what its Quit button calls. physics.paused is what the pause menu sets: no time is added to the simulation while it is true, so the world stays where it was and resumes from there.

docs.title: The mod
docs.text:
game/dev_mods/crate_panel is a mod: a mod.xml that depends on base_ui, a script, an RML fragment and its RCSS.

local hud = require("@base_ui/lib/hud")
local scene = require("@base_ui/lib/scene")

local panel = hud.add_panel("hud_right", fs.read_text("mod://crate_panel/panel.rml"), fs.read_text("mod://crate_panel/panel.rcss"))
panel:by_id("crate_boost"):listen("click", function() scene.boost() end)

It uses the game's modules (@base_ui/..., a dependency's, which a mod may require) and nothing in the base game mentions it: delete the folder and the panel is gone. It is Luau, RML and RCSS only, as every mod is. The mod listens on its own elements instead of writing onclick attributes in its fragment: an attribute a script writes runs as that script (as the mod, with the mod's limits, and without the base document's functions), so it could not call the game's functions anyway. What is not confined yet is what the UI may load: ui:load_document and ui:load_font read any mounted path, like the audio and models libraries, because the engine's classes do not know which mod called them; a document's <script src> is confined to what the document's owner may read.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Samples/UI/tests holds Luau tests of the pieces that need no UI (the formatting, the volume and the minimap arithmetic, the screen flow); run them by hand with Apogee.Runtime --luau-test Samples/UI. The things the sample uses are tested where they live: scripts and data models in documents (Tests/Apogee.UI.Tests, Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests), physics.paused (physics), game.quit (runtime).

docs.title: Viewer sample
docs.text:
Samples/Viewer (Apogee.Samples.Viewer) is the engine's first program that shows something: a procedural colonnade, six small glTF models on pedestals and 256 animated colored lights, drawn by the Forward+ renderer. It opens a window with the dev overlay, or renders offscreen (--headless) for screenshots. Everything scene-specific lives in the sample, next to its assets; the libraries it uses are Apogee.Platform, Content, Graphics, Rendering and DevTools.

dotnet run --project Samples/Viewer                 # the window
./build.sh aot && Bin/publish/viewer/Apogee.Samples.Viewer --help

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: WASD move, Q/E down and up, Shift is faster, hold the right mouse button to look, the wheel changes the speed, F1 shows or hides the dev overlay, Esc quits.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option --scene <courtyard\|file.gltf> what to show; a .gltf or .glb is lit with the light show --assets <dir> where the sample models are (default: Samples/Viewer/Assets, found by walking up from the program) --no-models leave the sample models out of the courtyard --lights <n> animated point lights, 256 by default --camera x,y,z,yaw,pitch start position in meters, angles in degrees --headless no window: render offscreen --frames <n> stop after n frames (headless default: 1) --size <w>x<h> window or image size (default 1280x720) --overlay draw the dev overlay in headless images --screenshot <file.png> headless: write the last frame --gpu <name> prefer the GPU whose name contains this (sets APOGEE_GPU) --no-vsync do not wait for vertical blank --watch window: use the shaders' source files (found in the repository above the program) and rebuild the pipelines that use a shader when you save it, with no hitch; an edit that does not compile keeps the old image and shows the error in red in the overlay

Exit codes: 0 fine, 1 bad arguments, 2 failure (no GPU, a file that does not load, a shader that does not compile), 3 the validation layer reported errors.

docs.title: Headless runs
docs.text:
Headless frames advance by a fixed 1/60 s, and the light show is a function of time only, so a given --frames always renders the same image on the same GPU:

Apogee.Samples.Viewer --gpu llvmpipe --headless --size 640x360 --frames 4 --screenshot viewer.png

The Viewer is a sample: people run it by hand, and neither CI nor any test runs it (there is no reference image to compare with). What the renderer must get right is tested, with its own fixtures, in Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests. ./build.sh aot-viewer publishes it with NativeAOT.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: The six models in Samples/Viewer/Assets are CC0 glTF-Sample-Assets files kept as Git LFS objects (see their README.md); where LFS was not pulled the courtyard still builds, without them. Larger scenes are not in the repository: Amazon's Lumberyard Bistro is CC BY 4.0 and a conversion to glTF is a local step, and Sponza and DamagedHelmet were left out because their licenses do not fit a repository that is freely redistributable.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Apogee.Audio is the game's sound: OpenAL Soft behind one AudioSystem, playing WAV, FLAC, MP3 and Ogg Vorbis files in 3D around the entity that has an AudioListener, on buses, with reverb zones and occlusion. In a game, scripts see it as the global audio.

OpenAL Soft is LGPL, so it is its own shared library beside the program (libopenal.so.1, OpenAL32.dll, libopenal.1.dylib in ThirdParty/openal-soft/lib), loaded at run time and replaceable: see Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for what a game that ships it does. Without the library audio.is_active is false: every call does nothing and returns an inert object, and the game runs in silence (the log says so once). The files are decoded by dr_wav, dr_flac, dr_mp3 and stb_vorbis in our audio_decode library (Native libraries).

local horn = audio:load_sound("res://sounds/horn.ogg")   -- a file from the game or a mod
local voice = horn:play("vehicles", 0.8, 1.0, false, truckEntity)   -- bus, volume, pitch, loop, entity
audio:get_bus("music").volume = 0.5

local music = audio:load_sound("res://music/field.ogg", true, false, true)   -- stream, is_3d, loop
music:play("music")

Another audio engine. There is no backend layer: the engine has one audio library. Middleware such as FMOD or Wwise is built around authored events, which a "play a file" API does not cover, so a shared seam would only get in the way; a game that needs one replaces Apogee.Audio.

docs.title: The system
docs.text:
new AudioSystem(world, options, files) (a session makes it for you): the device and context start with it; audio.is_active says whether they did (no library, a library that cannot start: both give an inactive system and a line in the log). Update(dt) is called once a frame after the world has progressed (ScriptSession.Progress does), because it reads world transforms.

AudioOptions: the output, the sample rate (48 kHz), and the Doppler and rolloff scales and the distance factor. - AudioOutput.Default is the platform's device, in real time. With no device at all the system mixes into nowhere and says so. - AudioOutput.None is OpenAL Soft's loopback device: nothing is played, but Update(dt) mixes the dt seconds it is given and drops the samples, so sounds start, loop and end exactly as they would be heard. Headless runs, script tests and the editor (when not playing) use it, and it needs no sound card. - AudioOutput.WavFile is the same, written to WavPath as a 32-bit float WAV when the system is disposed: what the tests record and measure.

audio.volume is the master volume (the listener's gain, which is also the volume of the master bus).

Files. Sounds are read through the game's virtual file system: res://, mod://<id>/, packs and zips, so a mod brings its sounds and a pack can hold them. Only virtual paths are read: a path with no scheme:// is an error, so a script cannot ask for a file by its place on the disk. (A mod can still read any res://, mod:// or user:// file: the audio classes do not know which mod called them, like the UI and model classes.) The format is told from the file's first bytes, not its name. A file that is missing or is not audio we read is an error with the reason. OpenAL's current context is process-wide: one audio system per process.

Loading. load_sound(path, stream, is_3d, loop) decodes the whole file into one OpenAL buffer, unless stream is true: then the file stays in memory and each voice decodes it as it plays, into four buffers of a quarter of a second (music, long ambience). Files with more than two channels are folded down to stereo.

docs.title: 3D, the listener and far from the origin
docs.text:
An entity with the AudioListener component (Index, 0 by default) is the ear: it looks along its local -Z with +Y up, as a camera does. Up to eight listeners (split screen). OpenAL's own listener stays at the origin. Each voice is placed relative to the nearest AudioListener, in that listener's frame, taken in double precision and then narrowed, so a source 10 000 km from the origin is as exact as one near it. The voice's velocity relative to that listener drives the Doppler effect (clamped to 300 m/s: a teleport must not shift the pitch to nonsense).

A voice is positional when its sound is 3D and it has an entity (the last argument of play): each frame it is placed at that entity's world transform. A sound loaded with is_3d = false is not. Sound fades with distance by OpenAL's inverse-distance rolloff, clamped: no quieter-than-full inside min_distance (1 m), no quieter than it is at max_distance (10 000 m). Set them on a sound (sound.min_distance, sound.max_distance: every voice it makes starts with them) or on one voice.

docs.title: Voices
docs.text: AudioVoice is what is playing: sound:play(bus, volume, pitch, loop, entity). volume, pitch, paused, is_playing, position (seconds), min_distance, max_distance, occlusion, muffling, stop(). Letting go: a sound that does not loop plays to its end whether you keep the voice or not; a looping sound is stopped when the voice is destroyed, which is when a script drops it, so keep the voice of whatever loops. Destroying a sound cuts every voice that is playing it.

docs.title: Buses
docs.text: audio:get_bus(name) returns the bus of that name (the same object each time): master or an empty name is the whole mix, and any other name is a bus of our own, made on first use, that sounds are played on (sound:play("vehicles")). volume, muted, set_paused(bool) and stop_all(). A voice's gain is its volume times its bus's times the master's. The old project's four buses (Music, Vehicles, Environment, UI) are the game's to make; the engine defines none.

docs.title: Reverb zones
docs.text: The ReverbZone component is a box centered on its entity (HalfExtents, scaled by the entity's scale) with a Preset, a Priority and a Level (dB added to the wet level). Where the first listener is in several, the highest priority wins, then the smallest. Only that zone applies; there is no crossfade (one EFX reverb effect carries it, and the change is heard at once). audio.current_reverb is the preset the listener hears now. The presets (generic, room, hallway, garage, barn, hangar, cave, forest, plain; off outside every zone) are our own approximations of those spaces, in ReverbPresets as OpenAL Soft's EAX reverb parameters, to be tuned by ear. Every voice sends to the one effect slot. Without the EFX extension (OpenAL Soft has it) there is no reverb and no occlusion filter.

docs.title: Occlusion
docs.text: A voice with occlusion = true and an entity, in an audio system with its physics set (audio.physics = physics; a session does), casts a ray from the nearest listener to the voice each frame and, when something blocks the way, puts a low-pass and an attenuation on its direct sound and its reverb send (OpenAL's filters), moving smoothly toward the target (8 · dt a frame). voice.muffling is how much (0 to 1). The ray ignores sensors and passes the voice's own body; it is one ray, so a source behind a thin pole is not muffled and behind a thick wall is.

docs.title: Not done
docs.text: HRTF settings (OpenAL Soft's own defaults apply), the other effects (echo, chorus…) from scripts (the C bindings have all of EFX), geometry-based occlusion, crossfading between zones, more than one reverb at a time, recording, .pck-style sound banks, and audio in the editor's own viewport (the editor plays sound in play mode only).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Audio.Tests mixes into a WAV file (AudioOutput.WavFile) and measures it, with no sound card, so they run in CI: a sound from the virtual file system is heard and ends, every format plays, only virtual paths are read, a stream plays to its end and a streamed loop goes on, a source on the left is louder in the left speaker and the sound follows when it moves, a far source is quieter and the distances of a voice change that, a bus scales what plays on it by exactly its gain (4:1 for 0.25), the master bus mutes the mix, mute and pause silence a bus, pitch and stop, destroying a sound cuts its voices, a reverb zone leaves a tail that no zone does not, zones are picked by priority then size, and a wall between the listener and the source muffles it (with the physics world's rays). Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests renders a source on the loopback device and tests the decoders. Tests/Luau/audio.test.luau runs the script surface, passing with or without the library, in the NativeAOT binary too.

docs.title: Content loading
docs.text: Apogee.Content is how the engine gets its files: the virtual file system (below), and the readers that turn model and texture files into plain CPU data that the renderer uploads (no GPU types except the PixelFormat enum). XML definitions, packs and mods build on the file system and come next.

docs.title: File system
docs.text:
A VirtualFileSystem gives the engine, and the scripts of mods, one view of where files are. Paths are scheme://a/b/c.txt:

Prefix Holds Writable res:// the game's content: its folders, and its packs and patch packs over them no user:// what the player's machine keeps for the game: saves, settings, downloaded mods yes mod://<id>/ one mod's own files no

The program decides what is mounted where, with Mount(prefix, source); a source is an IFileSource: a DirectorySource (a folder, read-only unless asked to be writable), a ZipSource (a zipped mod), and later a pack. A path is looked up in every source mounted at a prefix of it, the one mounted last first, so a mod's folder or a patch pack overrides what is under it. A source can also remove a file (a patch pack does): it is gone for everything mounted before that source. Prefixes nest (res://mods/cool over res://), and a folder that only exists because something is mounted below it (mod://) is listed.

var vfs = new VirtualFileSystem();
vfs.Mount("res://", new DirectorySource("Content"));
vfs.Mount("user://", new DirectorySource(VirtualFileSystem.DefaultUserDirectory("Acme", "Truck"), writable: true));
vfs.Mount("mod://cool", new ZipSource("mods/cool.zip"));

byte[] bytes = vfs.ReadAllBytes("res://textures/ground.png");
string text = vfs.ReadAllText("mod://cool/mod.xml");                 // UTF-8, without a byte order mark
foreach (string file in vfs.EnumerateFiles("res://defs", "*.xml", recursive: true)) { ... }   // sorted by ordinal order
vfs.WriteAllText("user://saves/slot1.xml", xml);                     // user:// only; res:// is read-only

Rules that keep a path meaning the same everywhere (and a script inside its mounts): a path has a lowercase scheme, / separators, and segments that are plain names: no . or .., no empty segment, no \ : * ? " < > | or control characters, nothing that ends in a dot or a space, and no Windows device name (nul, con.txt). A path that breaks a rule is a VfsException (an IOException) when it is read or written, and simply not there for Exists and its kin. Paths are case-sensitive, even on a file system that is not (a texture asked for as Ground.PNG would load on Windows and fail on Linux): write them as they are on disk, in lowercase by convention. Only a writable source takes a write, a missing file is a FileNotFoundException, and writes go through a temporary file so that a crash leaves the old one. Zip entries whose names break the rules are skipped (with a warning), so no entry can name a place outside the zip. A DirectorySource follows links inside its folder as the OS does: do not mount a folder that you do not trust to be free of links.

VfsPath has the helpers: Parse (strict), and lenient Normalize, Combine, DirectoryOf for resolving what a file refers to, where .. climbs but stops at the root of the scheme. TryGetPhysicalPath gives the real path of a file that a folder holds (to watch it, or for a library that only takes paths).

docs.title: What reads through it
docs.text:
• Scripts: new LuauVm(new LuauVmOptions { Files = new VfsScriptFiles(vfs) }) and vm.AddRoot("res://") (or "mod://cool"): require("./x"), .luaurc aliases and init.luau work on virtual paths, and chunk names, errors and OwnerOfModule see them (res://main.luau:12).
  • Models: ContentOptions.ReadFile = vfs.ReadAllBytes and GltfLoader.Load("res://models/car.gltf", options). The textures and the external .bin buffers a model refers to are read through it too (cgltf is given our allocator and file reader), relative to the model, so a model in a pack or a zip loads like one on disk.
  • Textures: ImageDecoder and Ktx2Loader take bytes: pass them vfs.ReadAllBytes(path).
  • Not yet: shaders. Slang compiles from real files and finds its imports itself, so the engine's shaders stay next to the program.

docs.title: glTF models
docs.text:
ModelData model = GltfLoader.Load("Models/Sponza/Sponza.gltf", new ContentOptions
{
    TextureCaps = new TextureCaps(Bc: device.SupportsBc, Astc: device.SupportsAstc),
});

GltfLoader reads .gltf (with its .bin and images) and .glb, and turns the default scene into a ModelData:

  • Meshes — one MeshData per glTF primitive that the scene uses: Vertex[] (48 bytes: position, normal, tangent+handedness, UV0 — the struct the vertex shader pulls from a buffer), uint[] indices, a material index and bounds. A mesh used by several nodes is loaded once.
  • Instances — each mesh placed in the world with its node hierarchy's world matrix (System.Numerics row-vector convention).
  • Materials — glTF's metallic-roughness model: factors and TextureRefs (texture index, UV set, KHR_texture_transform), emissive already multiplied by KHR_materials_emissive_strength, alpha mode and cutoff, double-sided, KHR_materials_unlit.
  • Textures — decoded and ready to upload (below). The same image used as a base color (sRGB) and as a normal map (linear) is two entries.
  • Lights — KHR_lights_punctual lights in world space (position, direction, color, intensity in lux or candela, range, cone angles).

What the file leaves out is filled in as glTF specifies: no normals gives flat normals; a normal-mapped material without tangents gets them computed from the UVs. By default (OptimizeMeshes) meshoptimizer merges duplicate vertices and reorders both buffers for the vertex cache and memory fetch, keeping exactly the same triangles. Triangle strips and fans become lists; points and lines are skipped with a warning. Only TEXCOORD_0 is read. Draco and EXT_meshopt_compression models are refused with an error that says so; any problem with a file is a ContentException naming the file.

docs.title: Textures
docs.text:
PNG, JPEG, BMP and TGA go through stb_image to RGBA8 with a full mip chain, built with a box filter; sRGB images are averaged in linear light, as the GPU's filtering does, and alpha never is. KTX 2 files (the glTF KHR_texture_basisu extension, or any .ktx2) are read by libktx, and Basis Universal data is transcoded at load to what the GPU has: BC7 (TextureCaps.Bc), else ASTC 4x4 (TextureCaps.Astc), else RGBA8. The file's own mip levels are kept. A TextureData carries the PixelFormat (the sRGB variant for base color and emissive, linear for the rest — decided by how the material uses it, not by the file), the size, the bytes of every mip, and the sampler state (filter, mipmaps, wrap).

Png.Encode(width, height, rgba) writes a PNG, for screenshots and test files.

docs.title: Definitions and schemas
docs.text: A game's data is XML: definitions (a crate, a machine, a crop) that mods can add to, change and remove, checked against schemas (XSD) that say what a valid one looks like. Apogee.Content reads both (Apogee.Content.Xml) and gives code and scripts typed data, with the line of every mistake.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
A definition is an element with an id. Its name is its type; type and id together identify it.

<!-- res://data/crates.xml: one definition, or a list of them under any root -->
<Crates>
  <Crate id="wooden" weight="12.5">
    <Tag>fragile</Tag>
    <Tag>stackable</Tag>
  </Crate>
  <Crate id="steel" weight="80"/>
</Crates>

A file holds one definition (its root has an id) or a list (the root's children are the definitions). DefDatabase.Load(files, folders, schemas) reads the .xml files of the folders you give it, in load order: the folders in order, in each folder its files sorted by name and then its subfolders the same way. In a game the folders come from the packages (base game first, then mods in dependency order).

What a later file may do with a definition:

Written Effect <Crate id="x" …/> again replaces it (it keeps its place in the list), with a warning that names both files <Crate id="x" patch="true" …/> patches it: see below <Crate id="x" remove="true"/> removes it

A patch or a removal of a definition that is not there is a warning, and does nothing. A patch merges into the definition (DefDatabase.Merge): its attributes replace the definition's (and add new ones), its text replaces the text, and its children are matched with the definition's children by name and id, or, with no id, by name and place (the second <Tag/> of a patch is the second <Tag> of the definition, even when the patch removed the first). A matched child is merged the same way; a child with remove="true" takes its match away; a child that matches nothing is added at the end. The patch and remove attributes are not kept.

<Crate id="wooden" patch="true" weight="14"><Tag remove="true"/><Tag append="true">reinforced</Tag></Crate>

Every Def knows Type, Id, its merged Node, its decoded Value, and Sources: the file that defined it and each file that patched it (with package, path, line), so a mod that patches a definition can find the files beside the original. Comments are not read.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
Everything wrong goes in database.Problems, each with a severity, the file and line, a path inside the definition, and a message:

mod://base/data/crates.xml:2: Crate.weight (wooden): 'heavy' is not a number
mod://base/data/crates.xml:4: Crate (steel): 'colour' is not an attribute of <Crate> (it has: id, weight).
mod://mod/data/crates.xml:1: warning: Crate: replaces Crate 'wooden' defined in mod://base/data/crates.xml (package 'base').

Errors are content that does not match its schema, a file that is not well-formed XML, a definition without an id. Warnings are things that load but are odd: a replacement, a patch of nothing, a type with no schema. A definition with errors is still in the database, with what could be made of it (a value that does not convert stays as text), so one mistake does not take a whole game down; the caller decides what to do with HasErrors. A problem in a patched definition names the file of the line it is on.

docs.title: Schemas
docs.text:
SchemaSet loads .xsd files (LoadFile, LoadFolder, LoadText), with the files they xs:include (found beside them, read once). A package brings the schema of the kinds of definitions it adds. The engine reads the part of XSD that content needs, and says so when a schema asks for more (<xs:key> is not supported, with the file and line), so a schema never means less than it says:

  • element, attribute (type, default, fixed, use; minOccurs, maxOccurs; elements may use ref), complexType with sequence, choice, all, group, attributeGroup, complexContent and simpleContent extensions, any, anyAttribute;
  • simpleType restrictions with enumeration, minInclusive, maxInclusive, minExclusive, maxExclusive, pattern (a regular expression that must match all of the text, with a time limit), minLength, maxLength, length, and list;
  • the built-in types: strings (string, token, ID, date…), boolean, decimal, float, double, and the integers with their ranges (int, long, byte, unsignedByte, positiveInteger…), and the engine's own vector3 (three numbers, "1 2.5 -3" or "1, 2.5, -3", decoded as a DefVector and a vector in Luau);
  • annotation with documentation (kept, for tools) and appinfo (the two conventions below). There are no namespaces: names are plain.

Order is not checked. Children may come in any order; each element is checked for how often it appears. The members of a choice have no minimum (any one may be the one chosen), and a repeated choice stands for "any order".

docs.title: What a definition decodes to (SchemaSet.Decode)
docs.text:
An element with a complex type is a record: its attributes, typed (numbers, booleans, text; a list type is a list), with the defaults of the attributes it leaves out, and its child elements by name. A child that may appear more than once is a list. An element that holds only one repeatable element (<Units><Unit/><Unit/></Units>) is that list. An element with a simple type is its value. simpleContent (text with attributes) is a record with the attributes and value, or just the value if it has no attributes. The example above decodes to:

{id: "wooden", weight: 12.5, Tag: ["fragile", "stackable"]}

Numbers are doubles, so whole numbers beyond 2^53 lose precision. Two conventions, written in the declaration's xs:annotation/xs:appinfo:

  • map: a container of <entry key="…"> items is a record by the keys (<Prices><entry key="wheat" value="2.5"/></Prices> is {wheat: 2.5}); an entry with nothing but key and value gives the value, any other entry is its record without the key. A key used twice is a problem.
  • defaults: an element that is left out is decoded as an empty one, so the defaults of its attributes apply, and a list that is left out is empty (without it a missing element or list is simply not there).

An open element (one with xs:any) is how a package adds a kind of child to another package's definition. Each child is checked against the global element named <open element>.<child> when the schemas have one (<components><motor power="90"/></components> is described by an element named components.motor), and kept as it is otherwise: attributes as text, children by name (a repeated name is a list), text as value. xs:anyAttribute keeps unknown attributes as text.

patch, remove, append, xmlns and xsi:… attributes are accepted on any element. An element the schemas have no declaration for decodes the same generic way, with no problems (DecodeResult.Declared is false), which is how a database without schemas reads everything.

docs.title: From Luau
docs.text:
Two global libraries (hand-written natives, declared in apogee.d.luau):

-- defs: the game's definitions, set with LuauVm.Defs (a game sets it when it has loaded its content)
local crate = defs.get("Crate", "wooden")          -- a table, or nil: crate.weight, crate.Tag[1]
for _, c in defs.all("Crate") do print(c.id) end   -- in load order
defs.types()                                       -- {"Barrel", "Crate"}
for _, s in defs.sources("Crate", "wooden") do print(s.package, s.path, s.line, s.role) end   -- "definition", "replacement", "patch"
for _, p in defs.problems() do print(p.severity, p.file, p.line, p.message) end

-- xml: plain XML text to and from tables
local node = xml.decode('<Crate id="a"><Tag>x</Tag></Crate>')   -- { name, attrs, order, children, text, line }
local text = xml.encode(node)

A definition's table is made the first time it is asked for and is read-only all the way down (assigning to it is an error), and it is the same table for every script, so scripts cannot change each other's view of the game; copy what you need to change. Setting LuauVm.Defs again (a reload) makes later calls see the new definitions, and tables that scripts already hold stay as they were. Without a database the library is there and finds nothing. xml.encode writes attributes in the order of order and then the rest sorted by name, so the text is the same every time; elements nest at most 128 deep, both ways.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: the XML reader and writer (lines, entities, a DTD refused), each schema feature with the exact problem messages, the merge rules including place counting and removal, and the database (load order, replace, patch, remove, sources, problems with file and line, kinds without a schema). Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests runs xml and defs from scripts (read-only tables, identity, sources and problems, reloads), and Tests/Luau/xml.test.luau runs them in the NativeAOT binary.

docs.title: Hot reload
docs.text:
While a game runs in development (and in the editor, which uses the same pieces), changing a file takes effect without a restart: a script you saved, a definition, an image.

Apogee.Runtime --game Samples/Mods --watch

--watch goes with --game. It makes res:// writable (so that a changed asset can be imported again into res://imported) and reloads, every frame it has something to do:

What changed What happens a .luau file that a script has required the module is run again and updated in place (below) a definition or a schema in a package's Content or Schema folder the definitions are read again, LuauVm.Defs is replaced, the defs.on_change listeners are called a .glb, .gltf, .bin, image or .import.xml imported again when the project has been imported (imported/index.xml), then HotReloader.AssetsChanged says which, for the host to load them again a .slang file imported again when the project has been imported (so its .ashader stays current), then HotReloader.ShadersChanged says which. The runtime hands them to its ShaderLibrary, and the renderers rebuild the pipelines that use them, off the render thread and swapped in at a frame boundary (Rendering); a shader that does not compile keeps the old pipelines and shows its error in the dev overlay a package's mod.xml, or an entry script (a package's <Script>, which runs once) listed as needs a restart, with a warning in the log

Files and folders that start with a dot, editors' temporary files (~, .tmp, .swp), and imported/ itself are ignored. Zips and packs are not watched (they do not change under a running game).

docs.title: Modules are updated where they are
docs.text:
LuauVm.ReloadModule runs the changed file again and then makes the table that every script got from require be the new module: it gets the new fields and loses the ones the new code does not have (and the new metatable). So every script that required the module sees the new functions, without being reloaded itself.

  • If the new code fails (syntax error, runtime error, timeout) nothing changes: the old module stays, and so does everything it registered. Fixing the file reloads it. The error and its line are in the log and in ReloadReport.Failures.
  • What a module registers while it loads is taken back and registered again by the new run: functions given to devtools.on_gui, signal connections, world:systems, defs.on_change listeners. (What a script registers later, from an event handler, is the script's to manage.) If the new run fails halfway, what it had registered is removed again and the old registrations stay.
  • A function copied into a local stays the old one: local f = module.f keeps the old function after a reload. Read module.f when you call it (or call module.f() directly).
  • State: the functions of the new module work on the new module table, while holders keep the old one, so a counter kept as a plain field (M.count) would split in two. Keep state in a table of its own and hand it over in on_reload(new, old), which the module may define and which is called before the update:
local M = { state = { count = 0 } }
function M.on_reload(new, old) new.state = old.state end   -- the new code carries on with the old state
function M.inc() M.state.count += 1 end
return M
  • A module that returns a frozen table (table.freeze) or something that is not a table is replaced in the cache only: scripts that already hold the old one keep it, new requires get the new one.
  • A module that nothing has required yet is not loaded by a change (it would run code nobody asked for).

docs.title: From code
docs.text:
using var reloader = new HotReloader(files, vm, packages);        // watches every folder behind the mounts
reloader.AssetsChanged += paths => { /* load the assets again */ };

// each frame, on the thread that owns the VM:
ReloadReport report = reloader.Poll();        // modules, DefsReloaded, assets, shaders, NeedsRestart, Failures

VfsWatcher is the part that notices changes: it reports virtual paths (a file in res://packages/core is also mod://core/…, and both are reported), waits until a path has been quiet for 150 ms (saving a file is usually several events) and gives each path once. A new folder is scanned, because the operating system starts watching it a moment after it exists.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only what require loaded is reloaded; an entry script needs a restart. Entities and components a script created stay as they are.
  • Pipelines are rebuilt from shaders, not state: a pipeline that a shader edit made differently (a different push constant layout, say) still has to agree with the code that draws with it. Texture and model reloading is the host's, from AssetsChanged.
  • While watching, base-game scripts can write res:// (mods still cannot: their fs rules do not change).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests: module updates (identity, removed fields, the old module kept when the new one fails to compile or run, on_reload, a failing on_reload, frozen and non-table modules, listeners and signal connections moved to the new code, a module that failed its first load leaving nothing registered) and HotReloader over real files (a module edit, a broken edit then a fix, definitions and schemas, changes that need a restart, modules nothing required, an image imported again, sources and shaders without an import). Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: the watcher (debounce, once, new and deleted files, ignored names, package views, zips). Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests: --watch, and a game's shader edits reaching its ShaderLibrary. Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests: a shader edit changing the rendered image (with its before and after), only the pipelines that use the file rebuilt, a broken edit then a fix, rebuilds while frames are in flight, changes during a build. Tests/Apogee.DevTools.Tests: the same for the overlay's shader, and the error section.

docs.title: Asset import
docs.text:
Source assets (glTF models, PNG and JPEG images, Slang shaders) are made for artists; a game wants its own formats, ready to load. Importing turns one into the other and keeps the result, so that it is done once, not at every start.

Apogee.Runtime --import Samples/Mods/res            # import what changed (in the folder's imported/)
Apogee.Runtime --import Samples/Mods/res --force    # import everything again
./build.sh pack Samples/Mods/res Bin/data/game.pack --cooked   # pack the artifacts instead of the sources they replace

docs.title: What it makes
GPU texture compression
docs.text:
Textures are cooked to Basis Universal UASTC inside KTX 2: one file for every platform, which Ktx2Loader transcodes when it loads to what the GPU samples (BC7 on desktop, ASTC 4x4 on mobile and Apple, RGBA8 where neither exists; TextureCaps says which). The encoder is the one in libktx (KTX-Software 4.4.2, Native libraries); BasisEncoder drives it:

  • Colour and data maps: UASTC level 2 (the default speed/quality trade-off) with RDO at quality 1.0, which shapes the blocks so that zstd squeezes them further, then zstd level 18 over the levels.
  • Normal maps (a material's normal texture inside a model, or an image whose settings say normalMap="true"): UASTC level 3, no RDO, and linear whatever srgb says: errors in a normal show as lighting noise, so these take the slower and more accurate settings. They stay RGB, so shaders read them as they always did. (libktx has a "normal map" mode that keeps two channels as RRRG, which would need the shaders and a BC5 target to go with it; it is not used.)
  • sRGB or linear is written in the file (the data format descriptor's transfer function); ContentLoader reads it from there, so a caller cannot get it wrong. The mip chain is the one the importer built (sRGB averaged in linear light).
  • A texture with a side under 4 pixels stays RGBA8 (a block would be bigger than the texture). compression="none" in the settings keeps RGBA8 for anything, such as a UI image that must not show block artifacts.
  • The encoder is deterministic (the same bytes on any number of cores) and slow, which is what the import cache is for: nothing is encoded again until the image, its settings or the encoder settings (part of the importer's fingerprint) change.

Measured on the 11 MB BoomBox.glb sample (four 2048 x 2048 PNGs; Linux, 28 threads, Release):

RGBA8 + zstd (compression="none") UASTC (the default) .amodel artifact 11.7 MB 5.5 MB (5.2 MiB) in a --cooked pack 11.7 MB 5.5 MB textures on the GPU (all levels) 85.3 MiB 21.3 MiB (BC7: 4x less) first import 1.0 s 18.7 s (139 s of CPU) import with nothing changed 0.07 s 0.07 s

The artifact used to be about the size of its source; now it is half, and a GPU holds a quarter of the memory.

docs.title: When something is imported again
docs.text: Each artifact has a key: the SHA-256 of the importer's version, the asset's .import.xml settings, the asset itself, and every file the import read for it. --import makes an artifact again only when its key is different, so changing a texture of a model, or a model's buffer, re-imports the model, and touching nothing re-imports nothing. An artifact whose source is gone is deleted. A failed import (a file that is not a PNG, a settings file that is wrong) is reported with its file, does not stop the others, exits with code 2, and leaves the artifact the game had (and its index entry) until the source is fixed.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
An <asset>.import.xml next to an asset (checked against the engine's schema) changes how it is imported; every attribute is optional:

<Import srgb="false" mips="false" optimize="false"/>

srgb (default true) is for images: colour maps are sRGB, normal maps, roughness and masks are linear. mips (default true) builds the mip chain. compression is uastc (the default) or none, for images and for the textures of a model; normalMap (default false) says that an image is a normal map (linear, encoded for accuracy). optimize (default true) is for models: merge duplicate vertices and reorder for the GPU's vertex cache. A model's textures take their sRGB or linear setting, and whether they are normal maps, from how its materials use them.

For a shader, <Variant> children each list the preprocessor defines of one more version to compile (the version with no defines is always compiled); the shader is loaded in a variant by passing the same defines to ShaderLibrary.Load:

<Import>
  <Variant><Define name="SHADOWS"/><Define name="QUALITY" value="3"/></Variant>
</Import>

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
ContentLoader is what a game calls: it takes the artifact when there is one and the source otherwise, so the same call works in the editor (sources), in a development run that has imported (artifacts) and in a shipped game (artifacts in a pack). A mod's files are not imported by the game, but a mod may be imported as a folder of its own and ship its imported/ (a mod that brings compiled shaders does); the loader finds it at mod://id/imported:

var content = new ContentLoader(files);
ModelData car = content.LoadModel("res://models/car.gltf");
TextureData ground = content.LoadTexture("res://textures/ground.png", srgb: true, caps);

It does not check that an artifact is current: importing is the step that does (and hot reload, in the editor, runs it when a file changes). The textures of an imported model or image are transcoded for the GPU in ContentOptions.TextureCaps / the caps argument, as those of a source model are.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text: --pack … --cooked leaves out every source that has an artifact, the files it was made from and its .import.xml, and packs the rest with imported/. It needs an import first. A shipped game therefore holds models/car.gltf.amodel and textures/ground.png.ktx2, not the glTF, the .bin and the PNGs, and ContentLoader.LoadModel("res://models/car.gltf") finds the artifact by the path of the source it replaced.

docs.title: Shaders
docs.text: Shipped games never load the Slang compiler. ./build.sh aot publishes the runtime and then runs Apogee.Runtime --import on its Shaders folder, which writes Shaders/imported/*.ashader; the renderers load those (ShaderLibrary, Rendering). In development nothing needs importing: a shader without an artifact is compiled and cached, as before. The bundle records the engine's shader ABI, so a mod's old compiled shader is refused with "import it again" rather than crashing the driver; to make a mod's shaders, import the mod's folder with the engine's dev runtime. CI runs the published runtime with the compiler libraries and every .slang source deleted, running the fixture game, to prove it.

docs.title: What gets cooked, and what does not (the plan)
docs.text:
A rule first: source formats always load. Mods are Luau and data, are never imported, and ship as folders or zips; the editor works on sources. So every loader keeps a source path (as ContentLoader does), and cooking is only an optimization for the base game: a faster, sometimes smaller artifact that is a cache of the source. No format exists only cooked.

Use a standard container where there is one, and an engine format only where there is none. So no .atex: textures stay KTX 2, which the engine already reads (including GPU-compressed data that is transcoded at load). That leaves .amodel as the one engine-specific binary so far, because glTF is an interchange format and there is no standard runtime one.

Kind Authored as Cooked? Artifact Models glTF yes, done .amodel (meshoptimizer) Textures PNG, JPEG yes, done: Basis UASTC in KTX 2, transcoded to BC7/ASTC/RGBA8 at load .ktx2 Shaders Slang yes, done: SPIR-V and Metal shading language and reflection ahead of time, in one bundle (DXIL has a slot), so a shipped game does not carry the compiler .ashader Materials XML definition (a Material type with a schema: textures by path, factors, alpha mode) not for now. They are small data, which mods must be able to author and patch like any definition; a model's built-in materials are already in .amodel none (an .amat only if profiling asks) Scenes, prefabs XML: entities and their components, written and read through the reflection registry not for now, and the same for everything that is a definition. Later, one generic cook: the decoded tree of any XML file (DefValue) as a binary file, so that scenes, prefabs and definitions share one importer and one loader generic binary, e.g. .abin Audio WAV, FLAC, MP3 and Ogg Vorbis, decoded when loaded (streamed if asked) already compressed by the formats; a cook would only trade load time for size none Scripts Luau no (a bytecode cache could come later; it is not needed to ship) none

How it grows. AssetImporter is a small registry. An importer (IAssetImporter) is a name, the extensions it takes, a fingerprint (part of the key: its version, and the versions and options of the tools it calls, such as Slang's, so changing what it writes imports again), and a function from the source and its settings to an artifact, or to nothing for a file that is not an asset on its own. It reads files through the ImportContext, which records them as the artifact's dependencies. new AssetImporter(files, importers) runs them in the order of the list (a file an earlier importer read is not imported by a later one); AssetImporter.Defaults is models and images and the runtime adds ShaderImporter, which lives in Apogee.Rendering because Content does not reference Graphics. A new kind of asset is a new importer and a Load… that takes its artifact; the index, the keys, the sidecar settings, --import and --pack --cooked stay as they are.

What is open for you to decide: whether a .amat is ever worth having. It blocks nothing.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: GPU compression (transcoding to BC7, ASTC and RGBA8 and how close it stays, the colour space read from the file, normal maps, determinism, the sidecar, a model's textures and the caps of the loader), the registry (order, an asset that is not one, what an earlier importer read, the fingerprint, a package's own artifacts, shader variants in the settings), the KTX 2 writer read back by libktx's reader (sRGB and linear, odd sizes, one level or a chain, the data format descriptor), the model file (every field bit for bit, deterministic, a mesh that is not a triangle list, damaged and foreign files), and the importer (artifacts and the index, nothing imported twice, a change to the source, a dependency or the settings, deleted sources, failures that keep the old artifact, hidden folders, a damaged index, settings checked against their schema) and ContentLoader (the artifact is the one used, a source otherwise, a mod's files). Tests/Apogee.Graphics.Tests: the shader bundle (variants, damaged files, another ABI, backends that are not written yet). Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests: the shader importer and ShaderLibrary (dependencies, variants, the compiler never started when an artifact exists, no compiler no artifact, a mod's artifacts). Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests runs --import and --pack --cooked end to end, for shaders too.

docs.title: Status and re-importing one asset
docs.text: AssetImporter.StatusOf("models/car.glb") says where one asset stands (AssetStatus: NotImportable, NotImported, UpToDate, or Stale when the file, its .import.xml or what the import read changed) and Reimport(source) imports just that asset again, leaving the rest of the index as it is. The editor's asset browser uses them.

docs.title: Packages and mods
docs.text:
The game's content and the mods that change it are all packages: a folder (or a .zip) with a mod.xml at its root. The game's own packages are base packages; mods are packages too, with the same layout and the same tools, so the base game is just the first thing that loads. Mods are Luau and data, never native code.

my_mod/
  mod.xml          what it is, what it needs, what it brings
  main.luau        scripts listed in mod.xml
  data/*.xml       definitions (see Definitions and schemas)
  schemas/*.xsd    schemas for the definitions it adds

docs.title: mod.xml
docs.text:
<Mod id="bigger_crates" name="Bigger Crates" version="1.2.0" author="Ada" description="Crates, but bigger."
     apiVersion="1" gameVersion=">=1.0 <3">
  <Dependency id="base_game" version="^1.0"/>
  <Script path="main.luau"/>
  <Content path="data"/>
  <Schema path="schemas"/>
</Mod>
id lowercase letters, digits and underscores, up to 64; the name of the package's folder (or of its .zip without the extension). Not engine, self, res, user or mod. version major.minor.patch; missing parts are 0, a leading v and a -suffix are ignored apiVersion the package API it was written for (default 1); a package that needs a newer one than the engine has does not load gameVersion which versions of the game it works with (a version range, default any) Dependency a package that must be there, and which versions of it (a range, default any) Script a .luau file inside the package, run when it loads, in the order written Content, Schema folders of definitions and of schemas inside the package

Paths are plain relative paths inside the package: no .., no drive or scheme. The manifest is checked against the engine's schema (mod.xsd), then for what a schema cannot say; every problem comes with the file and line.

Version ranges are comparators separated by spaces or commas, all of which must hold: >=1.2, <=, >, <, =1.2 (or 1.2), ^1.2.3 (at least that, below the next version of its first non-zero part: <2.0.0; ^0.2.3 is <0.3.0), ~1.2.3 (below the next minor: <1.3.0), * (any).

docs.title: Finding, solving and mounting
docs.text:
PackageSet.Load(files) looks in:

Where Kind Can the player switch it off? res://packages/<id>/ base no res://dev_mods/<id>/ dev (a development build's mods) yes user://mods/<id>/ and user://mods/<id>.zip the player's mods yes workshop://<id>/ the player's Steam Workshop mods (when Steam runs; see Steam) yes

The player's switched-off mods are in user://mods.xml (<Mods><Disabled id="cool"/></Mods>), which only the game writes (UserModSettings), never a mod. There is one package per id: the first one found wins, and a later one with the same id is ignored with a problem.

A package does not load, with a reason you can show the player, when: it needs a newer package API or another game version, the player switched it off, a dependency is missing, does not load, or is out of its version range (this cascades through whatever depends on it), it is part of a dependency cycle, or it is a base package that needs a mod. What loads is ordered dependencies first, base packages before mods, and otherwise by id, so the order is the same on every machine. Everything that loads is mounted at mod://<id>/ in the file system, whatever it is made of, so a package's files have one address everywhere (mod://bigger_crates/data/x.xml).

using PackageSet packages = PackageSet.Load(files, new PackageOptions { GameVersion = new PackageVersion(1, 4, 0) });

foreach (SolvedPackage p in packages.Packages)
    Console.WriteLine($"{p.Id} {p.Manifest.Version}: {(p.Enabled ? "loads" : p.Reason)}");   // "needs 'base_game', which is not installed"

DefDatabase defs = packages.LoadDefs();    // the packages' schemas and content folders, in load order
foreach (var (package, path) in packages.Scripts) { /* run the scripts */ }

Trouble with the search itself (a mod.xml that does not parse, an id that is not its folder's name, a zip that is not a zip, a schema that is wrong) is in packages.Problems, not an exception: one broken mod does not stop the game. PackageSolver.Solve is the same decision on a plain list of candidates, which is what the tests drive.

docs.title: Running packages in Luau (PackageLoader)
docs.text:
PackageLoader (in Apogee.Scripting) runs the packages of a PackageSet in a VM. A game wires its hooks into the VM's options and then loads:

var loader = new PackageLoader(files, packages);
var vm = new LuauVm(new LuauVmOptions
{
    Files = new VfsScriptFiles(files),          // scripts are read through the file system
    FileSystem = files,                         // the fs library
    OwnerOfModule = loader.OwnerOfModule,       // a module runs as the owner of the package it is in
    CanLoadModule = loader.CanLoadModule,       // require confinement
    CanAccessFile = loader.CanAccessFile,       // fs confinement
});
vm.Defs = packages.LoadDefs();
IReadOnlyList<PackageRunResult> results = loader.Load(vm);
  • Order and owners. Scripts run packages in load order, each package's <Script>s in the order written. A base package's scripts run as the VM's base owner; a mod gets an owner of its own (PackageLoaderOptions: a soft memory limit, 256 MiB by default, and a time budget per call, 2 s), so one mod cannot use up the memory or the frame of the others, and it cannot use classes marked ModsBlocked. A module runs as the owner of the package it is in, whoever required it: a mod that requires a base-game module does not give it the mod's limits.
  • Aliases. @<id>/… is an alias for each package (require("@base_game/lib/util")), in every script. A .luaurc alias of the same name wins.
  • Confinement. A mod may require files of its own package, of the packages it depends on (however far), and res://; ../other_mod/x resolves to another mod's folder and is refused, and so is @other_mod/x. The base game may require anything.
  • Failure. A script that raises an error stops its package: the error is logged and in PackageRunResult.Error, the package's remaining scripts and the packages that need it are not run, and everything else goes on. A mod that never returns is stopped by its time budget. Content a package brought stays loaded.

docs.title: The fs library
docs.text:
Scripts read and write through the virtual file system with virtual paths only (res://…, user://…, mod://<id>/…):

local text, err = fs.read_text("mod://my_mod/config.xml")      -- text, or nil and a message
local ok, err = fs.write_text("user://moddata/my_mod/save.xml", xml.encode(node))
fs.exists(path)  fs.read_bytes(path)  fs.write_bytes(path, data)  fs.list(dir, "*.xml", true)  fs.list_dirs(dir)  fs.make_dir(path)  fs.remove(path)

Functions return nil and a message instead of raising an error for what can go wrong. A mod may read res://, its own package and its dependencies', and user://moddata/<its id>/, and may write only user://moddata/<its id>/ (folders are made as needed): the game's content is read-only to it, and so are the player's saves and other mods' data. The base game may write wherever the file system allows (user://). Messages name the virtual path (user://x: access denied, res://y: not found), never a path on the disk, and a path that is not valid (.., a backslash, a drive) is refused before anything is looked up. fs.exists says false for what a script may not see.

docs.title: Shaders in a mod
docs.text: A mod may bring Slang shaders. The shipped game has no shader compiler, so a mod's shaders must be compiled by the modder: run the engine's dev runtime on the mod's folder (Apogee.Runtime --import <mod folder>) and ship the result with the mod. The compiled files are in the mod's imported/ folder (imported/shaders/x.slang.ashader and an index.xml), which ShaderLibrary and ContentLoader find at mod://id/imported. A bundle records the engine's shader ABI; after an engine update that changes it, the game says to import the mod again. In development, where the compiler is present, a mod's .slang source loads without importing. See Asset import.

docs.title: Apogee.Runtime --game <folder>
docs.text:
Apogee.Runtime --game Samples/Mods [--user <folder>] [--headless --frames 60 | --headless --screenshot out.png | (a window)]

The folder is res:// (its packages/ hold the game's packages), user:// is --user or the platform's folder for the game's name (the player's mods are in user://mods). The runtime logs every package and why one does not load, loads the definitions and their problems, runs the scripts, and then runs the frame loop of --run. A mod that fails is logged and left out; a base package that fails is an error of the game (exit code 2).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: versions and ranges, the manifest (every field, every kind of problem), the solver (each reason to disable, cascade, cycles, order independent of discovery order, duplicate ids) and PackageSet over real folders and a zip (places, mounting, switched-off mods, problems, definitions built from the packages, disposal). Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests runs PackageLoader over real folders (order, owners and limits, aliases, require and fs confinement including that no real path leaks, failures that stay inside their package, a runaway mod stopped by its budget, definitions seen by scripts), and Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests runs --game end to end.

docs.title: Packs
docs.text: A pack is one file (or a few) that holds a game's content: compressed with zstd, optionally encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and mounted in the file system like a folder. A shipped game's res:// is its packs; during development it is a folder. Mods are not packs: they stay folders or zips so that players can make them without tools.

docs.title: Making one
docs.text:
./build.sh pack Samples/Mods/res Bin/data/game.pack                      # every file under the folder (Apogee.Runtime --pack, with .env loaded)
./build.sh pack Content Bin/data/game.pack --split-mb 1024 --level 15      # parts of about 1 GiB, a smaller (slower) compression
./build.sh pack Content Bin/data/patch.pack --base Bin/data/game.pack      # a patch pack

./build.sh pack runs Apogee.Runtime --pack (the engine's host program has the content library and the native libraries, and the editor and the export step use the same PackWriter); the wrapper loads .env, so APOGEE_PACK_KEY applies. Run Apogee.Runtime --pack <folder> <out.pack> yourself to pack without the wrapper. Paths in the pack are relative to the folder (packages/core/mod.xml); files and folders whose name starts with a dot are left out; every name must be valid in a virtual path (no .., no nul…), and the tool says which are not. From code: PackWriter (Add, AddFile, Remove, Finish).

  • Compression. Each file is compressed with zstd when it has 64 bytes or more and that saves at least 10%; the rest (PNG, KTX2, OGG…) is stored as it is. --level is zstd's 1 to 22 (default 12). Large files are compressed on several threads.
  • Splitting. A pack grows to --split-mb (default 1536) and then continues in the next part: game.pack, game_001.pack, game_002.pack… A file is never split, so one that is bigger than the limit gets a part to itself. Opening the first part finds the others; a part that is missing is an error that says which.
  • Patch packs. With --base the packs you name (in order, with the same key) are what the game has already: the new pack holds only the files that are new or different, and a removal for each file that is gone. Mounted over the base, it replaces, adds and removes.

docs.title: Using one
docs.text:
PackKey? key = PackKey.FromEnvironment();                    // null when APOGEE_PACK_KEY is not set
using var pack = PackSource.Open("data/game.pack", key);     // the key is ignored for a pack that is not encrypted
files.Mount("res://", pack);                                  // later mounts override earlier ones: a patch pack goes after

Apogee.Runtime --game <folder> mounts the folder as res:// and then every *.pack in <folder>/data, by name (so patch.pack goes over game.pack), with the key from the environment, before it looks for packages. Reads are safe from several threads; a file is read, decrypted, decompressed and checked when it is asked for, a file that is neither compressed nor encrypted is streamed without being read whole (and without its hash checked).

docs.title: Encryption and the key
docs.text:
If APOGEE_PACK_KEY is set (64 hexadecimal digits: 32 bytes) the pack is encrypted; if it is not, it is not. No key is set up yet: nothing in the repository or the CI has one, so packs are plain. When you want one, put it in .env (which git ignores and the ./build.sh wrapper loads), make the same key available to everything that makes or opens packs (the editor, the tools, the shipped game, a CI secret), and never commit it or print it (a PackKey writes itself as PackKey(…)). A pack made with one key cannot be read with another, and changing the key means making the packs again.

What it does, in detail (PackFormat has the layout):

  • Each part has a random 32-byte salt; the key that seals a part is HKDF-SHA256(key, salt), so the pack key never encrypts anything directly and two packs of the same files differ.
  • Every file and the index is its own AES-256-GCM blob (nonce | tag | ciphertext, a random nonce each time). A wrong key, or a single changed byte, fails the check instead of producing garbage. The file's path is authenticated with it, so a file cannot be moved to another path in the pack.
  • The first four bytes of the pack are APGK without a key, and with one a few bytes of a hash of the key: an encrypted pack has no signature to search for, and opening one with the wrong key, or with none, is an error that says so (without the key in it).
  • Compression comes first and encryption after it (encrypted data does not compress). Without a key, damage is found by the zstd checksum of a compressed file and by a hash (the first 16 bytes of the SHA-256 of the file) that is checked for every file read whole.

AES-GCM comes from the platform: Windows and macOS have it, and on Linux it needs OpenSSL (libssl), which desktops and Steam's runtime have.

What it is not. A game has to be able to open its own packs, so the key is in the game; a determined person can get it out. The encryption keeps the content from being taken apart casually and makes a changed pack fail to load. It is not copy protection.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: the key, a round trip of every kind of file (empty, text, noise, nested), compression only where it pays, mounting, streaming, encryption (the content and the magic are not in the file, a salt per pack, no key and a wrong key), tampering (a flipped byte in a file or the index of a sealed pack, in a stored and in a compressed file of a plain one, a truncated file, a part missing), split parts (also a file bigger than a part, and sealed), patch packs, path rules, and many threads reading at once. Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests runs a game from a pack with a patch pack over it, and an encrypted game with the key from the environment.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: Apogee.Core: the small things every other library uses.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Log.Info("Category", "message") (also Trace, Debug, Warn, Error) writes a LogEntry to every registered ILogSink. Sinks can be called from any thread. Log.MinimumLevel filters, Log.IsEnabled(level) avoids building a message that would be dropped. ConsoleSink is the stock sink.

Log.AddSink(new ConsoleSink());
Log.Info("Runtime", "started");

docs.title: Arena
docs.text: Arena is a fixed-size bump allocator over unmanaged memory. Allocate<T>(count) returns a zeroed Span<T> that stays valid (the memory never moves) until Reset(mark); take Mark before, reset to it after, to free a scope. It is not thread safe: use one per thread or per job.

docs.title: NativeList
docs.text: NativeList<T> is a growable list in unmanaged memory for unmanaged elements: Add, RemoveAtSwapBack, a ref indexer and AsSpan(). Dispose it.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text: JobSystem is a worker pool: Schedule(group, job) queues a job on a JobGroup, group.Wait() returns when all of its jobs ran and rethrows the first failure. ParallelFor(count, batchSize, body) splits a range across the workers and waits.

docs.title: ECS
docs.text: Apogee.Ecs wraps a Flecs world (Apogee.Native.Flecs). World is an EngineObject, so scripts get a handle to it, and its [Method]s (create_entity, lookup, progress…) are in the registry. Use a world from one thread.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
A component is an unmanaged struct marked [Component] (see Reflection); its fields are the memory layout:

[Component] public struct Position { public Vector3 Value; }
[Component] public struct Health { public int Current; public int Max; }
[Component] public struct Frozen { }                       // no fields: a tag

using var world = new World();
Entity e = world.CreateEntity("hero");
world.Set(e, new Health { Current = 5, Max = 10 });
ref readonly Health health = ref world.Get<Health>(e);      // valid until the next structural change
world.Ensure<Health>(e).Current = 8;                       // a writable reference; the component is added when missing
world.Modified<Health>(e);                                 // tell observers about it
world.Add<Frozen>(e);                                      // tags: Add, Has, Remove

The first use of a component registers it in the world: an entity with the component's name, its size and alignment, and its fields as Flecs reflection data (world.ToJson(value) prints {"Current":5,"Max":10}; Flecs' own tools can read it too). Entity ids are Entity structs. Ids are never reused as such: deleting an entity and creating another gives a different id, and IsAlive is false for the old one.

docs.title: Components a script defines
docs.text: world.DefineComponent("Spin", [("speed", FieldKind.Float32), ("axis", FieldKind.Vector3)]) lays the fields out in name order (each aligned to its own size, a vector to four bytes), so a schema always gives the same layout. The same schema again returns the same component; another schema under a known name is an error. GetComponentInfo(id) gives the layout, and FieldAccess.Read/Write (in Apogee.Reflection) read and write a field of the component's memory as a Value, with range checks. The pointer API (GetPointer, EnsurePointer, SetPointer) works on any component id.

docs.title: Editing: hierarchy, copies, snapshots and scenes
docs.text:
What an editor needs of a world, in World.Editing.cs and World.Scene.cs. "User entities" are the ones a game or an editor made (IsUserEntity): not Flecs' own entities (modules, systems, observers), not the entities of registered components and the reflection data under them, not what is marked EditorOnly (the editor's own camera) or under such an entity.

  • Hierarchy: Roots(), Children(entity) (in creation order) and Subtree(entity) (parents first). ComponentsOf(entity) lists the components and tags the registry describes (not relationship pairs or the name), with their ComponentInfo; Components is every component the world has registered. SetParent and GetParent were there before; Trs.InLocalOf gives the local transform that keeps an entity where it is under a new parent.
  • Copies: Clone(entity, parent?) copies the components and the whole branch under the same parent, naming the copies name (copy), name (copy 2) so they stay unique.
  • Snapshots: Snapshot() takes every user entity (ids with their generation, names, parents, component bytes), SnapshotTree(entity) one branch. Restore(snapshot) puts the world back: user entities that are not in it are destroyed, the ones that are come back under the same ids (made alive again with ecs_make_alive when they were destroyed) with their components, names and parents as they were; RestoreEntities(snapshot) only brings back and overwrites, destroying nothing (an undo of a deletion). The same ids are what keep a selection and an undo history valid across a play session. A snapshot is bytes: a component that holds a handle of the run (a physics body's id) comes back with the old value, so such components are left to the code that made them.
  • Scenes (.ascene): SaveScene() writes the user entities as JSON text, SaveScene(entity) one branch, and LoadScene(text, parent?) creates the entities (under parent when given) and returns them in the order of the file. The format is ours, written field by field from the registry's descriptions with Utf8JsonWriter and read with JsonDocument: no reflection, so it works in NativeAOT. Flecs' own JSON was not used: it would carry the entities the engine registers for its types and systems. An entity has a number in the file, its parent and entity-typed fields refer to those numbers (a reference to an entity that is not in the scene is saved as null), and 64-bit values that a JSON number cannot hold go as text. Components a script defined are written with their schema ("components") and defined again when the scene is loaded into a world that has not heard of them. On loading, a component or a field the world does not have is logged and skipped, a name that is taken gets a free one (name 2), and text that is not a scene is a FormatException. WorldTransform is derived and never saved; IgnoreInScenes(name) leaves others out (the host does it for physics Body), and RegisterSceneConverter(component, field, write, read) saves a handle as what it names (the host saves ModelRenderer.Model, a number in this run's model library, as the model's path).
  • From scripts: world:save_scene() returns the text, world:load_scene(text, parent?) the list of entities it made, world:roots() and world:children(entity) the hierarchy. A script reads and writes the file itself with fs.read_text and fs.write_text, which keeps the confinement of a mod's files.

docs.title: Transforms
docs.text: Every world has Transform (local to the parent) and WorldTransform (in the world, computed top down once a frame by a system that every world installs), with a Double3 position: see Math and the double-precision world. A query term can read a component from the entity's parent with new QueryTerm(id, QueryOperator.Optional, QuerySource.ParentCascade): the field is a single element shared by the table (view.FieldPointer(index, size)), and parents are visited before their children. World.ComputeWorldTransform(entity) computes the world placement now, from the entity's Transform and its parents', for code that changes transforms and needs the result before the next Progress (physics placing a body it was just given).

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
using Query<Position, Velocity> moving = world.Query<Position, Velocity>();
moving.Each((Entity e, ref Position p, ref Velocity v) => p.Value += v.Value);
int count = moving.Count();

A query matches the entities that have all of the components (up to four typed ones; CreateQuery takes any number of QueryTerms, with QueryOperator.Not to exclude a component). It is cached by Flecs. Iterating defers structural changes (adding or removing components, deleting entities): they are applied when the iteration is over, so a callback may do them without breaking it. ForEachTable gives a TableView for each table: Entities, Count, and Field<T>(index) for the component of the term with that index. Dispose a query when done with it; the world disposes the rest.

docs.title: Systems and observers
docs.text:
world.AddSystem<Position, Velocity>("Move", Phase.OnUpdate, (Entity e, ref Position p, ref Velocity v) =>
    p.Value += v.Value * world.DeltaTime);
world.Progress(1f / 60);

Progress runs one frame: the phases in order (OnLoad, PostLoad, PreUpdate, OnUpdate, OnValidate, PostUpdate, PreStore, OnStore), and within a phase the systems in the order they were added. AddSystem also takes terms and a TableAction for the raw form scripts use. Destroy the system's entity to remove it.

An observer runs at once when its event happens to an entity that matches: AddObserver<Health>("Watch", ObserverEvent.OnSet, …) (also OnAdd and OnRemove).

Exceptions never unwind through Flecs. A system or observer that throws is recorded, the others still run, and Progress throws when the frame is done: the exception itself when there was one, an AggregateException when there were several.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Flecs copies the names it is given (entities, struct members), and a system's callback is kept alive by a GCHandle that Flecs frees together with the system; a world that is destroyed frees them all. This is checked under NativeAOT by the runtime's smoke test, which CI runs.
  • Relationship pairs are World.Pair(first, second); the child-of relation and the other builtin ids are Ecs.ChildOf… in the Flecs binding.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Ecs.Tests (needs the flecs native library): the transform hierarchy (TransformTests), registration and reflection JSON, set/get/ensure, tags, runtime components, names and parents, ids that stay dead, queries (with Not, with structural changes inside), systems in phases, failing systems, observers, and disposal; and EditingTests: which entities are the user's, hierarchy order, the components of an entity, clones, snapshots and restoring (ids that come back, names that swapped, a deleted branch), and scenes (a round trip with the hierarchy, references, doubles and script components, converters, unknown things, bad files). The scene round trip also runs in the NativeAOT smoke test (Apogee.Runtime with no arguments) and from Luau (Tests/Luau/ecs.test.luau).

docs.title: Interop
docs.text: Apogee.Interop is what the generated bindings stand on.

docs.title: NativeLibraries
docs.text: Generated DllImports name a logical library (SDL3, flecs). Each binding assembly registers the file names to try per operating system (NativeLibraries.Register, called from the generated *.Library.g.cs). Resolution tries, per candidate: next to the executable, then runtimes/<rid>/native, then the system search. TryLoad lets a test or a tool ask whether a library is installed without failing.

docs.title: CBool
docs.text: CBool is a one-byte C bool/uint8_t flag with implicit conversions to and from bool, so signatures stay blittable (a managed bool is not).

docs.title: Utf8
docs.text:
Utf8.ToZeroTerminated(string) gives the bytes of a C string (pin them with fixed to pass them to native code) and Utf8.FromPointer(byte*) reads one back (null stays null).

fixed (byte* name = Utf8.ToZeroTerminated("Apogee"))
{
    SDL.SetWindowTitle(window, name);
}
string? error = Utf8.FromPointer(SDL.GetError());

docs.title: Math and the double-precision world
docs.text: Everything the GPU and the shaders see is float; the world is not. A float has 24 bits of precision, so 5.8 km from the origin (the corner of an 8192 m map) it moves in 0.5 mm steps, which shows as jitter in physics and in the picture. So positions are double, and every other quantity (directions, rotations, scales, velocities, everything on the GPU) stays float.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
The engine does not have a math library of its own. It uses System.Numerics (Vector2/3/4, Quaternion, Matrix4x4, Plane): the JIT and NativeAOT treat those as SIMD intrinsic types (a Vector3 lives in one register and +, Dot, Normalize compile to a few vector instructions), which a struct of our own would only match by wrapping them. Apogee.Core.Numerics adds what System.Numerics has no type for:

Type What it is Double3 A world position: three doubles, 24 bytes, scalar code (positions are added and subtracted, not crunched in bulk). Converts implicitly from Vector3 and explicitly to it. Trs A placement: Double3 position, Quaternion rotation, Vector3 scale. InWorldOf(parent), TransformPoint, InverseTransformPoint, TransformVector, ToMatrix(origin).

Conventions (the same as the renderer's): right-handed, +Y up, an object or camera looks down -Z, angles are radians, matrices are row-major and used with row vectors (Vector3.Transform(v, m); a * b applies a first), and quaternions compose as in mathematics: (q1 * q2) * v == q1 * (q2 * v), so q2 applies first.

docs.title: Relative to an origin
docs.text:
Double3.RelativeTo(origin) subtracts in double and then narrows to float, so the result is exact however far both points are from the world's origin:

Vector3 onScreen = enemy.Position.RelativeTo(camera.Position);     // a few meters, precise to a micrometre, 10 000 km from the origin
Matrix4x4 world = placement.ToMatrix(camera.Position);             // the translation is relative to the camera

That is how positions reach the GPU: the renderer works camera-relative (see Rendering: Camera.Position and a scene's Origin are Double3). Jolt is built with JPH_DOUBLE_PRECISION (see Native libraries), so that body positions are double too.

docs.title: Transforms in the ECS
docs.text:
Transform (Position: Double3, Rotation: Quaternion, Scale: Vector3) is a component of every world. It is local: relative to the entity's parent (the ChildOf relationship), and in the world for an entity with no parent. Set the scale to one (Transform.Identity, Transform.At(position)): a zeroed transform, which is what Add gives, has no size.

WorldTransform is the same placement in world space, and the transform system computes it once a frame (in the PostUpdate phase) top down: a Flecs query with the parent's WorldTransform as a cascade term, so parents are always done before their children, whatever order they were created in. Adding a Transform adds its WorldTransform (Flecs' With trait). Read WorldTransform; do not write it.

Entity truck = world.CreateEntity("truck");
Entity wheel = world.CreateEntity("wheel", parent: truck);
world.Set(truck, Transform.At(new Double3(5_000_000, 0, 0)));
world.Set(wheel, new Transform(new Double3(1, 0.4, 2), Quaternion.Identity, Vector3.One));
world.Progress(0.016f);
Double3 where = world.Get<WorldTransform>(wheel).Position;       // (5 000 001, 0.4, 2)

Limits. Scale may differ per axis, but there is no shear: a child's world scale is the product of its own and its parent's, which is exact when the parent's scale is uniform or its rotation lines up with the child's axes (the rule most engines use). The child's position inside its parent is narrowed to float while it is rotated, so keep children within about ten kilometres of their parent; the parent itself can be anywhere.

docs.title: In scripts
docs.text:
Luau's vector is three floats (LUA_VECTOR_SIZE 3), so scripts see positions as vectors: a Double3 is narrowed when it goes into Luau and widened when it comes back. A float is good to about a millimetre at 8 km from the origin, which is enough for gameplay logic, and nothing is lost where it matters, in the physics and the renderer, which keep the doubles. A script that needs an exact far position works with offsets from a known place instead.

Quat is an immutable userdata:

local turn = Quat.axisAngle(Vector3(0, 1, 0), math.rad(90))      -- Quat.new(x, y, z, w), Quat.euler(vector(pitch, yaw, roll)), Quat.lookAt(forward, up?)
turn * Vector3(0, 0, 1)                                          -- rotates a vector: (1, 0, 0)
turn * other                                                     -- composes: `other` applies first
turn:inverse(), turn:normalized(), turn:slerp(other, t), turn:dot(other), turn:toEuler()
turn.x, turn.y, turn.z, turn.w; Quat.identity; turn == other

The built-in components are reachable by name: world:component("Transform") and world:component("WorldTransform"), with fields Position, Rotation and Scale. A component a script defines can have fields of type "dvec3" (a Double3, seen as a vector) and "quat".

docs.title: In the registry and in files
docs.text:
• [Component] structs may have Double3 and Quaternion fields (FieldKind.Double3, FieldKind.Quaternion), and [Property]/[Method] members may use both types. A Double3 member crosses to scripts as ValueKind.Vector3, a Quaternion as ValueKind.Quaternion. Flecs knows both as struct types, so its JSON keeps all 17 digits of a position.
  • Value carries a quaternion in the spare float next to a vector's z (a Value is 32 bytes); it has no room for a Double3, which is why positions cross as vectors.
  • In XML definitions a vector3 attribute (type="xs:vector3"; any prefix) is three numbers, at="1 2.5 -3" (spaces or commas), decoded as a DefVector and a vector in Luau.

docs.title: Tests
