docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Core.Tests (Double3, Trs: composing, inverting, precision at 10 000 km, the camera-relative matrix), Tests/Apogee.Ecs.Tests (propagation through three levels created in any order, reparenting, the With trait, the layout and the JSON of the components), Tests/Apogee.Reflection.Tests (the new field kinds, members and values), Tests/Luau/quat.test.luau (Quat and the transform from a script), the vector3 case of Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests and, in Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests, the golden scene rendered 100 km and 10 000 km from the origin.

docs.title: Profiling, SIMD and the shipped instruction set
docs.text: The rule for speed is measure, then write SIMD where a measurement says so. System.Numerics is already intrinsic (see Math), so most code needs nothing. This chapter says how to look, what the shipped programs are compiled for, and where hand-written vector code exists.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
• The dev overlay (Dev tools): the CPU frame time history, the GPU time of each pass (FrameLoop.Timings, from timestamp queries, per frame in flight), the render graph and the draw, culled and light counts. Start here: it says whether a frame is CPU- or GPU-bound.
  • RenderDoc shows the same pass names (frame.Scope(name) and recorder.Label(name) are debug labels).
  • CoreCLR (the editor and dotnet run): dotnet-trace collect -- <program> and dotnet-counters monitor (install them with dotnet tool install -g dotnet-trace dotnet-counters).
  • NativeAOT (a shipped build): a native program, so the platform's profiler reads it: perf record -g on Linux, Instruments on macOS, Windows Performance Analyzer or Visual Studio on Windows. ./build.sh aot keeps the symbols (Apogee.Runtime.dbg next to the program on Linux, .pdb files on Windows).
  • Micro-benchmarks: ./build.sh bench [filter] runs BenchmarkDotNet over Samples/Benchmarks (a sample: benchmarks are run by hand) in Release (the raw results go to Bin/benchmarks, which is not committed) (for example ./build.sh bench '*Culling*' --job short). BenchmarkDotNet is used there only (MIT, a test dependency, never shipped), and CI builds the project but does not run it: benchmarks are noisy on shared machines. Remember that BenchmarkDotNet's NativeAOT mode compiles for the CPU it runs on, which is not what a game ships with; to measure the shipped baseline publish a small program with -p:PublishAot=true instead.

docs.title: The instruction set of a shipped game
docs.text:
The JIT asks the CPU which instructions exist when the program starts. NativeAOT cannot: it compiles for a fixed set, and a CPU without it does not start the program. Measured with a small program on an AVX2 machine:

IlcInstructionSet Vector128.IsHardwareAccelerated Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated, Avx2.IsSupported, Fma.IsSupported (not set) true false x86-64-v2 true false x86-64-v3 true true

So the default of x64 is x86-64-v2 (SSE4.2 and POPCNT, practically every PC since 2009), and AVX2 code is simply compiled out of a default NativeAOT build; it is not a run-time check. Our choice, in Directory.Build.props for PublishAot builds:

  • x64: x86-64-v2, written down so that it is a decision. -p:ApogeeAotInstructionSet=x86-64-v3 builds for AVX2, BMI and FMA (Intel since Haswell in 2013, AMD since Excavator in 2015 and Zen) at the price of the older CPUs, which then do not start the game; the next section says what that buys.
  • osx-arm64: apple-m1 (atomics, CRC, rounding multiply, dot products): every Apple-silicon Mac has at least that.
  • Other arm64 and anything else keep the compiler's default (ARMv8.0 with NEON).

The CoreCLR editor and development runs use the JIT and so do get AVX2 on a CPU that has it. That is why the code that can use 256-bit vectors checks Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated and falls back.

docs.title: Where there is SIMD
docs.text:
Only where it was measured to pay, and with a scalar twin that the tests compare it with.

Frustum culling (Apogee.Core.Numerics.FrustumCulling, used by SceneRenderer): the bounds of every draw are kept as six arrays (centers and half extents, structure of arrays, padded to a multiple of eight), and each frame the five planes of the camera's view volume are tested against all of them, four or eight boxes per instruction, producing a bit per draw. The three kernels (CullScalar, CullVector128, CullVector256) do the same arithmetic in the same order, so they set the same bits, which FrustumCullingTests checks on random boxes and frusta; Cull picks the widest that is hardware accelerated. Because the scene's boxes are relative to its origin, the frustum is moved to them with Frustum.Offset (the plane constants absorb the offset) and the arrays never change.

Measured for 100 000 boxes (Core i7-14700K, .NET 10):

scalar Vector128 (NativeAOT x86-64-v2, the shipped default) Vector256 (NativeAOT x86-64-v3; CoreCLR) time 1.66 ms 0.18 ms (9x) 0.064 ms (26x)

So a shipped game culls 100 000 draws in under a fifth of a millisecond without AVX2, and AVX2 would save about 0.1 ms more per 100 000: not worth turning players away. For 1 000 boxes the whole cull is about 1.5 µs (128-bit). ./build.sh bench '*Culling*' reproduces the table; *RelativePosition* measures Double3.RelativeTo (100 000 positions: about 0.11 ms, scalar double code, which is fast enough that it has no SIMD twin).

Not done, on purpose (nothing measured yet, so nothing written): density-map sweeps and the instancer (terrain), skinning, particles. They get a benchmark first.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text: Apogee.Reflection is the registry of everything scripts, serialization and inspectors see: classes with properties, methods and signals, enums, ECS components and script libraries. It is written by a Roslyn source generator (Apogee.Reflection.Generator), so there is no runtime reflection and it works under NativeAOT.

docs.title: Describing a class
docs.text:
A class derives from EngineObject, is partial, and is marked [ApogeeClass]. Members are opted in:

public enum Mode { Idle, FastMove }

/// <summary>Something that moves.</summary>
[ApogeeClass(Creatable = true)]
public partial class Actor : EngineObject
{
    /// <summary>How fast it goes, in meters per second.</summary>
    [Property] public float Speed { get; set; } = 2;
    [Property] public Mode Mode { get; set; }
    [Property] public int Count { get; private set; }              // no public setter: read-only

    [Method] public bool TryMove(Vector3 to, float speed = 1f) { … }
    [Method] public (int, string) Pair() => (7, "seven");            // a tuple is several results in a script
    [Method] public static int Twice(int x) => x * 2;

    [Signal] public Signal<int, string> Damaged { get; } = new();
}
  • Names in scripts are snake_case (TryMove → try_move, FastMove → "fast_move"); Name = "…" on an attribute overrides it. Classes keep their C# name ([ApogeeClass(Name = "…")]).
  • Options: Scriptable = false keeps the class out of scripts, ModsBlocked = true refuses its objects to mods, and Creatable = true gives scripts a new() (it needs a parameterless constructor).
  • Documentation: the <summary> above a member is copied into the registry, for the generated .d.luau and the inspectors.
  • Types a member may have: bool, the integer types, float, double, string, Vector3, Double3 (seen as a vector in scripts), Quaternion, enums (a [Flags] enum is a list of names in scripts), Entity, Value (any), ScriptFunction, EngineObject classes, and T[], List<T> and IReadOnlyList<T> of those. T? is nullable. Anything else is error APG002 that names the member, as are non-partial classes (APG001), two members with one script name (APG003), a component that is not an unmanaged struct or has an unsupported field (APG004) and a member that cannot be described, such as a ref parameter or a signal of the wrong type (APG005). A type with an error writes nothing, so the first error is the only one.

docs.title: Components and libraries
docs.text:
[Component]
public struct Position { public Vector3 Value; }               // fields: bool, integers, float, double, Vector3, Double3, Quaternion, Entity

[Component] public struct Frozen { }                           // no fields: a tag

[ScriptLibrary("imgui")]
public static partial class ImGuiLibrary
{
    [Method] public static bool Button(string label) { … }
}

A component's ComponentInfo has its size, alignment and every field's offset, taken from the compiled struct. A library is a global table of its static [Method]s in scripts.

docs.title: What an inspector shows
docs.text:
[Property] carries hints for inspectors, on a class's properties and on a component's fields (FieldDef.Meta, PropertyDef.Meta: an InspectorMeta). All are optional:

[Component]
public struct Engine
{
    [Property(Min = 0, Max = 100, Step = 0.5, Category = "Power")] public float Throttle;   // a slider from 0 to 100 under the heading "Power"
    [Property(Min = 0)] public int Gear;                                                    // a drag field that does not go below 0
    [Property(Hidden = true)] public uint Handle;                                           // an inspector does not show it
    [Property(ReadOnly = true)] public double Hours;                                        // shown, not editable
}

Min, Max and Step are hints for widgets: they do not stop a script or a file from setting another value. InspectorMeta.HasRange says both ends are given (a slider can be drawn), RangeText is 0 to 100 for the generated Luau definitions, which add (Range: 0 to 1.) to the doc of a property. A field without [Property] has no hints. A component a script defines gives them in a table: world:component("Vehicle", { speed = { type = "f32", min = 0, max = 90, step = 0.5, category = "Motion" }, gear = "i32", token = { type = "u32", hidden = true } }); the plain name = "type" form still works.

docs.title: Using the registry
docs.text:
TypeRegistry.GetClass("Actor") gives a ClassInfo; FindProperty("speed"), FindMethod("try_move") and FindSignal("damaged") look a member up by its script name, inherited ones included. Everything crosses as a Value, a 24-byte struct with no boxing:

var results = new Value[1];
actor.Class.FindMethod("try_move")!.Invoke(actor, [Value.Vector(target), Value.Float(2)], results);
bool moved = results[0].ToBool();

MethodDef.Invoke checks the argument count; the To… methods check kind and range and throw a ValueException whose message a script can show (expected number, got string, 300 is out of range for byte). Registration happens in a module initializer of each assembly that has described types, so the registry is complete before the first lookup.

docs.title: Objects and handles
docs.text: Every EngineObject takes a slot in one table: its Handle is an index and a generation (SlotTable<T> in Apogee.Core). Scripts hold the handle, never the object. Destroy() frees the slot and bumps the generation, so a handle to a destroyed object, or to one whose slot was reused, is recognised (attempt to use a destroyed object). An object a script creates is destroyed when the script lets go of it unless the engine calls Adopt() on it (see Scripting).

docs.title: Signals
docs.text: Signal, Signal<T1> … Signal<T1, T2, T3, T4>: Connect(handler) returns a Connection (Disconnect(), IsConnected) and Emit(…) calls a snapshot of the handlers, so a handler may disconnect itself while it runs. A handler that throws is logged and the others still run; the emitter never sees it. SignalDef.Connect connects a handler that receives the arguments as Values.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Reflection.Tests compiles C# snippets with the generator (CSharpGeneratorDriver), checks the generated text and the diagnostics, loads the result and drives it through the registry; it also tests Value, handles, signals and the registry itself.

docs.title: Graphics
docs.text: Apogee.Graphics is the GPU layer. The renderer, the dev tools and the content pipeline talk to a small portable API: GraphicsDevice and the objects it makes (buffers, images, samplers, pipelines, a command recorder, a swapchain and a frame loop). Each graphics API implements it in its own namespace: Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan and Apogee.Graphics.Metal. The renderer on top of it is in Rendering.

docs.title: Backends: the seam
docs.text:
Everything above the backends is abstract classes with the portable surface, and each backend has one sealed class for each:

Portable (Apogee.Graphics) Vulkan (Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan) What it hides GraphicsDevice VulkanDevice instance, physical device choice, queue, memory allocator, the window's surface GpuBuffer, GpuImage, ImageView, GpuSampler VulkanBuffer, VulkanImage, VulkanImageView, VulkanSampler VkBuffer, VkImage and views (VMA allocations) Pipeline VulkanPipeline pipeline objects and the shared pipeline layout CommandRecorder VulkanCommandRecorder command buffers, barriers (VulkanStates maps an ImageState to layouts, stages and accesses), dynamic rendering BindlessHeap VulkanBindlessHeap the descriptor set of texture, sampler and storage-image arrays ImmediateContext VulkanImmediateContext a command buffer and a fence for loading and tools Swapchain, FrameLoop VulkanSwapchain, VulkanFrameLoop acquiring and presenting, the timeline semaphore of the frames in flight, timestamp queries

The portable names of things are the engine's own: PixelFormat (in Apogee.Core.Graphics; its numbers are Vulkan's VkFormat numbers, which are also the vkFormat of a KTX 2 file, so a texture's format is read by a cast, and another backend maps the ones it supports with a table), BufferUsage, ImageUsage, SampleCount, CullMode, FrontFace, CompareOp, PrimitiveTopology, Filter, MipmapMode, AddressMode and IndexFormat (all with Vulkan's numbers too), and ShaderCode (the compiled code of one entry point and which ShaderBackend it is for). Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan.VulkanConvert turns them into Vulkan's enums; the barrier states (ImageState, BufferState) were already abstract. A device refuses ShaderCode of another backend.

A test keeps the seam closed. BackendSeamTests reads the public surface of Apogee.Graphics, Apogee.Rendering, Apogee.DevTools, Apogee.Content and Apogee.Platform by reflection and fails on any signature that names a type of Apogee.Native.Vulkan, outside Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan. Code that does need Vulkan (the backend's own tests, tools) casts: (VulkanDevice)device.

Creating a device.

using var window = new Window("My game", 1280, 720, WindowOptions.Resizable | GraphicsDevice.RequiredWindowOptions());   // a window is made for one API
using var device = GraphicsDevice.Create(new GraphicsDeviceOptions { Window = window });                              // no window: headless
using var swapchain = device.CreateSwapchain(vsync: true);
using var loop = device.CreateFrameLoop(swapchain);

GraphicsDeviceOptions.Backend chooses the API; when it is null the platform's is used (GraphicsDevice.DefaultBackend: Metal on macOS, Vulkan elsewhere; APOGEE_GRAPHICS=vulkan|metal overrides it for development). TryCreate returns the reason instead of throwing, for a machine without a usable GPU or driver (GraphicsException is what the creation functions throw). GraphicsDevice.EnumerateDevices lists every GPU with the reasons it cannot be used. device.Name, Kind, Backend, ShaderBackend and the capabilities (SupportsBc, SupportsAstc, SupportsAnisotropy, MaxSamplerAnisotropy) are portable; device.ValidationErrorCount / TakeValidationErrors() count what the API's validation layer reported, which is how the tests fail on any validation error.

docs.title: Other backends
docs.text: Direct3D 12 is not planned: Vulkan already covers Windows (AMD, NVIDIA and Intel ship Vulkan 1.3 drivers), Linux and the Steam Deck. The seam does not rule one out (push constants of 128 bytes fit root constants, the bindless heap maps to a descriptor heap, the render graph's states are abstract, and the shader bundle reserves a slot for DXIL), but the engine's shaders read buffers through pointers (device addresses), which HLSL does not have.

docs.title: The Metal backend
docs.text:
Status: written, never run on a GPU (help wanted). It compiles, the shim builds on macOS CI, Apple's compiler accepts every shader, and the native bindings are tested; GitHub's macOS runners have no Metal 3 GPU, so the device, rendering and swapchain code has not run.

Apogee.Graphics.Metal is the default on macOS. It needs macOS 15, Metal 3 and tier 2 argument buffers, which is Apple silicon and the Intel Macs of 2017 and later; EnumerateDevices says why a GPU does not qualify. Metal is Objective-C, so it is reached through a small C API, Native/metal_c (see ThirdParty/README.md), bound by Apogee.Native.Metal. Nothing Objective-C crosses it: objects are opaque handles, and completion is a shared event's value rather than a block.

Portable Metal GpuBuffer MTLBuffer: shared (mapped for life) for upload and readback; device-local is private, filled through a staging buffer. Its Address is gpuAddress, which is what the push constants carry GpuImage, ImageView, GpuSampler MTLTexture and MTLSamplerState; PixelFormat is mapped by a table in the shim BindlessHeap one argument buffer: 16 384 texture gpuResourceIDs, then 256 sampler ids, 8 bytes each (slot 0 is a white texel and a linear-repeat sampler) CommandRecorder an MTLCommandBuffer; the render, compute or blit encoder a command needs is opened on demand and ended by the next kind of command or by a barrier Pipeline MTLRenderPipelineState / MTLComputePipelineState from the bundle's MSL (compiled with newLibraryWithSource when loaded); a compute pipeline's thread-group size comes from Slang's reflection Swapchain, FrameLoop a CAMetalLayer (SDL creates it for a WindowOptions.Metal window) and an MTLSharedEvent as the timeline, with the same frames in flight as Vulkan

Two things differ from Vulkan and shape the code:

  • Residency. Buffers are reached by address and textures by the argument buffer, so Metal does not know the GPU uses them. Every buffer and texture is added to one MTLResidencySet when it is made (this is why macOS 15 is the minimum), and the set is committed before a submission when something was added.
  • Hazards. Metal does not order what shaders reach through an address. Encoders are chained with an MTLFence (each waits for the one before), which is what the render graph's barriers mean on Metal. Image layouts do not exist, so Barrier only ends the current encoder.

Not done yet: GPU timings (FrameLoop.Timings is empty on Metal), Metal's binary archive cache for compiled shader libraries. The Metal tests (MetalBackendTests, and every shared GPU test when the device is Metal) skip without a qualifying GPU, unless APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1. How to check a build on a Mac: Metal on a Mac; the open tasks: Help wanted.

docs.title: The Vulkan backend: instance and device
docs.text:
GraphicsDevice.Create makes a VulkanInstance and, for a window, its VkSurfaceKHR (through SDL), and the VulkanDevice owns both; a caller that keeps its own instance uses VulkanDevice.Create(instance, options).

VulkanInstance asks for Vulkan 1.3, turns on the Khronos validation layer when it is installed (APOGEE_VULKAN_VALIDATION=0 turns it off, =1 makes a missing layer an error), and installs a debug messenger: warnings and errors from the layers and the driver go to the log, and ErrorCount / TakeErrors() count them. On macOS the loader's portability enumeration is enabled so MoltenVK is listed.

The device picks the best GPU that meets the engine's baseline: Vulkan 1.3 with dynamic rendering, synchronization2, maintenance4, buffer device addresses, timeline semaphores and descriptor indexing (runtime arrays, partially bound, sampled images update after bind, non-uniform indexing), plus a graphics and compute queue that can present to the window when one is given. Discrete GPUs win over integrated ones, then virtual, then software. PreferredDeviceName or APOGEE_GPU=llvmpipe picks by name (a substring), and a GPU that fails the baseline is skipped with its reason.

The device owns the VMA allocator (created with bufferDeviceAddress; VMA loads Vulkan through the device's own entry points), and VulkanDevice.SetDebugName names objects for the validation layer and RenderDoc.

docs.title: Buffers, images, samplers
docs.text:
All GPU memory comes from VMA through three small classes. GpuBuffer always gets a device address (buffer.Address), which is how shaders reach buffers: a pointer in push constants, no descriptors. MemoryKind says where it lives: DeviceLocal (fastest, filled by copying), Upload (the CPU writes it, the GPU reads it; mapped for its whole life) and Readback.

using GpuBuffer vertices = device.CreateBuffer(vertexBytes, BufferUsage.Storage, "mesh vertices");   // uploads through staging
using GpuBuffer perFrame = device.CreateBuffer(256, BufferUsage.Uniform, MemoryKind.Upload);
perFrame.Write(frameConstants);

using GpuImage albedo = device.CreateImage(new ImageDescription(PixelFormat.R8G8B8A8Srgb, 1024, 1024, ImageUsage.Sampled, MipLevels: 11));
device.UploadImage(albedo, texels, regions, ImageState.ShaderRead);

GpuImage knows its description, has a view of everything (the depth aspect only, for depth-stencil formats) and makes extra views for one mip or layer. Memory from VMA is not zeroed. UploadBuffer, UploadImage, ReadBuffer and ReadImage go through staging and wait for the GPU: they are for loading, tools and tests, not for every frame (per-frame data goes in Upload buffers). ImmediateContext (device.Immediate.Submit(recorder => …)) is the same machinery for your own one-off GPU work, and is safe from several threads.

docs.title: Resource states and barriers
docs.text: An image or buffer is always in one ImageState / BufferState (ShaderRead, ColorAttachment, StorageReadWrite, …), and ResourceStates.Describe maps each to the Vulkan layout, pipeline stages and access mask. CommandRecorder.Barriers records any number of transitions as one synchronization2 vkCmdPipelineBarrier2; the render graph computes them from what each pass declares. recorder.Label("Shadow pass") opens a named group that shows up in RenderDoc and in validation messages.

docs.title: The bindless heap
docs.text: Every pipeline has the same layout: descriptor set 0 is device.Bindless, three big arrays (sampled images, samplers, storage images, partially bound and update-after-bind) that shaders index with integers, plus 128 bytes of push constants. AddSampledImage(image) returns the index to read it with, RemoveSampledImage frees it for reuse. Slot 0 of the images and samplers is a white texel and a linear repeat sampler, so an unset index still reads something sane.

docs.title: Shaders
docs.text:
Shaders are Slang. In development they are compiled at run time by ShaderCompiler; a shipped game never loads the compiler: its shaders were compiled ahead of time by the importer (below) and are loaded from their artifacts. ShaderCompiler targets Vulkan 1.3 (SPIR-V 1.6) or Metal (below) with row-major matrices, and entry points keep their names.

var compiler = new ShaderCompiler(new ShaderCompilerOptions { SearchPaths = [shaderFolder], CacheDirectory = cacheFolder });
CompiledShader shader = compiler.CompileFile(Path.Combine(shaderFolder, "tonemap.slang"));   // throws ShaderCompileException with file:line
using Pipeline pipeline = device.CreateComputePipeline(shader.Code("main"), "tonemap");     // the code of the compiler's backend, as the device runs it

A CompiledShader has the code of each entry point for one backend (Spirv(entry), Msl(entry) or Code(entry) for a pipeline), Slang's reflection of the program as JSON, warnings, and the list of files it read. CompileSource(name, text) compiles text. The cache (CacheDirectory) keeps SPIR-V between runs (the Vulkan build only): an entry is named by a hash of the source, the options and the Slang version, and remembers the hash of every file the compile read, so editing an imported module invalidates it. A corrupt or unwritable cache only costs a recompile. Compiles are serialized process-wide: Slang's global session is not safe to use from two threads at once.

docs.title: Compiled ahead of time: ShaderBundle
docs.text:
Apogee.Runtime --import <folder> compiles every .slang module that has a [shader(…)] entry point into imported/<path>.ashader (the importer is ShaderImporter in Apogee.Rendering, see Asset import). A bundle holds one or more variants of the module, each the module compiled with one set of preprocessor defines (the variant without defines is always there; more are listed in the shader's .import.xml), and for each variant its reflection and the code of every entry point per backend. The importer writes SPIR-V and Metal shading language into the same file; a reader takes the code of the backend of its device (ShaderBundle.Read(…, backend), ShaderLibrary.Load(path, backend: device.ShaderBackend)) and skips the others, and the format reserves DXIL (Direct3D 12). A shader that does not compile for every backend fails the import, so it is found on the author's machine and not on a Mac. Specialization constants need no variant: they stay in the SPIR-V and are in the reflection (pipelines do not set them yet).

A bundle records ShaderAbi.Version (2: it added the Metal code and the bindless parameter block), which is bumped when the shared pipeline layout below changes, on any backend, and an engine refuses a bundle of another version with "import it again" instead of crashing in the driver. That matters for mods, which may ship their own compiled shaders (a mod's folder imported with --import; mod://id/imported).

ShaderCache stores its entries as bundles, so there is one format on disk.

docs.title: Metal: the same shaders
docs.text:
ShaderCompilerOptions.Backend = ShaderBackend.Msl makes the compiler produce Metal shading language source instead of SPIR-V (text, so any machine can make it; the Metal driver compiles it when the shader is loaded). It is the same Slang source for both backends, which is why the engine's shaders follow a few rules, checked by MetalShaderTests:

  • Buffers are pointers (Foo* in the push constants), which Slang writes as device Foo* in MSL: nothing to change.
  • The push constants are Metal buffer 0 (setBytes), and the bindless textures and samplers are one argument buffer, buffer 1. In Slang they are ParameterBlock<BindlessResources> gBindless (arrays of 16 384 textures and 256 samplers, which on Vulkan come out as exactly the engine's bindless descriptor set 0, bindings 0 and 1), with gTextures and gSamplers as macros for its members. Metal has no descriptor sets and Slang numbers buffers in declaration order, so the compiler defines APOGEE_METAL for the Metal build only, and the shaders pin the indices with : register(b0) / : register(b1) (PUSH_SLOT, BINDLESS_SLOT in common.slang). The Vulkan build never sees those annotations: the same register annotations changed the SPIR-V's bindings and crashed lavapipe.
  • No other buffer, texture or sampler is bound directly: everything else is reached through an address or an index.

AppleCompilesEveryEngineShaderToMetal hands every entry point to Apple's compiler (xcrun metal -c) when it runs on a Mac with Xcode; the macOS CI job requires it. Slang's reflection is that of the SPIR-V build; the bundle keeps the first backend's.

All pipelines share one layout (the bindless set and 128 bytes of push constants), so a pipeline is just shaders plus state. CreateGraphicsPipeline takes a GraphicsPipelineDescription: geometry is pulled from buffers by the vertex shader (no vertex input state), depth is reverse-Z (near plane = 1, so the compare is greater-or-equal, and the clear value is 0), blending is one of Opaque, Alpha, Premultiplied, Additive, and rendering is dynamic rendering into attachments of the given formats.

Buffers are reached through pointers: put a buffer's Address in the push constants and read it in Slang as a pointer.

struct Push { float* output; uint count; float scale; };
[[vk::push_constant]] ConstantBuffer<Push> push;

[shader("compute")] [numthreads(64, 1, 1)]
void main(uint3 id : SV_DispatchThreadID) { if (id.x < push.count) push.output[id.x] = id.x * push.scale; }

recorder.BindPipeline(pipeline);                  // also binds the bindless set
recorder.PushConstants(new Push { Output = buffer.Address, Count = n, Scale = 0.5f });
recorder.Dispatch((n + 63) / 64);

For drawing, BeginRendering(width, height, colorTargets, depthTarget) starts a pass and sets viewport and scissor, Draw/DrawIndexed draw, EndRendering ends it; images are moved to ColorAttachment/DepthAttachment with Barriers first.

docs.title: Swapchain and the frame loop
docs.text:
using var swapchain = device.CreateSwapchain(vsync: true);
using var loop = device.CreateFrameLoop(swapchain);

while (!window.CloseRequested)
{
    PlatformHost.PumpEvents();
    Frame? frame = loop.BeginFrame();           // null: minimized, or the swapchain was just recreated
    if (frame is null) continue;

    Backbuffer back = frame.Backbuffer!.Value;   // starts in ImageState.Undefined
    using (frame.Scope("Clear"))
    {
        frame.Recorder.Barrier(new ImageBarrier(back.Image, ImageState.Undefined, ImageState.ColorAttachment));
        frame.Recorder.BeginRendering(back.Width, back.Height, [new ColorTarget(back.View, Clear: true)]);
        frame.Recorder.EndRendering();
        frame.Recorder.Barrier(new ImageBarrier(back.Image, ImageState.ColorAttachment, ImageState.Present));
    }
    loop.EndFrame(frame);                        // submits, then presents
}
loop.WaitIdle();

Swapchain picks a UNORM format (B8G8R8A8 or R8G8B8A8; shaders write sRGB-encoded values themselves, which lets the dev overlay draw onto it directly), FIFO presentation (mailbox or immediate without vsync), and the window's size. A resized window, an out-of-date or suboptimal result all recreate it; a minimized window skips frames. Present semaphores are per image, so one is never signalled while an earlier present still waits on it.

FrameLoop keeps two frames in flight. Each has its own command pool and buffer, upload arena, timer queries and acquire semaphore, and one timeline semaphore counts finished submissions, so BeginFrame waits only for the frame that used its slot two frames ago. Without a swapchain it runs headless: the same frames with no window image, for screenshots, tests and servers.

  • frame.Allocate(size) gives per-frame host-visible memory with a GPU address (a 4 MB arena per frame, reset when the slot is reused): per-draw constants, instance data. It is valid until the GPU finishes the frame.
  • frame.Defer(resource) disposes something once the GPU has finished the frame, which is how a transient resource a frame's commands use is freed.
  • frame.Scope("Shadow pass") is a RenderDoc debug label plus a GPU timer; loop.Timings lists the sections of the most recent finished frame in order, with their GPU milliseconds.

The window tests open a real window, so they only run with APOGEE_WINDOW_TESTS=1 ./build.sh test.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: The GPU tests share one device and fail on any validation error. They skip without a GPU, unless APOGEE_REQUIRE_VULKAN=1 (CI, on lavapipe) or, with the Metal backend, APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1. Run them on a specific GPU with APOGEE_GPU=nvidia ./build.sh test or APOGEE_GPU=llvmpipe ./build.sh test.

docs.title: Metal
docs.text:
The Metal backend (Graphics) was written without a Mac in front of the developer, and has never run on a GPU. The macOS jobs of the CI build it on every push and run the tests that can run there; a Mac that meets the baseline can check the rest. This page is for whoever has one, and the open tasks are in Help wanted.

Needs: macOS 15 or later, and a Mac with Metal 3 and tier 2 argument buffers: an Apple silicon Mac, or an Intel Mac from 2017 on with a recent GPU. The same checks apply to both.

docs.title: What CI does
docs.text:
• Builds metal_c (the Objective-C shim), the bindings and the backend, and runs the native binding tests (Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests) against the real library.
  • Compiles every engine shader's Metal shading language with Apple's own compiler (xcrun metal -c; AppleCompilesEveryEngineShaderToMetal).
  • Runs Apogee.Runtime --gpu-info. If the runner's GPU meets the baseline (the line metal: … ok), the GPU tests are required to run on it (APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1); if not, they skip and the log says why.
  • Does all of this on an Apple-silicon runner and an Intel one, and uploads each NativeAOT build as the artifact apogee-osx-arm64 / apogee-osx-x64. When the probe finds a qualifying GPU it also renders the fixture game on Metal (uploaded as metal-screenshots-*).

docs.title: Checking on a Mac
docs.text:
Clone the repository, download the artifact for your Mac (apogee-osx-arm64 or apogee-osx-x64) from the CI run and unzip it into Bin/publish (so that Bin/publish/runtime exists). A downloaded binary needs chmod +x Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime and xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine Bin/publish first. Then, from the repository's root:

Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime --gpu-info                       # which GPUs, and whether they qualify; send this line first
Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime --game Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame --user /tmp/game-user --headless --size 640x360 --frames 10 --screenshot game.png
Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime --run Samples/Scripting/main.luau --headless --size 640x360 --frames 30 --screenshot scripting.png   # a sample, run by hand
Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime --luau-test Tests/Luau

Then a window, which tests the swapchain: run the lighting sample (./build.sh aot-viewer, then Bin/publish/viewer/Apogee.Samples.Viewer) and look at it for a few seconds (fly with the mouse and WASD; resize the window).

Report (an issue, or a pull request with the fix) the output of --gpu-info, the PNGs, and anything printed in the terminal. There are no reference images: a few pixels of difference at edges between GPUs is the rasterizer, a black or garbled image is a bug.

To run the engine's tests from a checkout instead: APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1 ./build.sh test (a missing or unqualified GPU is then a failure, not a skip).

docs.title: What is not covered
docs.text:
GPU timings (Timings is empty on Metal: Metal samples counters only at encoder boundaries, and not on every GPU) and a binary archive cache for shader libraries.

The images are compared with the references that Mesa's software rasterizer made, so the Metal tests allow a mean difference of 2 (worst channel 64) instead of Vulkan's 0.5 (24); APOGEE_IMAGE_TOLERANCE=<mean> sets it. These numbers are a guess until a real Mac has measured the difference: report the "mean difference" lines, and the bound can be tightened (or the Metal reference images split off).

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text: The renderer is built on Graphics: a render graph, the Forward+ lighting pipeline and the dev overlay.

docs.title: The render graph
docs.text:
A frame's rendering is a graph of passes over images and buffers. A pass says how it uses each resource; the graph works out what runs, where the memory comes from, and every barrier. You build a new graph every frame (it is cheap); the memory persists in a pool.

using var pool = new TransientPool(device);                       // lives as long as the renderer

void RenderFrame(Frame frame, Backbuffer back)
{
    var graph = new RenderGraph(device, pool);
    ImageHandle backbuffer = graph.ImportBackbuffer(back);        // starts undefined, ends ready to present
    ImageHandle hdr = graph.CreateImage("HDR color", new ImageDescription(PixelFormat.R16G16B16A16Sfloat, back.Width, back.Height,
        ImageUsage.ColorAttachment | ImageUsage.Sampled));

    graph.AddPass("Scene", PassType.Graphics, pass =>
    {
        pass.WriteColor(hdr, clear: new Vector4(0, 0, 0, 1));     // the graph begins and ends the rendering
        pass.Execute(ctx => DrawScene(ctx.Recorder));
    });
    graph.AddPass("Tonemap", PassType.Graphics, pass =>
    {
        pass.ReadSampled(hdr);
        pass.WriteColor(backbuffer, clear: Vector4.Zero);
        pass.Execute(ctx => Tonemap(ctx.Recorder, ctx.Image(hdr).SampledIndex));    // the bindless index to read it by
    });
    graph.Execute(frame);
}

Declaring. AddPass(name, type, setup) runs setup immediately; it declares uses on the PassBuilder and sets the callback that records the commands (pass.Execute). Images: ReadSampled, WriteColor, WriteDepth, ReadDepth, WriteStorage, ReadWriteStorage, CopyFrom, CopyTo. Buffers: Read, Write, ReadWrite, CopyFrom, CopyTo. The difference between write and read-write matters: a write replaces everything (so whatever wrote it earlier is no longer needed, and a fresh transient can be written first), a read-write needs the previous contents. Attachments are begun and ended by the graph for graphics passes, with clear (give a value) or load (give none); depth is reverse-Z, so its default clear is 0. A pass the graph cannot see the effect of calls NoCull().

Compiling (graph.Compile(), done by Execute if you did not) is pure and needs no GPU:

  1. Culling. Walking back from the outputs (the backbuffer, and imports marked output: true), a pass runs only if it writes something that is needed; what it reads becomes needed. A pass that overwrites a resource completely makes earlier writers of it unneeded.
  2. Validation. A read of something no earlier pass wrote is a RenderGraphException, as are one resource used two ways in a pass, attachments of different sizes, and attachments in a compute pass.
  3. Memory. Transients whose lifetimes do not overlap and whose descriptions are equal share one image (buffers: equal size and usage).
  4. Barriers. In front of each pass, one batched barrier brings each resource from its last state to the one the pass declared. Reading a resource again in the same state needs none; anything after a write does, even in the same state. Imported resources leave in the state you gave (Present for the backbuffer). graph.Plan describes the result (ToString() prints it for the dev overlay).

Executing. Each live pass runs inside frame.Scope(name), so it is a RenderDoc label and a GPU timer. PassContext resolves handles: ctx.Image(h) gives the VkImage, view, size and, for transients created with Sampled / Storage usage, the bindless index to read or write it by; ctx.Buffer(h) gives the GpuBuffer (use .Address in push constants).

Transients come from TransientPool, one set per frame in flight, so a steady-state frame allocates nothing; resources unused for eight frames are freed. A transient image with Sampled or Storage usage keeps its bindless slot for as long as it lives. Limits: images are tracked as a whole (every mip and layer in one state), transients have one mip and no multisampling, and everything runs on the one queue.

new RenderGraph() without a device can only be compiled, which is how the planner is unit tested.

docs.title: Where shaders come from: ShaderLibrary
docs.text: Renderers get their shaders from a ShaderLibrary (SceneRenderer(device, shaders); the default is ShaderLibrary.Standard(cacheDirectory), the Shaders folder next to the program mounted as shaders://). Load("shaders://forward.slang") takes the compiled artifact when the folder was imported (imported/forward.slang.ashader, made by Apogee.Runtime --import, which ./build.sh aot runs on the published programs) and never touches the Slang compiler. A module without an artifact is compiled (development), if the compiler library is there; if it is not, the error says to import the folder. A mod's shaders are loaded the same way from mod://id/… and its own imported/.

docs.title: Rebuilding pipelines when a shader changes
docs.text:
ShaderLibrary.NotifyChanged(paths) takes the virtual paths of changed files (HotReloader.ShadersChanged reports them, or a VfsWatcher over the shaders' folders) and raises ModulesChanged with the modules it had loaded that are one of those files or were made from one (the files a compile read are in CompiledShader.Dependencies, the artifact's in the index), so an edit to common.slang reaches every shader that imports it. SceneRenderer and ImGuiRenderer keep their pipelines in ReloadablePipelines<T> groups, one per shader module (the two cluster shaders are one group), and only the groups that use a changed module are rebuilt:

  1. Off the render thread. The change starts a build on another thread: the module is compiled through the library and the pipelines are made (pipeline creation needs no external synchronization). The frame is not held up; the renderer keeps drawing with the pipelines it has. Changes that arrive during a build start one more right after it.
  2. Swapped at a frame boundary. Render (or AddPasses) calls Apply(frame) first: if a build has finished, its pipelines become the current ones there, so a frame never mixes old and new.
  3. Destroyed when the GPU is done. The old pipelines go through frame.Defer, which frees them when that frame's slot comes round again, after the frames that used them have completed. The tests record several frames without waiting, rebuild in the middle, and the validation layer must stay silent (it does not when the old pipelines are destroyed at once).
  4. A shader that does not compile changes nothing. The old pipelines stay, the error (file, line, message) is logged and held in ShaderLibrary.Errors for the dev overlay, and the next edit that compiles clears it. Pipelines that are made lazily per target format are made again for the formats already seen, in the same build.

The runtime's --watch mounts the shaders' source folders when it runs from the repository, and the viewer's --watch does the same, so saving a .slang file changes the picture of the running program.

docs.title: Forward+
docs.text:
SceneRenderer draws a RenderScene (a ModelData on the GPU) with a Camera, using a render graph it builds every frame.

using var renderer = new SceneRenderer(device, cacheDirectory: shaderCache);     // loads the shaders in <program>/Shaders (compiled ahead of time, else compiled now)
using RenderScene scene = renderer.CreateScene(GltfLoader.Load("Sponza.gltf", options));
var camera = new Camera { Position = new Vector3(0, 2, 8) };
camera.LookAt(Vector3.Zero);

Frame frame = loop.BeginFrame()!;
renderer.Render(frame, scene, camera, RenderTarget.Window(frame.Backbuffer!.Value), new RenderSettings { Exposure = 1f });
loop.EndFrame(frame);

The frame. Depth prepass (opaque and alpha-masked geometry into a reverse-Z D32 image) → Build clusters (only when the projection changed) → Cull lights → Forward (PBR into an RGBA16F image, opaque and masked, then blended surfaces far to near, depth-tested against the prepass) → Tonemap (exposure, the Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapper, and the sRGB transfer function, into the target). renderer.LastPlan is the graph and LastStats the draw, light and cluster counts.

Clusters. The view is cut into 16 x 9 cells over the screen and 24 slices in depth, spaced exponentially between the camera's Near and ClusterFar (a slice is thin close to the camera and long far away, so every cell holds a similar amount of space as seen from the eye). A compute shader builds each cluster's view-space box; another tests every light's sphere against every box and keeps at most 64 lights per cluster in a fixed-size list, so there are no atomics and nothing to clear. The forward shader finds the pixel's cluster from its screen position and depth and loops over only those lights. ClusterGrid has the same arithmetic on the CPU. A cluster's bounds are per frame-in-flight and are rebuilt only when the projection changes. Spot lights are culled by their bounding sphere (the cone is applied when shading).

Lighting. glTF metallic-roughness materials with Cook-Torrance GGX: Smith visibility, Schlick Fresnel, Lambert diffuse, base color, metallic-roughness, normal, occlusion and emissive textures with KHR_texture_transform, alpha mask and blend, double-sided, and unlit. Lights are point and spot (RenderScene.Lights, editable every frame; intensity is candela, falling off as the inverse square and reaching zero exactly at the light's radius, which is its glTF range or where it fades below a faint threshold) plus one directional sun (SunDirection, SunColor) and a two-colour ambient. No shadows and no image-based lighting yet, so a smooth metal reflects only the lights. RenderSettings.Debug = DebugView.ClusterLights tints each pixel by its cluster's light count (dark: none; blue to red: one to eight or more).

Conventions. Right-handed, +Y up, a camera looking down -Z at yaw 0. Reverse-Z with an infinite far plane: depth 1 at the near plane, 0 at infinity, compare greater-or-equal. The projection flips y (Vulkan's normalized y points down), which keeps the image and so the winding: front faces are counter-clockwise, as in glTF. Matrices are row-major and used with row vectors, as in System.Numerics.

Culling. Before the passes are recorded, every draw's bounds (the mesh's box carried to the camera's axes, written each frame into six float arrays together with the instance) are tested against the camera's view volume (Frustum: left, right, bottom, top and the near plane; the far plane is at infinity) with SIMD, and only the draws inside go into the depth and forward passes. It is exact for the planes, so it never drops a draw that touches the view and may keep one near a corner that is not visible. LastStats.Culled counts what was left out, RenderSettings.CullDraws = false turns it off to compare (CullingTests requires the same picture either way, and that a camera turned away culls everything). The measurements and the instruction set shipped games are built for are in Profiling and SIMD. The per-pass lists of draws are reused from frame to frame instead of allocated.

A double-precision world, rendered camera-relative. Camera.Position and RenderScene.Origin are Double3 (see Math): renderer.CreateScene(model, at: new Double3(5_000_000, 0, 2_000_000)) puts a model 5 000 km out, and the model's own coordinates (instances, lights, bounds) stay relative to that origin. Nothing on the GPU is in world coordinates. Each frame:

  • Camera.View has the camera at the origin (rotation only; camera.WorldToView(point) takes a world point there, subtracting in double first);
  • the renderer writes the frame slot's instance records with their translation (placement position - camera.Position) + offset, subtracted in double and then narrowed, so a scene 10 000 km away is as precise as one at the origin (the instance buffer is per frame in flight, like the cluster buffers, and grows when a frame needs more; the matrices' linear part is stored once at load);
  • lights and the blend sort are moved the same way, and GpuFrameData.CameraPosition is zero, which the shaders (that subtract it from a surface position) need no change for.

ForwardPlusTests.TheSceneLooksTheSameFarFromTheWorldsOrigin renders the golden scene at the origin, at 100 km and at 10 000 km and requires the same picture.

Data for the shaders. One GpuFrameData per frame (in the frame's upload arena) holds the matrices, the screen, the sun, and the addresses of the instance (rewritten every frame), light and cluster buffers; a draw pushes the frame's address, the instance number and the addresses of the vertices and materials of its model (a model has buffers of its own). Shaders/common.slang is the Slang side of GpuStructs.cs; the structs use only 16-byte aligned members (and the vertex is twelve explicit floats) so that every layout rule agrees, and tests pin the sizes and offsets.

Tests. The planner and the math run without a GPU. On a GPU: a GPU-vs-CPU comparison of the light lists of all 3456 clusters (every light that is inside by a margin must be listed, every listed light inside by a margin), the sky tone-mapped exactly like the CPU twin, lights brighten what they should and nothing beyond their radius, spot cones, the sun, alpha mask and blend, double-sided surfaces, the heatmap, the 64-light cap, 600 lights, and a golden image rendered by the software rasterizer (Golden/forward_plus.png; APOGEE_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 rewrites it). The discrete GPU matches it to a mean of 0.02 out of 255.

docs.title: Drawing a world of entities
docs.text:
A RenderScene is one model with its own lights. A game draws entities: any number of models, each placed by an entity, lit by light entities, seen through a camera entity. The pieces:

  • GpuModel is a ModelData on the GPU: its vertex, index and material buffers, its textures in the bindless heap, and a record per mesh instance (ModelNode: its matrices without the translation, its box, its first index). It is placed any number of times at no cost but one instance record per mesh. renderer.CreateModel(data) makes one; a RenderScene is a GpuModel plus an origin, a sun and lights.
  • ModelLibrary gives models ids: Load(path) returns the same id for the same path, however many entities show it, and reads the model through the virtual file system (imported .amodel when there is one). Ids exist before there is a GPU, because a game's scripts run before the renderer is made: the model is read and uploaded the first time a frame needs it (Attach(renderer, caps) says where), a file that does not load is logged once and draws nothing, and Reload(path) swaps a changed file in under the same id (the runtime does it for the --watch run, after the importer). Detach() frees the GPU side before the device goes. Scripts see the library as the global models: models:load("res://packages/car/car.glb"). It reads any mounted path, as audio does: the engine's classes do not know which mod called them.
  • Components (Components.cs, all visible to scripts and, later, the editor): ModelRenderer { Model } draws the model at the entity's WorldTransform (position, rotation and scale place every mesh); Light { Color, Intensity, Range, InnerCone, OuterCone, Kind } is a point, spot or (kind 0) directional light shining along the entity's -Z, and the first directional one is the sun; CameraComponent { FovDegrees, Near, ClusterFar } is a lens, and the entity that also has the MainCamera tag is the eye. The lights a model came with move with its entity.
  • RenderWorld(world, models) reads those entities when a frame is rendered (queries over WorldTransform, so what the systems moved this frame is what is drawn; nothing is copied or kept in sync) and SceneRenderer.Render(frame, renderWorld, camera, target) draws it. renderWorld.TryGetMainCamera(camera) fills a Camera from the main camera entity (roll is ignored: yaw, then pitch). DefaultSunDirection, DefaultSunColor and the ambient colours are what a world without a directional light uses.

Both kinds of scene go through one renderer core. It gathers placements (a model, a double-precision position, a rotation, a scale) and lights, writes one GpuInstance per mesh instance with the placement's rotation and scale composed in (normals take S^-1 * R, so non-uniform scale lights correctly) and its translation relative to the camera, builds the boxes from the same numbers, culls, and draws by pass. A draw binds its model's index buffer when the model changes and pushes the model's vertex and material addresses, so many models share one frame without sharing buffers.

In the runtime. --game and --run draw the world through its main camera when it has one, with the ImGui frame over it; the scene renderer is not even made (and its shaders not compiled) until then, so a script that only has panels keeps drawing them over the plain background, exactly as before. Without a GPU (--headless without --screenshot) ids and entities exist and nothing is drawn.

local Transform, ModelRenderer = world:component("Transform"), world:component("ModelRenderer")
local CameraComponent, MainCamera = world:component("CameraComponent"), world:component("MainCamera")

local car = models:load("res://packages/garage/car.glb")
local e = world:create_entity("car")
world:set(e, Transform, { Position = Vector3(0, 0, 0), Rotation = Quat.identity, Scale = Vector3(1, 1, 1) })
world:set(e, ModelRenderer, { Model = car })

local eye = world:create_entity("eye")
world:set(eye, Transform, { Position = Vector3(0, 1.5, 6), Rotation = Quat.identity, Scale = Vector3(1, 1, 1) })
world:set(eye, CameraComponent, { FovDegrees = 60, Near = 0.05, ClusterFar = 100 })
world:add(eye, MainCamera)

RenderWorldTests check, on a GPU, that an entity draws what a scene of the same model draws, that five entities share one model (draw counts), that scale and rotation place the model, that lights and the sun light the world, that an unknown or removed id draws nothing, that a model 3 000 km out looks the same as at the origin, that the main camera entity drives the camera, and that models load once per path and reload in place; WorldRenderingTests run a game folder with a model, a light and a camera through --headless --screenshot.

docs.title: Debug drawing
docs.text:
DebugDraw (in Apogee.Core, so anything can add to it without knowing about rendering) is immediate mode: lines and triangles in double-precision world positions that live for one frame. Line, Triangle, Box (turned, or from two corners), Circle, Sphere, Arrow and Axes add them; colors are bytes r, g, b, a as a uint (DebugColor.Rgba, DebugColor.Red, ...). It keeps at most Capacity (a million) lines and as many triangles and counts the rest in Dropped, so a loop that draws too much costs detail, not memory. Physics adds to it with PhysicsWorld.DrawDebug (physics); scripts use the debug_draw library (debug_draw.line(from, to, color), box, sphere, arrow, axes; a color is a vector of red, green and blue from 0 to 1, white without one), called every frame for as long as the picture should stay.

RenderSettings.DebugDraw is the instance to draw; the renderer reads it and does not clear it (whoever fills it clears it: the runtime does after every frame). When it is not empty a pass, Debug draw, is added between the forward pass and tone mapping: it loads the HDR image, depth-tests against the scene's depth without writing it, and so draws over the lit picture before exposure and the tone mapper, which is why a color means what it says (debug_draw.slang takes the colors as sRGB and the tone mapper encodes them back).

  • Lines are quads of two triangles, widened to RenderSettings.DebugLineWidth pixels (1.5 by default) in the vertex shader: hardware line width is not portable (Metal has none). A quad cannot be left to the clipper, so the shader cuts a line at the near plane itself, and a line wholly behind the camera is not drawn. The part of a line that is behind something is drawn again without the depth test, at DebugHiddenAlpha (0.25; 0 hides it).
  • Triangles are drawn solid with flat shading from a light at the eye, so a face looking at the camera is bright and one seen edge-on is dim.
  • Camera-relative, like the scene: DebugDrawRenderer writes the positions as offsets from the camera, subtracting in double first, so a line 3 000 km out lands on the same pixels as one at the origin (DebugDrawRenderingTests render both). The buffers are per frame in flight and grow when a frame needs more.

DebugDrawRenderingTests read pixels back: a line is a stripe of its color and a wider one covers more, hidden parts follow DebugHiddenAlpha, a line behind the camera changes nothing and one crossing the near plane is cut there, triangles are shaded, and an empty DebugDraw adds no pass.

docs.title: Native bindings
docs.text:
Raw bindings for each C library are generated by our own tool, Tools/Apogee.Build/Bindings (ClangSharp.Interop over libclang). Output goes to Source/Apogee.Native.<Lib>/Generated/ and is committed; nothing in Generated/ is edited by hand.

./build.sh bindings           # all libraries
./build.sh bindings sdl flecs # some

Each library has a JSON config in Tools/Apogee.Build/Bindings/Configs/: headers and include directories, ownDirs (declarations found elsewhere are foreign and not bound), prefixes and suffixes to strip, renames, macro groups that become [Flags] enums, and regexes for functions and constants to leave out. What was skipped, and why, is written to Bin/bindings/<lib>.skipped.txt.

A config can name a type that another binding defines (foreignTypes, a regex on C names mapped to a namespace): it is then referenced and not bound again, by the name that binding gives it (the same stripPrefixes and renames, as rmlui.json and cimgui.json have). Enum members lose the common prefix they share with their enum (JPH_MotionType_Static is MotionType.Static), and members whose C name starts with an underscore (_JPH_MotionType_Count, _JPH_MotionType_Force32: reserved names, not values) are left out.

Vulkan is generated from the Khronos registry ("kind": "vulkan") rather than headers, and loads commands through vkGetInstanceProcAddr into VkGlobalCommands, VkInstanceCommands and VkDeviceCommands.

Steamworks ("kind": "steam") is generated from Valve's steam_api.json and the S_API declarations of its flat API, because the headers are C++: the config names the interfaces to bind (interfaces) and the core functions (includeFunctions). libclang parses the headers only to measure the structs, once with Linux's 4-byte callback packing and once as Windows (8), and the structs whose size differs are emitted with Pack = SteamPack.Callback (Native libraries).

docs.title: What is generated
docs.text: Blittable structs, unmanaged function pointers for callbacks, opaque handles as readonly structs, DllImports with ExactSpelling (runtime marshalling is disabled in every binding assembly), a module initializer that registers the library with NativeLibraries, and a Sizes table of every struct's C size.

docs.title: Build defines
docs.text: The headers are read with the defines the native library is built with ("defines" in the config, and the same ones in Native/<lib>/CMakeLists.txt). Struct layouts can depend on them: Flecs has more fields in ecs_ref_t and ecs_map_t in a debug build, so its binding is generated with FLECS_NDEBUG and the library is always compiled with it. The struct size test cannot catch this, because it compares with what clang saw, not with the compiled library; FlecsRefsHaveTheLayoutOfTheCompiledLibrary calls a function that returns such a struct by value.

docs.title: Exported variables
docs.text:
extern variables (extern const ecs_entity_t EcsOnUpdate;) become ref properties that look the symbol up by name the first time they are used, so the value is always the library's, filled in by its init function:

ulong phase = Ecs.OnUpdate;        // ref readonly ulong: the variable is const in C
Ecs.ComponentId                    // ecs_id(EcsComponent), the symbol FLECS_IDEcsComponentID_

globalRenames (regex → replacement, first match wins, applied before the usual stripping) maps odd symbol names; excludeGlobals leaves out variables the library does not export (debug-only ones, or ones declared without a definition). Arrays are not bound. A variable whose name is a function's keeps the full C name (EcsDelete next to Delete).

docs.title: Array parameters
docs.text: A C parameter written as an array (float color[4]) is a pointer to its first element: the binding takes float*, not an inline array by value (libclang reports the written type, and passing the bytes where an address is expected crashes). Fields of structs are different: they are fixed buffers or inline arrays.

docs.title: Types from another binding
docs.text:
A library whose headers use another library's types (VMA uses Vulkan's) lists them in foreignTypes: a regex on the C type name and the C# namespace of the binding assembly that has it under the same name.

"foreignTypes": { "^Vk": "Apogee.Native.Vulkan" },
"typeMap": { "VkBufferUsageFlags": "VkBufferUsageFlagBits", "VkBool32": "uint", "VkDeviceSize": "ulong" }

Those types are referenced (the generated files get a using for the namespace, and the project references the other binding), never generated again. The Vulkan binding names flags typedefs differently from C (VkBufferUsageFlags is the VkBufferUsageFlagBits enum, VkBool32 is uint), so those go in typeMap, which is looked at first. A name that the other assembly lacks is a compile error in the generated code, not a silent void*.

docs.title: Vulkan structure types
docs.text:
Every Vulkan struct that starts with sType has a parameterless constructor that sets it from the registry, so new VkRenderingInfo { … } is correct by default:

var rendering = new VkRenderingInfo { LayerCount = 1, RenderArea = area };   // SType is VkStructureType.RenderingInfo

default(T), stackalloc and arrays of the struct do not run it: set SType yourself there (or loop over the array).

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Tests/Apogee.Build.Tests runs the generator on fixture headers and on the Vulkan registry, and checks that the committed Vulkan bindings are what the generator writes now (it needs clang; the tests skip without it).

Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests checks, for every binding assembly, that every entry point resolves in the native library, that every exported variable is found, that every struct size equals the one clang computed, and calls into each library. Library assemblies are skipped, with a message, when the native library is not installed.

docs.title: Native libraries
docs.text: What is bound and how to use it. Where each library comes from and how it was built is in ThirdParty/README.md.

docs.title: Luau (Apogee.Native.Luau)
docs.text:
The VM, the compiler and the native code generator in one library, plus our layer over them, Native/luau/apogee_luau.h. Luau is built with LUA_USE_LONGJMP: an error is a longjmp to the nearest protected call, and a longjmp must never cross a managed frame. So the binding leaves out what raises an error on input a script controls: lua_error, lua_call, the luaL_check*/luaL_opt* family, lua_gettable/lua_getfield and the other calls that run metamethods, lua_yield, and lua_pushcclosurek. What is bound can raise only on a programming error (writing to a read-only table, pushing without Checkstack) or when memory runs out, and the layer deals with that one.

State* state = Lua.NewVm(memoryLimit: 64 * 1024 * 1024);          // allocator, interrupt and accounting installed
Lua.LuaLOpenlibs(state);
Lua.PushManagedFunction(state, &Add, name, 0);                       // [UnmanagedCallersOnly] static int Add(State*)
Lua.Rawsetfield(state, Lua.Globalsindex, name);
if (Lua.LoadSource(state, chunk, source, size, 0) == CallResult.Ok)  // compiles, loads, native code for --!native chunks
    result = Lua.ProtectedCall(state, 0, 1, budgetMilliseconds);     // traceback on errors, time budget, memory errors
Lua.CloseVm(state);
  • A managed function returns its number of results, or Lua.Raise with the error value on top of the stack; the wrapper turns that into lua_error once managed code has returned. Its own upvalues start at index 2 (Globalsindex - 2).
  • Memory: NewVm takes a hard limit (SetMemoryLimit changes it: set it after the libraries are open). An allocation over it fails, and Luau raises the memory error, only while Luau code is the topmost thing running. One made by a managed function, or by the host outside a call, is never refused (nothing could catch the error, or it would unwind managed code); the error is raised when the managed function returns. SetCategoryLimit is a soft limit for a memory category (Setmemcat), raised at the next call or loop iteration, which is how each script owner gets its own cap in one VM.
  • Time: the budget of ProtectedCall/ProtectedResume (or SetTimeBudget) is armed by the outermost call. Once it has passed every call and loop iteration raises, so pcall in a script cannot swallow it. A long native function (string.rep) is not interrupted.
  • Bytecode from LuauCompile is freed with Lua.Free: it comes from the library's C runtime, which is not necessarily the caller's. LoadSource keeps it inside the library.
  • Native code (--!native, Luau::CodeGen) is on where the machine supports it (x64 and arm64); NativeEnabled says. It needs executable memory: a macOS app that is signed with the hardened runtime needs the allow-jit entitlement.
  • One state belongs to one thread at a time.

docs.title: Vulkan Memory Allocator (Apogee.Native.Vma)
docs.text:
VMA suballocates GPU memory. Its binding is Vma (functions) plus Allocator, Allocation, Pool… (the opaque structs behind VMA's handles; you only hold pointers to them).

var functions = new VulkanFunctions { VkGetInstanceProcAddr = …, VkGetDeviceProcAddr = … };
var info = new AllocatorCreateInfo
{
    PhysicalDevice = physicalDevice, Device = device, Instance = instance,
    VulkanApiVersion = Vk.ApiVersion13, PVulkanFunctions = &functions,
};
Allocator* allocator;
Vma.CreateAllocator(&info, &allocator);

The library is built without static Vulkan functions: it loads the rest through the two pointers you pass, so it works with whatever Vulkan loader the process uses. Flag typedefs are the *FlagBits enums (AllocationCreateFlagBits), already [Flags].

VirtualBlock needs no GPU: it hands out offsets from a range (used for sub-allocating our own buffers, and in tests).

docs.title: meshoptimizer (Apogee.Native.Meshopt)
docs.text:
Mesh processing: vertex deduplication, vertex cache / overdraw / vertex fetch optimization, simplification, meshlets and quantization. The binding is Meshopt and keeps the C spelling of the parameters. The content loader runs every mesh through it at import: GenerateVertexRemap → RemapIndexBuffer/RemapVertexBuffer → OptimizeVertexCache → OptimizeVertexFetch.

nuint unique = Meshopt.GenerateVertexRemap(remap, indices, indexCount, vertices, vertexCount, vertexSize);
Meshopt.RemapIndexBuffer(indices, indices, indexCount, remap);
Meshopt.OptimizeVertexCache(indices, indices, indexCount, unique);

docs.title: zstd (Apogee.Native.Zstd)
docs.text:
Compression, for packs and for libktx's KTX 2 supercompression. The binding is Zstd and covers the stable API of zstd.h and zstd_errors.h: one-shot Compress/Decompress (with CompressBound and GetFrameContentSize to size the buffers), streaming through CompressStream2/DecompressStream with InBuffer/OutBuffer, contexts (CreateCCtx, CCtxSetParameter), and dictionaries (CreateCDict/CreateDDict). Functions that fail return a size that IsError recognizes; GetErrorName and GetErrorCode say what happened. The library is built with worker threads, so CParameter.NbWorkers compresses on several threads.

byte[] frame = new byte[(int)Zstd.CompressBound((nuint)data.Length)];
nuint size = Zstd.Compress(target, (nuint)frame.Length, source, (nuint)data.Length, 3);
if (Zstd.IsError(size) != 0) throw new InvalidDataException(Marshal.PtrToStringUTF8((IntPtr)Zstd.GetErrorName(size)));

Zstd.ContentSizeUnknown and ContentSizeError are what GetFrameContentSize returns for a frame that does not say its size and for non-frames. libktx links this library (they have to sit next to each other, which the build arranges), so a zstd-compressed KTX 2 file is inflated by the same code.

docs.title: FreeType (Apogee.Native.FreeType)
docs.text:
Font rasterization, for the dev tools' text now (Dear ImGui's FreeType loader) and for RmlUi's. The binding is class FT over the public headers of the modules we build: loading a face (NewMemoryFace, NewFace), sizes, glyph loading and rendering (LoadChar, RenderGlyph, with the Load… flags and the RenderMode enum: anti-aliased, light, monochrome, LCD and signed distance fields), outlines, strokes, glyph and bitmap helpers, variable fonts (ftmm) and colour tables. The names drop the FT_ prefix (FT_Init_FreeType is FT.InitFreeType); FT_Library is LibraryRec* and FT_Face is FtFaceRec*; a C long is CLong.

LibraryRec* library;
FT.InitFreeType(&library);
FtFaceRec* face;
fixed (byte* font = fontBytes)   // the face reads this memory for as long as it lives: keep it pinned (or in native memory)
{
    FT.NewMemoryFace(library, font, new CLong(fontBytes.Length), new CLong(0), &face);
    FT.SetPixelSizes(face, 0, 16);
    FT.LoadChar(face, new CULong('A'), FT.LoadRender);
    Bitmap bitmap = face->Glyph->Bitmap;               // Rows, Width, Pitch, Buffer: 8-bit coverage
}

Every function returns an FT_Error: zero is success. The modules are TrueType and OpenType (tt, cff, sfnt), Type 1, CID and Type 42, the PostScript helpers, the auto-hinter, and the smooth, monochrome and SDF renderers; zlib is FreeType's own copy (WOFF 1 fonts and .gz files). Left out: the bitmap and Windows fonts, PFR, the SVG and colour-PNG glyphs, WOFF 2 (brotli) and HarfBuzz; ThirdParty/README.md lists them and how the library is configured (Native/freetype/apogee_ftoption.h, apogee_ftmodule.h). FreeType is used under the FreeType License (BSD-style, with a credit clause: a game that ships the library says so in its credits, see Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Dear ImGui's font atlas is rasterized by it: cimgui links this library (they sit next to each other) and ImGui makes it the default font loader. FreeTypeSmokeTests renders a glyph of a font loaded from memory through every renderer, and the common binding tests check the entry points and struct sizes.

docs.title: cgltf (Apogee.Native.Cgltf)
docs.text:
A glTF 2.0 parser (.gltf and .glb). Cgltf.Parse reads a file from memory and Cgltf.ParseFile from a path; both give a Data* that owns the parsed document and that you release with Cgltf.Free. Cgltf.LoadBuffers reads the binary buffers (external files and data URIs), Cgltf.Validate checks the document, and Cgltf.AccessorUnpackFloats / AccessorReadIndex read accessor data whatever its component type.

var options = new Options();
Data* data;
if (Cgltf.Parse(&options, bytes, size, &data) == Result.Success && Cgltf.LoadBuffers(&options, data, path) == Result.Success)
{
    Accessor* positions = data->Meshes[0].Primitives[0].Attributes[0].Data;
    Cgltf.AccessorUnpackFloats(positions, destination, floatCount);
}
Cgltf.Free(data);

The names are the C names without cgltf_; its booleans are plain ints.

Keep the parsed memory alive

For a .glb cgltf's buffers, and for any file its strings, point into the memory you passed to Parse, so that memory has to stay valid until Free. Pinning a managed array only for the call works under CoreCLR by luck (the array does not move) and breaks under NativeAOT. GltfLoader copies the file into native memory and frees it after Free.

docs.title: stb_image (Apogee.Native.Stb)
docs.text:
Decodes the common image formats (PNG, JPEG, BMP, TGA, GIF, PSD, HDR, PIC, PNM) from memory. The class is Stbi.

int width, height, channelsInFile;
byte* pixels = Stbi.LoadFromMemory(data, length, &width, &height, &channelsInFile, Stbi.RgbAlpha);
if (pixels == null) throw new InvalidDataException(Marshal.PtrToStringUTF8((IntPtr)Stbi.FailureReason()));
// …upload width * height * 4 bytes…
Stbi.ImageFree(pixels);

Asking for Stbi.RgbAlpha always gives four 8-bit channels, whatever the file has. Stbi.InfoFromMemory reads the size without decoding. There is no file API: read the bytes through the engine's file system first.

docs.title: libktx (Apogee.Native.Ktx)
docs.text:
Reads KTX 1 and KTX 2 textures, and writes KTX 2 with the Basis Universal encoder. Basis Universal data (ETC1S/BasisLZ and UASTC) is transcoded to whatever the GPU supports. The asset importer encodes UASTC with ktxTexture2_CompressBasisEx and supercompresses it with ktxTexture2_DeflateZstd (BasisEncoder, Asset import); the game only loads, but the encoder is in the same library (libktx is 2.1 MB on Linux with it; a shipped game never calls the encoder). Not built: the ASTC encoder (UASTC is transcoded to ASTC instead), and the OpenGL/Vulkan upload (the renderer uploads the bytes itself).

Texture2* texture;
Ktx.Texture2CreateFromMemory(bytes, size, TextureCreateFlagBits.LoadImageData, &texture);
if (Ktx.Texture2NeedsTranscoding(texture))
{
    // BC7 on desktop GPUs, ASTC 4x4 on mobile and Apple, RGBA8 as the fallback that always works.
    Ktx.Texture2TranscodeBasis(texture, TranscodeFmt.TtfBc7Rgba, 0);
}
nuint offset;
Ktx.Texture2GetImageOffset(texture, level, layer, face, &offset);   // texture->PData + offset: that level's bytes, texture->VkFormat: their format
Ktx.Texture2Destroy(texture);

Names are the C names without ktx, with the _ after Texture2 dropped (Texture2CreateFromMemory); enums lose _e.

docs.title: Slang (Apogee.Native.Slang)
docs.text:
The shader compiler. Slang's own API is C++ and COM, so the binding is over a small C API of ours (Native/slang_c) that compiles Slang source to SPIR-V for Vulkan 1.3 (SPIR-V 1.6, row-major matrices, entry points keep their names). The compiler library ships with the game: shaders compile at run time, and a mod can bring its own .slang files.

Session* session;
var desc = new SessionDesc { SearchPaths = paths, SearchPathCount = pathCount, Optimization = 1 };
Slang.SessionCreate(&desc, &session);

Result* result;
Slang.Compile(session, moduleName, path, source, null, 0, &result);   // entry points: all the module defines
if (Slang.ResultStatus(result) < 0) Log.Error("Shaders", Marshal.PtrToStringUTF8((IntPtr)Slang.ResultDiagnostics(result)));
byte* spirv = (byte*)Slang.ResultSpirv(result, 0, &size);              // entry point 0
Slang.ResultDestroy(result);

Passing source = null loads <moduleName>.slang from the search paths. Besides the code, a result carries the diagnostics (warnings too), the program's reflection as Slang's JSON, and the files the compile read, which is what a shader cache keys on.

docs.title: Jolt Physics (Apogee.Native.Jolt)
docs.text:
Jolt Physics, behind our own C API, Native/jolt/apogee_jolt.h (about 80 functions, written for what the engine needs; no third-party wrapper), in one shared library, jolt. The binding is a class Jolt (Jolt.WorldCreate, Jolt.BodyCreate) with structs that keep their Aj prefix (AjBodyDesc, AjVec3, AjWorld*) because BodyDesc, VehicleDesc and World are the engine's own names for other things. Physics is the engine's use of it; this is the raw binding.

The API is handles and plain structs: a world owns its job system, temp allocator, collision layer filters and event queue; shapes are reference counted (ShapeBox, ShapeMesh, ShapeStaticCompound, MutableCompound… each returns one reference that ShapeRelease gives back); bodies are made from an AjBodyDesc (layers, mask, motion, mass, damping, sensor, events, bullet) and are 32-bit ids; there are queries (Raycast, CastSphere, OverlapSphere, OverlapBox, with a layer mask and an ignored body, filtered natively), a character (CharacterCreate, CharacterStep), vehicles (VehicleCreate from a flat AjVehicleDesc, then VehicleSetGearbox, VehicleDriveWheeled, VehicleGetWheelState…) and a drawbar joint. Nothing throws; functions that can fail return false or null.

How it is built decides what the binding means, so these are fixed in Native/jolt/CMakeLists.txt:

  • Double precision (JPH_DOUBLE_PRECISION): AjRVec3 is three doubles, and so are the positions in every call (BodyGetPose, Raycast, AjEvent.Position). Rotations, scales, velocities and everything else are floats. It is the physics side of the double world (see Math).
  • Cross-platform determinism (JPH_CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC): the same inputs give the same results on Windows, Linux and macOS, on any CPU and with any number of threads (no fused multiply-add, strict float contraction). It costs about 8% of the simulation. Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests/JoltSmokeTests simulates a pile of bodies and compares the bits of their final positions with a recorded hash; it was the same on SSE 4.2 and AVX2 builds, with 1, 2 and 7 threads, and before and after the move from JoltC to our own API.
  • 32-bit object layers (JPH_OBJECT_LAYER_BITS=32): the low 16 bits are a body's group (its 14 layers, plus a marker for static and one for sensor bodies, which only choose the broad phase tree), the high 16 its mask. Two bodies collide when each is in a layer the other's mask holds; static bodies never collide with each other.
  • Instruction set: SSE 4.2 (the engine's x86-64-v2 baseline). cmake -DAPOGEE_JOLT_AVX2=ON builds for AVX2, BMI, LZCNT and F16C, any CPU since Haswell, and Jolt's code is then faster; the library picks its instruction set when it is built, there is no run-time dispatch. FMA is never used.
  • No C++ exceptions and no RTTI, as Jolt does not use them, and none may cross managed frames. No GPU compute, no profiler, no assertions in Release. The debug renderer is compiled in: aj_world_draw_debug collects what it draws (see Physics).
Jolt.Init();                                                     // registers Jolt's types; Jolt.Shutdown() at the end
var desc = new AjWorldDesc { MaxBodies = 10240, MaxBodyPairs = 65536, MaxContactConstraints = 20480, TempBufferBytes = 32 << 20, Threads = 4, EventCapacity = 4096,
                             VelocitySteps = 10, PositionSteps = 2, Gravity = new AjVec3 { Y = -9.81f } };
AjWorld* world = Jolt.WorldCreate(&desc);
AjShape* ball = Jolt.ShapeSphere(0.5f);
uint body = Jolt.BodyCreate(world, &bodyDesc);                   // bodyDesc.Shape = ball
Jolt.WorldUpdate(world, 1f / 60);                                // one collision step

Events. Jolt calls its contact and activation listeners on its worker threads, inside WorldUpdate, where managed code must not run. The world's listeners only append to a queue in native memory (a mutex, and a fixed capacity: what does not fit is counted, EventsDropped), and EventsTake copies them out after the update:

  • ContactAdded: two bodies started touching; the point (a double position), normal and depth are the first contact point's. ContactRemoved: they stopped (also when one of them goes to sleep: Jolt ends the contacts of a sleeping body).
  • BodyActivated and BodyDeactivated.
  • Only bodies that ask are reported (AjBodyDesc.Events); a sensor always reports its contacts, with Jolt.EventSensor in the flags. The UserData of a body is yours, whole, and comes back in the event.
  • IgnorePair(a, b) makes two bodies pass through each other (a truck and its trailer) until AllowPair; the world's contact validation looks the pair up only while some pair is ignored.

A step that needs more working memory than TempBufferBytes allocates from the heap instead of failing.

docs.title: RmlUi (Apogee.Native.RmlUi)
docs.text:
RmlUi 6.3 (HTML and CSS style game UI), behind our own C API, Native/rmlui/apogee_rmlui.h (85 functions), in one shared library, rmlui. RmlUi's own API is C++ with inheritance, templates and ownership by unique_ptr, which a C# program cannot call, so everything goes through handles and plain structs. RmlUi is compiled into the library as a static one would be (RMLUI_STATIC_LIB, hidden symbols): the library exports what the header declares and nothing else. Its font engine is FreeType, our own freetype library (it has to sit next to this one). The binding is a class Rml (Rml.ContextCreate, Rml.ElementAppendChild) with Ar-prefixed structs (ArHost, ArVertex, ArRect). UI is the engine's use of it; this is the raw binding.

  • The host. RmlUi needs a few things from its host, and ArHost is how it gets them: a table of function pointers (a C# program fills it with [UnmanagedCallersOnly] methods). Drawing: RmlUi compiles geometry (ArVertex lists, 20 bytes each, with the alpha already multiplied into the color) and asks for it to be drawn with a translation and a texture, under a scissor rectangle and a transform; textures come from load_texture (an image path) or generate_texture (RGBA pixels, for font atlases). System: time, a log, the mouse cursor, the clipboard.
