Files: read_file hands over a whole file to the library (ar_sink_write), which serves RmlUi's reads and seeks from memory, so every document, stylesheet and font is read through whatever file system the host has. Any function may be NULL; its work is then skipped (no drawing, no files).
  • Elements are handles, 64 bits with a generation, not pointers. A slot watches its element with RmlUi's observer pointer, so a handle to an element that has been destroyed (it was in a document that was unloaded, or in a branch someone destroyed) answers "not alive" and every call refuses it; a released slot that is used again does not answer to the old handle. An element made with DocumentCreateElement or DocumentCreateText is owned by its handle until ElementAppendChild or ElementInsertBefore puts it in a tree (RmlUi's ElementPtr rule), ElementRemoveChild gives it back, ElementDestroy ends it. Handles that calls return are the caller's to ElementRelease; so are the ones an event gives (EventTarget, EventCurrent).
  • Events. ElementAddListener(element, "click", capture) returns a token, and every event reaches the host's one on_event(user, token, event) synchronously, with the type, target, current element, phase and the event's parameters (EventGetString, EventGetNumber: mouse_x, key_identifier, value...), and EventStopPropagation. A listener dies with its element or at ElementRemoveListener; the only place one is freed is RmlUi's OnDetach.
  • Text results (ElementGetId, TextGet...) are written into a caller's buffer with the length the whole text needs, like snprintf; -1 is "no such thing".
  • Input is ContextMouseMove, ContextMouseButton, ContextMouseWheel, ContextKey (ArKey is RmlUi's key list, its values checked at compile time) and ContextText; each returns false when a document consumed the input.
  • Scripts in documents. Every document is an ArDocument, so that <script> and <script src> reach the host (load_inline_script, load_external_script, with a document id that is the same for every call about the document until document_closed) and on* attributes become listeners whose code the host compiles (compile_inline_handler, when the first event comes: the attribute is read before the element is in its document). RmlUi runs the scripts of a document when its <head> is read, before the body.
  • Data models. DataModelCreate, DataModelBind (a top-level variable, by ref and ArDataKind), DataModelBindEvent (for data-event-*), DataModelDirty, DataModelIsDirty and DataModelRemove. The values stay the host's: RmlUi asks data_get, data_set, data_size and data_child with the refs the host gave out, so one VariableDefinition per kind serves every variable. ArVariant carries the value (nil, bool, integer, double, string).
  • A base stylesheet. RmlUi has no user-agent stylesheet: a div is display: inline and ignores its width and height until a stylesheet says div { display: block }. SetBaseStyle gives it one, put under the rules of every document loaded afterwards (in its head, so the text the body makes already has a font); the tests of this binding that do not set one write the rule themselves.
  • Fonts are copied (LoadFont keeps its own copy until after shutdown, which RmlUi requires of the memory).
  • Effects. The host gets what RmlUi 6 asks of a render interface beyond geometry: enable_clip_mask and render_to_clip_mask (an ArClipOperation, geometry and translation), layers (push_layer, composite_layers with the filter handles and a blend mode, pop_layer), save_layer_as_texture and save_layer_as_mask_image, filters (compile_filter gets an ArFilterDesc: a blur, a drop shadow, or a 4x5 color matrix that opacity, brightness, contrast, invert, grayscale, sepia, saturate and hue-rotate are turned into) and shaders (compile_shader gets an ArShaderDesc: a linear, radial or conic gradient with its stops), with render_shader and the matching releases. Every callback is optional: one left null is a feature RmlUi then draws without. backdrop-filter is not forwarded.
var host = new ArHost { Size = (uint)sizeof(ArHost), User = state, CompileGeometry = &CompileGeometry, RenderGeometry = &RenderGeometry, /* ... */ ReadFile = &ReadFile, OnEvent = &OnEvent };
Rml.Initialize(&host);                                           // once; Rml.Shutdown() at the end
ArContext* context = Rml.ContextCreate(name, 1280, 720);
ulong document = Rml.ContextLoadDocumentText(context, rml, url);
Rml.DocumentShow(document);
Rml.ContextUpdate(context);                                      // layout and animations
Rml.ContextRender(context);                                      // calls host.RenderGeometry for what is visible

Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests/RmlUiSmokeTests runs all of it against a recording host: layout in pixels, the geometry and its colors, text with a real font, building and editing a tree (and what a stale handle does), listeners (bubbling, capture, stopping, removal, parameters), clicking by pointer position, files and stylesheets through the host, images, added stylesheets, typing into a text field, the debugger, resizing.

docs.title: ImGuizmo, ImPlot and imnodes
docs.text:
Dear ImGui add-ons for the dev tools and the editor: ImGuizmo (3D manipulation gizmos and a view cube), ImPlot (plots) and imnodes (node editors). All three use ImGui's C++ API and its context, and the symbols of ImGui are hidden in cimgui, so they are compiled into the cimgui library (Native/imgui/CMakeLists.txt), each with a C API of ours over it (apogee_imguizmo.h, apogee_implot.h, apogee_imnodes.h: plain functions over floats, ints and opaque handles, no C++ types, no cimguizmo / cimplot / cimnodes). Three binding projects are generated from those headers, all on the library name cimgui: Apogee.Native.ImGuizmo (class Gizmo, functions Gizmo.Manipulate, Gizmo.ViewManipulate...), Apogee.Native.ImPlot (class Plot: Plot.BeginPlot, Plot.PlotLineF...) and Apogee.Native.ImNodes (class Nodes: Nodes.BeginNode, Nodes.Link...). Their enums are checked against the library's own at compile time (static_asserts in the shims).

  • They act on ImGui's current context, which is in the same library: make ImGui's context current, create an ImPlot and an imnodes context (Plot.CreateContext, Nodes.CreateContext), and make those current too. ImGuiHost does all of that.
  • ImPlot's templates are exported as _f (float) and _d (double) functions: Plot.PlotLineF(label, values, count, xScale, xStart, spec) and Plot.PlotLineXyD(label, xs, ys, count, spec), and the same for shaded areas (PlotShadedBetweenF is an area between two lines), bars and scatter. AplotSpec is the look of an item; Plot.DefaultSpec fills it with automatic colors.
  • ImGuizmo's matrices are 16 floats, column-major; Gizmo.Manipulate changes the object's matrix in place and can give the change since the drag began (deltaMatrix).
  • imnodes' ids are the caller's integers: nodes, attributes (pins) and links each have their own.
  • The library exports exactly the three headers and ImGui's cimgui.h: nm -D libcimgui.so | grep -c _Z is 0, no C++ symbol of ImGui, ImPlot or imnodes leaks.
  • Tests: the three bindings are in NativeBindingTests (every entry point resolves; they have no struct of a known size but ImPlot's AplotSpec), and Tests/Apogee.DevTools.Tests/ImGuiExtensionTests runs a headless frame through each.

docs.title: OpenAL Soft (Apogee.Native.OpenAL)
docs.text:
OpenAL 1.1 with OpenAL Soft's extensions, through its C API with no shim: class OpenAL. OpenAL Soft is LGPL, so it is its own shared library beside the program (see Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md); Audio is built on it.

  • Names keep the C names with the first letter in capitals: alGenBuffers is OpenAL.AlGenBuffers, alcOpenDevice is OpenAL.AlcOpenDevice, AL_SOURCE_RELATIVE is OpenAL.AlSourceRelative. The extensions OpenAL Soft exports as plain functions are bound too (AL_ALEXT_PROTOTYPES): EFX effects, filters and auxiliary slots (AlGenEffects, AlFilterf), and ALC_SOFT_loopback (AlcLoopbackOpenDeviceSOFT, AlcRenderSamplesSOFT), which renders to memory with no sound card.
  • Left out: the direct-context variants (...Direct), EAX, the debug extension, the functions the header declares that the library does not export, and the effect parameters' default, minimum and maximum (float macros).
  • Every call can leave an error that is read with AlGetError / AlcGetError; the audio system checks them where a failure matters.
ALCdevice* device = OpenAL.AlcLoopbackOpenDeviceSOFT(null);          // or AlcOpenDevice(null) for the speakers
int[] attributes = [OpenAL.AlcFormatChannelsSoft, OpenAL.AlcStereoSoft, OpenAL.AlcFormatTypeSoft, OpenAL.AlcFloatSoft, OpenAL.AlcFrequency, 48000, 0];
fixed (int* a = attributes) { context = OpenAL.AlcCreateContext(device, a); }
OpenAL.AlcMakeContextCurrent(context);
// ... buffers, sources, then, once per update on a loopback device:
OpenAL.AlcRenderSamplesSOFT(device, mix, 1024);

docs.title: Audio decoders (Apogee.Native.AudioDecode)
docs.text:
WAV, FLAC, Ogg Vorbis and MP3 behind four functions of ours (Native/audio_decode/apogee_audio.h, built from dr_libs and stb_vorbis): Open takes a whole file in memory and tells the format from its first bytes, Read gives interleaved 32-bit float samples at the file's channel count and sample rate, Rewind starts over, Close ends it. The memory must stay valid until Close. The files come from the engine's file system, so the decoders never touch the disk.

AaInfo info;
AaDecoder* decoder = AudioDecode.Open(bytes, (nuint)length, &info);   // null if it is not audio we can read
ulong frames = AudioDecode.Read(decoder, samples, 4096);              // 0 at the end
AudioDecode.Close(decoder);

docs.title: GameNetworkingSockets (Apogee.Native.Net)
docs.text:
Valve's GameNetworkingSockets behind our own small C API (Native/net/apogee_net.h, shim apogee_net), class Net: GNS's flat C API takes C++ references and structs packed differently by platform, which the shim's compiler lays out instead. A host owns a listen socket and connections (GNS's handles, as uint); Poll returns what happened as AnEvents (Incoming, Connected, Message, Disconnected), whose message bytes and strings stay valid until the next Poll, so managed code never runs inside a GNS callback or on one of its threads. Network is built on it; Tests/Apogee.Network.Tests is its test. Without libGameNetworkingSockets next to it the shim does not load (NativeLibraries.TryLoad fails) and networking is off.

Net.Init(error, size);                       // counted: every Init needs a Shutdown
AnHost* host = Net.HostCreate();
ushort port; Net.Listen(host, 27020, &port);
uint connection = Net.Connect(host, "127.0.0.1:27020"u8);
AnEvent* events = ...; int n = Net.Poll(host, events, 256);   // once a frame
Net.Send(host, connection, bytes, length, reliable: true, lane: 0);

docs.title: Steamworks (Apogee.Native.Steam)
docs.text:
Valve's flat C API (steam_api.dll / libsteam_api.so / libsteam_api.dylib), class Steam. The three libraries are Valve's redistributable_bin, committed unchanged (Git LFS, ThirdParty/steamworks/lib); the SDK headers are not (Valve's agreement lets us distribute only the redistributables), so the bindings are generated code and committed, and the headers are needed only to regenerate them (./build.sh sdk steam <zip>, then ./build.sh bindings steam). Without the library NativeLibraries.TryLoad fails and Steam is off.

The headers are C++, and the bindings are generated from what Valve publishes for other languages instead: steam_api.json (interfaces, structs, enums, constants) plus the S_API function declarations in steam_api_flat.h, steam_api.h and steam_api_common.h, with libclang measuring the structs ("kind": "steam", SteamApiParser).

  • Interfaces are opaque pointers. Steam.SteamUserV023() returns an ISteamUser* that Steam owns; its methods take it first (Steam.UserGetSteamID(user), the flat API's SteamAPI_ISteamUser_GetSteamID). Only the interfaces in steam.json are bound (user, friends, utils, apps, user stats, remote storage, UGC, screenshots, timeline); networking, matchmaking, Steam Input and the game server API are left out.
  • Callbacks use manual dispatch (ManualDispatchInit, ManualDispatchRunFrame, ManualDispatchGetNextCallback into a CallbackMsg, ManualDispatchGetAPICallResult), so nothing runs on Steam's threads. Every callback struct has its id as a constant (Steam.GameOverlayActivatedId).
  • Packing. Valve packs its callback structs to 4 bytes on Linux and macOS and to 8 on Windows, and a few structs are #pragma pack(4) or (2) on every system. The structs that depend on the system say Pack = SteamPack.Callback, a constant chosen when the project is built (APOGEE_STEAM_PACK8 for a Windows build), and the layout test checks the size clang computes for both packings (SteamLayout.CallbackPackSizes). Build the binding for the operating system it runs on.
  • Names lose Valve's Hungarian prefixes (m_unAppID is AppID, m_eResult is Result); _t and the E/I prefixes of enums and interfaces stay as Valve writes them.
  • Constants that are plain numbers (or a * b, a + b) are bound; strings and macros are skipped (Bin/bindings/steam.skipped.txt).
byte* message = stackalloc byte[1024];
if (Steam.InitFlat(message) == ESteamAPIInitResult.OK)       // Steam client running, steam_appid.txt next to the program in development
{
    Steam.ManualDispatchInit();
    ISteamUser* user = Steam.SteamUserV023();
    ulong id = Steam.UserGetSteamID(user);
}

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Apogee.Network connects the game to other programs over UDP: GameNetworkingSockets (GNS, Valve's open-source transport, BSD-3-Clause) behind one NetSystem, in scripts the global net. Connections are encrypted, messages are reliable (arrive once, in order) or not (may be lost, never twice), large messages are split and put back together, and lanes keep a slow message on one from holding up the others. There is no replication: what is sent, and what it means, is the game's.

The base game's only: NetSystem is ModsBlocked, as are connections. The library is a prebuilt, self-contained shared library beside the program (ThirdParty/gns/lib, see ThirdParty/README.md); without it net.is_active is false and every call does nothing and returns nothing, so a game that can also play alone works the same.

-- the server
local port = net:listen(27020)            -- 0: a free port; returns the port, or 0 if it is in use
net.connection_requested:connect(function(connection, address)
    if banned[address] then connection:refuse() end    -- accepted when the handlers return, unless one refused
end)
net.connected:connect(function(connection)
    connection:send('{"hello":"player"}')
end)
net.message:connect(function(connection, text, lane)
    local command = json.decode(text)
    ...
end)
net.disconnected:connect(function(connection, reason, code) ... end)

-- a client
local connection = net:connect("192.168.1.20:27020")    -- "[::1]:27020" for IPv6; a name is looked up first
net.connected:connect(function(c) c:send("hello") end)
connection:send(positionText, false)                  -- unreliable: for what is out of date a moment later

docs.title: The system
docs.text:
ScriptSession makes the NetSystem (the global net) and calls Update() once a frame, after Steam's and before the input and the world, so what arrived is a signal before the systems and scripts run. Nothing of the game runs on GNS's threads: the library's callbacks are queued and become signals inside Update, all on the calling thread, in this order: connections requested and made, then messages, then connections ended (a message sent just before a close is delivered before the close is announced). Opening a socket costs nothing until listen or connect is called. The system is disposed with the session.

  • listen(port) listens on a UDP port for IPv4 and IPv6 and returns the port (0 if it is in use). With 0 a free port from 49152 up is chosen. One port at a time; stop_listening(); listening_port.
  • connect(address) returns a NetConnection that is connecting, or nil when the address cannot be used. The outcome is a connected or a disconnected signal. A name in the address is looked up with the system's resolver, which can block for a moment; an IP address does not.
  • NetSystem.create() makes a system of its own (the tests talk to themselves over the loopback interface), NetSystem.create_inactive() one that does nothing, NetSystem.is_installed() says whether the library loads.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
NetConnection: address, is_incoming, state (connecting, connected, closed), ping (ms, -1 until known), quality (0 to 1), bytes_out and bytes_in (a second), send(text, reliable = true, lane = 0) (false when it could not be queued), configure_lanes(count), close(reason, linger = true) and refuse().

  • Messages are text in scripts: UTF-8, such as JSON. C# also has SendBytes(span, reliable, lane) and the event BytesReceived, which carry any bytes.
  • Lanes. configure_lanes(3) before the first message gives the connection three lanes of equal priority; each is in order on its own. Both sides configure the same number. The lane a message arrived on is the last argument of message.
  • Closing. close ends the connection and, with linger, sends what is still waiting first. The other side gets disconnected with the text and the code (1000 and up are the application's: a refused request is 1001). Here no signal comes (you asked for it). A connection that ended is closed and destroyed a frame later.
  • A connection that is not answered gives up after GNS's connect timeout (10 seconds) with a disconnected.

docs.title: With Steamworks
docs.text: GNS's interface is Steam's: ISteamNetworkingSockets in libsteam_api is the same class with the same functions, and the Steam Datagram Relay (connections by Steam id, through Valve's network, with no open port) is the same API with another way to address the peer. A Steam transport would therefore replace Native/net/apogee_net.cpp's calls (CreateListenSocketP2P, ConnectP2P, the identity instead of the IP address) and leave Apogee.Network, the scripts and these signals as they are. It is not built: the Steam wrappers of steam.md leave networking out on purpose (steam.json).

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text: GNS is C++ with a flat C API that takes C++ references and structs packed differently on each platform, so it is not bound as it is. Native/net/apogee_net.h is our own small C API over it (a host, connections as integers, an_poll returning events), compiled against GNS's headers (ThirdParty/gns/include) and linked to its shared library. Apogee.Native.Net is the generated binding of that header. Every GNS call is in apogee_net.cpp. ./build.sh native builds the shim when libGameNetworkingSockets is in Bin/native/<rid> or ThirdParty/gns/lib/<rid>, and skips it with a message otherwise.

docs.title: Not done
docs.text: Peer-to-peer connections and signaling, Steam's relay (above), the datagram-only ISteamNetworkingMessages, NAT punch-through, a server browser or lobby, and replication (entities, snapshots, prediction): the game builds those on messages. Messages in scripts are text only.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Network.Tests runs two network systems in one process over the loopback interface: a client connects and messages go both ways (reliable and unreliable, with non-ASCII text), 300 reliable messages arrive in order, bytes are not changed, a 200 kB message is split and put back together, a close is announced after the messages that came before it, a handler can refuse a connection (the other side sees code 1001), a connection to a port nobody listens on stays pending without blocking, lanes carry their number, addresses are parsed and names resolved, and an inactive system does nothing. Tests/Luau/net.test.luau runs the same through the script surface. They skip where the library is not installed; Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests checks the shim's entry points and struct sizes.

docs.title: Steam
docs.text:
Apogee.Steam connects a game to Steam: the player's name and language, the overlay, achievements, stats and leaderboards, rich presence, the timeline, cloud saves, and Workshop mods. In a game, scripts see it as the global steam (the SteamSystem class). It is the base game's: a mod cannot use it (ModsBlocked), and a base-game function a mod calls still acts as the base game.

Steam's library (steam_api) is Valve's redistributable and is in the repository; the Steam client is the player's. When Steam is not running, or the game was not started with an app id, steam.is_active is false and every call does nothing and answers with something inert (the log says why, once, and steam.status has the words), so a game works the same on a machine without Steam, under --headless, and in a test. A real, windowed run connects; --headless and tests do not.

if steam.is_active then
    print(steam.user_name, steam.language)          -- "Ada", "english"
end

steam:unlock_achievement("ACH_WIN_ONE_GAME")        -- shows the pop-up, and sends it to Steam
steam:set_stat_int("NumGames", steam:stat_int("NumGames") + 1)
steam:store_stats()                                  -- stats are in memory until stored

steam:set_rich_presence("status", "Delivering hay")  -- the line friends see
steam:add_timeline_event("Crash", "Hit a tree", "steam_death")

steam.overlay_activated:connect(function(open: boolean) paused = open end)

docs.title: The frame and the signals
docs.text:
ScriptSession.Progress calls steam:update() first in every frame. It uses Steam's manual dispatch: Steam's callbacks and the results of asynchronous calls are collected there, on the calling thread, and turn into signals. Nothing runs on a thread of Steam's. A script never waits: a call that needs Steam to answer returns at once, and a signal carries the answer.

Signal When overlay_activated(open) the overlay opened or closed: pause the game while it is open shutdown_requested() Steam is shutting down and wants the game to exit stats_received(ok), stats_stored(ok) the player's stats arrived; a store_stats finished achievement_stored(name, current, max) an achievement unlocked or progressed leaderboard_found(name, found), score_uploaded(name, ok, rank), scores_downloaded(name, users, ranks, scores) the answers of the leaderboard calls (ok false and no entries when it failed or Steam is off) text_input_dismissed(submitted, text) Steam's on-screen keyboard closed workshop_item_installed(id), workshop_item_downloaded(id, ok), workshop_subscribed(id, ok), workshop_unsubscribed(id, ok) Workshop

Steam's 64-bit ids (the player, a Workshop item) are decimal strings in scripts, because a script number cannot hold them.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• The user and the app: user_id, user_name, app_id, build_id, language (the language the player chose for the game, as Steam names it: english, french, schinese; a game can take it as the default language), ui_language, country, is_subscribed, is_steam_deck, is_big_picture, owns_dlc(app_id), is_dlc_installed(app_id).
  • Overlay: activate_overlay("friends" | "community" | "players" | "settings" | "stats" | "achievements" | ""), open_web_page(url), open_store(app_id), is_overlay_enabled, and show_text_input(description) for the Deck's on-screen keyboard.
  • Achievements and stats: achievement(name), unlock_achievement, clear_achievement, achievement_progress(name, current, max), achievement_names(), stat_int/stat_float, set_stat_int/set_stat_float, store_stats, reset_all_stats(achievements_too). Steam loads the stats when the game starts: stats_received says when. Achievements and stats are defined in Steamworks (the partner site), by name; this only sets them.
  • Leaderboards: find_leaderboard(name), upload_score(name, score, keep_best), download_scores(name, from, to, "global" | "around_user" | "friends"). A leaderboard that was not looked up yet is looked up by the call that needs it.
  • Rich presence: set_rich_presence(key, value) (status is the line shown in the friends list), clear_rich_presence().
  • Screenshots and the timeline: trigger_screenshot(), add_screenshot(path, width, height); add_timeline_event(title, description, icon, priority, offset_seconds, featured), set_timeline_state(text) and set_timeline_mode("playing" | "staging" | "menus" | "loading") give the player's Steam timeline (the game recording) its markers.

docs.title: Cloud saves
docs.text:
ScriptSession.StartGame mounts cloud:// in the game's file system. With Steam running and the cloud on (steam.is_cloud_enabled: the player has it on for the account and for the game) it is the player's Steam Cloud files for the game; otherwise it is a plain folder (<user folder>/cloud). A game saves to cloud:// in both cases, with the same code:

fs.write_text("cloud://slot1/save.json", json)       -- follows the player to their other machines
local text = fs.read_text("cloud://slot1/save.json")

Steam keeps cloud files flat, with / in their names, so a folder exists only as far as a file's name says; a write that Steam refuses (too big, or the space is used up) fails like a write to a full disk. steam:cloud_quota() gives the total space and what is left. The game must also turn the cloud on for its files in Steamworks (the app's Steam Cloud settings: a byte and a file count quota). What is saved in the plain folder while Steam was off is not copied into the cloud later.

docs.title: Workshop mods
docs.text:
A Workshop item is a mod: a folder with a mod.xml at its root, uploaded by its author, that Steam downloads and keeps up to date for subscribers. When Steam runs, the game mounts the installed items at workshop:// (Steam's own folders, read-only), each listed under its mod.xml id, and the package finder searches it (PackageOptions.ExtraUserModsPaths) next to user://mods: a Workshop mod is one of the player's mods in every way (the same solver, the same "switch it off" list in user://mods.xml, the same limits for mods). If an own mod and a Workshop item share an id, the one found first (the player's own) wins.

Mods are read when the game starts. workshop_item_installed(id) says a subscription finished installing: tell the player to restart. subscribe(id), unsubscribe(id), subscribed_items(), workshop_item_folder(id) and download_workshop_item(id) are there for a mod browser in the game's menu.

docs.title: Uploading a mod
docs.text:
cd path/with/steam_appid.txt          # the game's app id; the Steam client must be running and signed in as a partner of the game
Apogee.Runtime --workshop-upload Mods/my_mod --title "My mod" --description "What it does" --preview preview.png --tags Vehicles,Tools --visibility private
Apogee.Runtime --workshop-upload Mods/my_mod --title "My mod" ... --confirm      # this one really uploads
Apogee.Runtime --workshop-upload Mods/my_mod --item 1234567890 --note "Fixed the hitch" --confirm   # an update of an item

Uploading makes something visible under the author's Steam account, so without --confirm the command only prints what it would send. A new item starts private: change it to public on the Workshop page, or upload with --visibility public once it is ready. The first time, Steam wants the Workshop legal agreement accepted (the command prints the link). The folder must have a mod.xml; everything in it is sent.

docs.title: Starting a game under Steam
docs.text:
A game that ships on Steam has the game folder's steam_appid.txt (the app id alone on one line) or Steam's own launch to tell the app id. StartGame reads the file and asks Steam to relaunch the game through itself when it was started some other way (SteamAPI_RestartAppIfNecessary): the process then ends at once (RestartRequested). A steam_appid.txt next to the program turns that off, which is how you run it during development (Steam reads the app id from the file; use 480, Valve's Spacewar, to try the API without an app of your own). A watched game (--watch) never asks for a relaunch.

Steam Input is not wrapped: SDL sees Steam's virtual gamepad, so a player's Steam controller configuration works with the input actions as it is. Steam's networking and matchmaking are bound (Native libraries) but have no engine layer yet.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Tests/Apogee.Steam.Tests: the inactive system (every call), the Workshop source, workshop:// through the package finder, and the cloud's fallback folder. They need no Steam.
  • Against a real client (off by default): APOGEE_STEAM_TESTS=1 ./build.sh test with the Steam client running and signed in. They use Spacewar (480) and change that account's Spacewar stats and cloud files.
  • Tests/Luau/steam.test.luau: the same inactive behavior as scripts see it, in the runtime's Luau tests.

docs.title: Physics
docs.text:
Apogee.Physics is Jolt Physics for the ECS: entities get bodies, the simulation steps at a fixed rate, and the entities' transforms follow. The raw library is in Native libraries; this is what the engine makes of it. In a game, scripts see the world as the global physics.

local Transform = world:component("Transform")
local ground = world:create_entity("ground")
world:set(ground, Transform, { Position = Vector3(0, -1, 0), Rotation = Quat.identity, Scale = Vector3(1, 1, 1) })
local floor = BodyDesc.new()
floor.shape = PhysicsShape.box(Vector3(100, 1, 100))        -- half extents
floor.motion = "static"
physics:add_body(ground, floor)

local crate = world:create_entity("crate")
world:set(crate, Transform, { Position = Vector3(0, 5, 0), Rotation = Quat.identity, Scale = Vector3(1, 1, 1) })
local body = BodyDesc.new()
body.shape = PhysicsShape.box(Vector3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
body.mass = 20
body.events = true                                           -- report its contacts
physics:add_body(crate, body)

physics.contact_began:connect(function(a, b, point, normal) print("hit", a, b, point) end)
local hit, entity, point, normal, distance = physics:raycast(Vector3(0, 10, 0), Vector3(0, -1, 0), 50)

docs.title: The world and its frame
docs.text:
PhysicsWorld(ecsWorld, options) makes one simulation for an ECS world; a game session makes it for you. Call Update(deltaSeconds) once a frame, before World.Progress (ScriptSession.Progress does): the physics then writes the transforms of its bodies, the frame's systems and scripts see them, and the world's transform system composes the WorldTransforms as usual.

  • A fixed step, StepRate times a second (64 in the tests, 60 by default). Update adds the frame's time to an accumulator and runs as many steps as fit, at most MaxSubsteps (4): a slow frame loses time instead of spiralling. The results depend on the step rate, not on the frame rate or the number of threads.
  • stepping (Stepping in C#) is raised before each fixed step. Anything that must act once per step, vehicle controls above all, connects there, not to a per-frame callback.
  • Interpolation (Interpolate, on by default): the entity of a moving dynamic body shows the pose between its last two steps by how far the accumulator is into the next one, so motion is smooth at any frame rate, at the price of showing the past by up to one step. physics:pose(entity) is the exact pose of the last step. A body that comes to rest shows exactly where it is, not a blend.
  • Determinism: the library is built so that the same inputs give the same bits on every OS (see Native libraries), whatever ThreadCount is.
  • Options: MaxBodies (10 240), MaxBodyPairs, MaxContactConstraints, TempBufferBytes (32 MiB), Gravity, VelocitySteps 10, PositionSteps 2, EventCapacity (4096). These are the old project's settings.

docs.title: Bodies
docs.text:
A BodyDesc says what a body is: its shape, motion, mass (or a density, with the shape's volume), friction, restitution, damping, gravity_factor, layers and mask, whether it is a sensor, whether it reports events, allow_sleeping, bullet (sweep the whole path, so a fast body cannot tunnel through a thin wall) and its starting velocities. One description can make any number of bodies. physics:add_body(entity, desc) puts the body where the entity's transform is now; the entity gets a Transform if it has none, and a Body component (Id, Slot, Motion). Removing the component (physics:remove_body) or destroying the entity removes the body.

motion Meaning static Never moves (ground, walls). physics:teleport moves it, slowly. kinematic The game moves it: it goes to where its entity is by the end of each frame's steps, and pushes dynamic bodies (doors, lifts, platforms). dynamic The simulation moves it, and its entity follows.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text:
A PhysicsShape is made with a static function and shared by any number of bodies: box(halfExtents), sphere(radius), capsule(halfHeight, radius) and cylinder(halfHeight, radius) (along Y), convex_hull(points), mesh(vertices, indices) and height_field(heights, size, offset, scale) (static and kinematic bodies only), compound(children, positions, rotations), offset(shape, position, rotation) (moves the shape inside its own space, so a box can stand on the entity's origin) and scaled(shape, scale). Jolt counts references, so a shape that is dropped lives on in the bodies that use it. volume, center_of_mass and is_valid_scale(scale) say what it is. Dimensions are checked: a zero radius or a mesh index past the vertices is an error with the reason.

Scale. The entity's world scale is applied to the shape when the body is made (a scale a shape cannot take, such as a stretched sphere, is an error). Changing the scale later does not change the body: make it again.

docs.title: How a body fits the entity tree
docs.text: Transform is local to the parent and WorldTransform is computed top-down (see Math). A body takes its world pose from World.ComputeWorldTransform(entity) when it is made, and a dynamic body writes back a local Transform: its world pose from Jolt, taken into the space of its parent (parentWorld⁻¹ × pose, with the position subtraction done in double). The scale is left alone. So a crate under a moving platform entity falls in the world's space, and its local transform changes to match. A kinematic body reads its entity's world transform. The rule that keeps this simple: a body's ancestors must not be dynamic bodies (add_body refuses); a parent that is not a body, or is static or kinematic, is fine.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text: A body is in some of 14 collision layers (layers, a bit each: 1 is the default layer) and collides with the layers in its mask (all by default). Two bodies collide when each is in a layer the other's mask holds. Two more bits are the world's own and sort bodies into three broad-phase trees (static, sensor, moving); Jolt never collides two bodies that are both static or kinematic. The native layer builds the object layer from them, and the query filters (mask, ignore) run natively too: see Native/jolt/apogee_jolt.cpp.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Bodies that have events (and every sensor) report to the world's event queue (apogee_jolt), which is drained after each step on the main thread:

Signal Arguments contact_began the two entities, the contact point (a position) and the normal contact_ended the two entities (also when one of them goes to sleep: Jolt ends the contacts of a sleeping body) sensor_entered, sensor_exited the sensor's entity, then the other body_woke, body_slept the entity

A sensor (sensor = true) does not collide and is not pushed; it reports the bodies inside it. Events a step produced beyond EventCapacity are dropped and counted (dropped_events). A signal handler runs while the world is not inside Jolt, so it may add or remove bodies.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
All positions are in the world, in double precision, and layers are a mask; ignore is an entity the query passes through. Sensors are never hit.

  • raycast(origin, direction, maxDistance, mask?, ignore?) returns hit, entity, point, normal, distance.
  • cast_sphere(origin, direction, radius, maxDistance, mask?, ignore?) returns the same for the first body a swept sphere touches (point is on the body, distance how far the sphere got).
  • overlap_sphere(center, radius, mask?, ignore?) and overlap_box(center, rotation, halfExtents, mask?, ignore?) return the entities of the bodies that touch the shape, each once.

docs.title: Bodies from code
docs.text: get_linear_velocity, set_linear_velocity, get_angular_velocity, set_angular_velocity, add_force (newtons, for the next step only: call it every step), add_torque, add_impulse (newton seconds), wake, is_awake, pose (the exact pose), teleport(entity, position, rotation) (body and entity at once, no blend).

docs.title: Vehicles
docs.text: physics:create_vehicle and physics:create_hitch: see Vehicles and hitches. BodyDesc.center_of_mass and physics:get_mass(entity) are for them.

docs.title: Characters
docs.text: physics:create_character(entity, height, radius, layers?, mask?) makes a character controller (Jolt's CharacterVirtual): a capsule whose feet are at the entity's position that slides along walls, walks up stairs (steps up to 0.4 m) and slopes (up to max_slope_degrees, read-only, 50), sticks to the ground going down and stands on moving platforms. It is not a rigid body: dynamic bodies are pushed by it and do not push it. Set desired_velocity (the horizontal part counts; gravity and jumps decide the vertical one), call jump(speed) (from the ground only), read is_on_ground, ground_velocity, velocity and position. It steps with the world, and its entity follows, blended like a dynamic body. teleport(position) and set_rotation(rotation) move it; destroying it stops the following.

docs.title: Far from the origin
docs.text: Jolt is built with double positions, so a body, a ray or a character is as exact 10 000 km out as at the origin; the tests run the same scenes at x = 1e7. Rotations, scales, velocities and forces are floats. Scripts see positions as vectors, narrowed to float (see Math): a script that works that far out keeps its coordinates relative to something near.

docs.title: Pausing
docs.text: physics.paused = true stops the world: Update adds no time and runs no step, so bodies stay where they are, keep their velocities, and resume from there when it is false again. A pause menu sets it.

docs.title: Debug drawing
docs.text:
physics.debug_draw = true (or the Physics shapes checkbox in the dev overlay's Debug section) draws the world over the picture: every body's shape as wireframe, colored by what it is, the joints and drawbars, a vehicle's wheels and suspension, and the capsules of characters. In C#, PhysicsWorld.DrawDebug(DebugDraw draw, PhysicsDebugOptions? options, Double3 camera) adds the same to any DebugDraw; PhysicsDebugOptions chooses what: shapes (solid or wireframe), bounding boxes, centers of mass, velocities, constraints and their limits, characters. camera picks the level of detail of round shapes.

Jolt draws, and our C API only collects: aj_world_draw_debug runs Jolt's DebugRendererSimple into one process-wide collector (Jolt allows one debug renderer at a time; it is made on first use and freed by aj_shutdown), and aj_debug_lines / aj_debug_triangles hand its arrays over, so no managed code runs inside Jolt's drawing. DebugLine and DebugTriangle have the layout of the C structs (a test pins it), so the arrays are copied as they are. A character is not a body, so aj_character_draw_debug draws its capsule separately. Jolt's wireframe is the edges of the shape's triangle mesh (a box is its twelve triangles, so 36 lines), not just its outline.

docs.title: Not done
docs.text: Constraints (joints beyond the hitches), soft bodies, ragdolls, and changing a body's shape or scale after it is made. The Jolt library has all of them in its C API (Apogee.Native.Jolt).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Physics.Tests covers falling and resting, double precision 10 000 km out, parent spaces, kinematic carrying, scale, teleport, impulses and mass, the fixed step and interpolation, queries, events, sensors, layers, every shape, the character, debug drawing (the layout of its structs, a box's lines at their place 1 000 km out, solid and wireframe, bounding boxes, the character's capsule), and that the result is the same with 1 and 4 threads. Tests/Luau/physics.test.luau runs the script surface in the NativeAOT binary too.

docs.title: Vehicles and hitches
docs.text:
Vehicles tuned for heavy trucks, trailers and attachments: Jolt's wheeled and tracked VehicleConstraint, with the game owning the gearbox, plus the two ways to hitch things together. They are part of Physics (PhysicsWorld.CreateVehicle, CreateHitch); in a game, scripts reach them through the global physics.

local desc = VehicleDesc.new()
desc.engine_max_torque = 2500
desc.wheels = {}
for _, axle in { { z = 2.2, r = 0.55, steer = 35, share = 0.513 }, { z = -0.2, r = 0.8, steer = 0, share = 1.579 } } do
    for _, x in { 0.95, -0.95 } do
        local wheel = WheelDesc.new()
        wheel.position = Vector3(x, axle.r, axle.z)      -- the wheel's center with its suspension fully extended
        wheel.radius, wheel.powered, wheel.max_steer_angle, wheel.torque_share = axle.r, true, axle.steer, axle.share
        wheel.entity = wheelEntity[x][axle.z]            -- optional: follows the wheel each frame
        table.insert(desc.wheels, wheel)
    end
end
local truck = physics:create_vehicle(truckEntity, desc)   -- the entity has a dynamic body

truck.stepping:connect(function(dt)                  -- before every fixed step: the game drives
    truck.forward, truck.steering = throttle, steer
    truck.drive_ratio, truck.clutch = gearbox:ratio(), gearbox:clutch()
end)

docs.title: The vehicle
docs.text:
The vehicle's space is the body's: +Z forward, +Y up, +X to its left (glTF's). A wheel's position is where its center sits with the suspension extended; the suspension reaches suspension_length above that. WheelDesc: radius, width, suspension_length, suspension_frequency (Hz) and suspension_damping, max_steer_angle (degrees), steer_ratio, powered, max_brake_torque, max_handbrake_torque, friction (scales the tire's grip), torque_share and brake_factor. VehicleDesc: drive (wheels or tracks), wheels, the engine (engine_max_torque, engine_min_rpm, engine_max_rpm, engine_torque_curve, engine_inertia), differential_ratio, clutch_slip_rpm, track_brake_torque and max_pitch_roll_angle. A heavier body with a low center of mass (BodyDesc.center_of_mass) drives better.

The game owns the gearbox. Jolt's transmission stays in manual mode with one forward and one reverse gear, whose ratio is rewritten every step from drive_ratio (signed: negative reverses; 0 is neutral) and clutch (0 drives nothing, 1 is engaged; the clutch's strength comes from clutch_slip_rpm). The inputs are forward (throttle), steering (-1 to 1, positive toward +X), brake and handbrake. Set all of them in the stepping signal of the vehicle (or of the physics world): it runs before each step, then the vehicle gives the values to Jolt. A dynamic gearbox, an automatic with a torque converter, a CVT sweeping its ratio, ABS and engine braking are all game code on top of this (a game's own Luau scripts).

docs.title: What the port does for the powertrain
docs.text:
• Differentials: powered wheels at about the same Z (within 0.25 m) form an axle with one differential, the wheel with the larger X as its left one. Its ratio is differential_ratio scaled by the axle's wheel radius over the largest powered radius, so axles of smaller wheels turn them faster and every wheel covers the same ground.
  • Torque shares: the engine's torque goes to the axles by the torque_share of their wheels (an even split by default). By their load, the lightly loaded front axle of a truck would spin.
  • A vehicle with no powered wheel (a trailer) gets a dummy differential and stays in neutral whatever it is told.
  • Wheel inertia is that of a wheel of about 250 kg per meter of radius (0.5 · 250 · r · r²): Jolt's car default is knocked to a stop by the brakes in a single step on a truck.
  • The engine's torque curve is sampled at 17 points of rpm / max rpm; engine_peak_power_rpm is where torque times rpm peaks, found over 65 points.

docs.title: Steering
docs.text: Each wheel steers by max_steer_angle times the steering input times its steer_ratio (1 for front steering, -1 for rear steering, 1 on every axle for crab steering). A wheel with no steer angle is the fixed axle. With wheels of different ratios, Ackermann geometry applies: from two such wheels the vehicle finds the wheelbase and the pivot (the axle where the ratio is 0), and every steered wheel turns about the one turning center: the inner wheel of an axle more than the outer, at most 80°. (Jolt sets all wheels from one input before its casts; the port puts each wheel's angle in the wheel's settings and gives Jolt an input of 1, which comes to the same.)

docs.title: Tracks
docs.text: drive = "tracks": a track per side (+X is left) made of the wheels on that side, driven by its powered wheel (the sprocket), or the rearmost one. Steering slows one side (and reverses it at full lock); steering with no throttle turns on the spot, the two sides running opposite ways. track_brake_torque is a sprocket's brake.

docs.title: Readings
docs.text:
speed_kmh, engine_rpm, engine_torque, engine_load, engine_peak_power_rpm, gear_ratio, brake_capacity (what all the brakes give together), wheel_count; per wheel get_wheel_contact, get_wheel_compression (0 extended to 1), get_wheel_rpm, get_wheel_steer_degrees, get_wheel_contact_point, get_wheel_contact_normal, get_wheel_contact_entity; and get_wheel_readings(), four numbers per wheel for the assists: contact (1 or 0), angular velocity in rad/s, the load in newtons (the suspension's force; a vehicle's wheels together carry its weight) and the tire's grip. set_brake_factor(wheel, factor) scales one wheel's brake torque from the next step on (an ABS releases a locking wheel with it); physics:get_mass(entity) is the body's mass.

Wheel entities (WheelDesc.entity, usually children of the vehicle's entity) get their local Transform written after each update: their place on the suspension, steered and spinning, in the vehicle's space (wheel models have their axle along X). A vehicle ends when it is destroyed, its body goes or its entity does.

docs.title: Hitches
docs.text: A hitch is an entity under the vehicle's entity (any depth), whose transform is the hitch's frame in the vehicle's space. physics:create_hitch(hitchEntity, "mount" | "trailer") makes the Hitch; hitch:attach(entity, point, rotation) takes the attachment's entity and the attach point in the attachment's space, which meets the hitch's frame; it returns false if the hitch holds something. A hitch holds one body. The two never collide while hitched.

docs.title: Mount hitch: loader, crane, blade
docs.text:
The attachment becomes part of the truck. Its collision shape is added to the truck's body, which becomes a mutable compound of its own shape and one child per attachment (so the truck feels what the attachment hits, and several attachments can be mounted), its mass is added to the truck's (the inertia of the whole shape, scaled to the total mass), and the attachment's body is removed: its entity stays, as a child of the hitch entity at the inverse of the attach point, and the transform cascade carries it with the truck's interpolated pose. Lifting is moving the hitch entity: each step the compound child is moved to match (and the truck's center of mass moves with it). The attachment must be a dynamic or kinematic body without a vehicle.

hitch:detach() gives the attachment a body again where it is (the same shape and settings as before), moving as the point of the truck it was at (v + ω × r), takes its mass back, makes it a root entity in the world and restores the truck's own shape when nothing else is mounted. The same happens, as far as it can, when the truck's body is removed. Destroying the attachment's entity while it is mounted lets go of it. Destroying the truck's entity destroys the mounted attachment's entity too: it is a child of the hitch entity.

docs.title: Trailer hitch: drawbar, fifth wheel
docs.text: The trailer keeps its body (it may be a vehicle with wheels of its own, which stays in neutral) and a six-degrees-of-freedom joint holds the attach point to the hitch: the three linear axes are locked and the rotation is limited about the hitch's X, Y and Z by angular_limits (degrees; default 25, 75, 15: pitch, yaw, roll). The joint's frames are taken from the exact poses of the bodies when you attach, so attach after placing the trailer behind the truck; the joint pulls the two points together if they are apart. The pair do not collide (the native layer rejects every contact of the pair: aj_ignore_pair).

docs.title: Not done
docs.text: No hydraulics or linkage geometry (lift is the hitch entity's height, set by the game; what an attachment does is game code), no motorcycles (Jolt has the controller, the engine does not use it), no per-wheel slip reading and no hitch for more than one body.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Physics.Tests/VehicleTests.cs is the old vehicle.test.luau (the ratio drives it, neutral and an open clutch drive nothing, the step runs every step before the inputs, brake factors, the readings with the load equal to the weight, torque shares, a trailer in neutral) with Ackermann angles checked against cot(outer) − cot(inner) = track / wheelbase, rear and crab steering, wheel entities, a tracked vehicle turning on the spot. HitchTests.cs covers a scenario (a mounted attachment lifted 0.35 m, riding within 1 cm of the hitch, lowered and detached to rest on the ground; a trailer holding its drawbar within 5 cm through a turn and staying upright), plus the cleanup paths. Tests/Luau/physics.test.luau drives a vehicle and a mount hitch from a script, in the NativeAOT binary too.

docs.title: Input actions
docs.text:
Apogee.Input turns keys, mouse and gamepads into actions a game defines by name (jump, move_forward, lights). The game's code and mods ask for actions, never for keys, so a player can rebind everything and one gamepad works where another has different buttons. It is built for games with large action catalogs (about 45 actions).

  • InputActionMap: every action, its contexts, its defaults and what the player bound it to. Saves and loads the player's bindings.
  • InputActionRouter: routes input to the actions of the active contexts and reads their strength.
  • InputDevices: feeds a router from SDL's events (keyboard, mouse, gamepads).

In a game (--game, --run) scripts see one router as the global input, with its own map in input.map.

input.map:add_situation({ "world", "on_foot" })               -- contexts that are active together
input.map:add_situation({ "world", "vehicle" })
input.map:add_situation({ "menu" })
input.map:add_action("move_forward", { "on_foot", "vehicle" }, { "W", "Joy LY-" }, true)   -- analog: read by strength
input.map:add_action("lights", { "vehicle" }, { "L" }, false, "Toggle the headlights")
input.map:add_action("lights_back", { "vehicle" }, { "Alt+L" })

-- every frame, from what the player is doing:
input.contexts = if menu_open then { "menu" } else { "world", "vehicle" }

local throttle = input:get_strength("move_forward")           -- 0..1 (the mouse's motion: pixels of the frame)
input.action_fired:connect(function(action) print(action) end)   -- "lights" when L is pressed

docs.title: Contexts and situations
docs.text:
A context is a name the game chooses. An action works in the contexts it lists, and the router fires only the actions of input.contexts (none: no input at all). The game sets them every frame ({ "menu" } while a menu is open, { "world", "on_foot" } walking).

Situations say which contexts are active together, and are used only to find clashes: two actions clash when some situation has a context of each and they are bound to the same input. Without any situation, two actions clash when they share a context. Q for the camera in world and for a tab in menu is no clash when no situation holds both. get_conflicts(action, binding) tells what would clash if an action were bound to a text, and get_all_conflicts() lists the clashes among the current bindings, each as action<TAB>other<TAB>binding.

An analog action is read with get_strength and never fires; it clashes with any other action on its input whatever the modifiers. The others fire action_fired and also answer is_held (strength at least half) and get_strength (0 or 1).

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text:
A binding is text, the form players see in a settings file: [Hold |Double ][Ctrl+][Shift+][Alt+]input.

Input Written Keys by position on a US QWERTY keyboard, so AZERTY players get ZQSD for WASD: A..Z, 0..9, F1..F24, Enter, Escape, Backspace, Tab, Space, Minus, Equal, BracketLeft, BracketRight, Backslash, Semicolon, Apostrophe, Grave, Comma, Period, Slash, IntlBackslash, CapsLock, PrintScreen, ScrollLock, Pause, Insert, Home, PageUp, Delete, End, PageDown, Left, Right, Up, Down, NumLock, Kp0..Kp9, KpDivide, KpMultiply, KpMinus, KpPlus, KpEnter, KpPeriod, Menu, and Ctrl, Shift, Alt, Meta (left and right are one input) Mouse Mouse Left, Mouse Right, Mouse Middle, Mouse Wheel Up, Mouse Wheel Down, Mouse Back, Mouse Forward, and its motion Mouse X-, Mouse X+, Mouse Y-, Mouse Y+ Gamepad (Xbox names) Joy A, Joy B, Joy X, Joy Y, Joy LB, Joy RB, Joy Back, Joy Start, Joy Guide, Joy L3, Joy R3, Joy Up, Joy Down, Joy Left, Joy Right, sticks Joy LX- .. Joy RY+ (Y+ is down), triggers Joy LT, Joy RT

Names are case-insensitive when read and written as listed. Ctrl+, Shift+ and Alt+ go with keys and mouse buttons, not gamepad inputs. normalize_binding(text) writes a text the canonical way and raises an error (with what is wrong) for one that does not read; binding_error(text) returns that message or ""; parse_binding(text) returns the input, the modifiers (a list: { "ctrl", "shift" }) and the trigger ("press", "hold", "double_tap").

SDL's gamepad mapping decides which physical button is Joy A (the south one, so a PlayStation controller's cross). Steam Input's virtual gamepad arrives the same way, so a player's Steam controller configuration keeps working with no engine support.

docs.title: What the router does
docs.text:
• The most specific modifiers win. Of the bindings on an input whose modifiers are all held, only those with the most modifiers fire: Shift+Tab does not also fire Tab, and W still fires while Shift is held for running.
  • Hold. A key that also has a Hold binding fires its press on a quick release instead; held for 0.4 s it fires the hold, and its release then fires nothing.
  • Double tap. A key with a Double binding waits 0.3 s for a second tap before it fires its press.
  • Axes. Sticks and triggers have a dead zone of 0.2 (the rest is scaled to 0..1). A stick direction pushed past 0.5 also acts as a button and is released below 0.4, so a stick can fire actions and move a menu. The mouse's motion adds up in pixels until the end of the frame (end_frame, which the runtime calls).
  • Panels and text boxes. InputDevices takes KeyboardCaptured and MouseCaptured functions (the runtime gives it the dev overlay's WantsKeyboard and WantsMouse): while true, new presses and the mouse's motion are not routed. Releases always are, so a key that was pressed before a text box got focus cannot stay down. Losing the window's focus releases everything.
  • Changing contexts drops what was waiting (a hold that had not come due, a first tap).

docs.title: Rebinding
docs.text:
input:listen()                                               -- the next input is not routed: it is reported
input.captured:connect(function(binding) print(binding) end)  -- "Shift+F", "Joy LY-", "Mouse Wheel Up"
input.map:set_bindings("lights", { binding, "Joy RB" })

A key goes by the modifiers held with it; a modifier key alone does not count (the router waits for the key it goes with); a stick or trigger counts when pushed past half way. get_label(action) is what to show the player: the binding as their keyboard names it (Z on AZERTY for a W binding, & for a key that types it), its gamepad button (Pad A) when a gamepad was used last, or – when unbound; InputActionRouter.label_binding(text) does the same for any text (Hold Ctrl+Left mouse).

The player's bindings are saved as what differs from the defaults, as text (map:save_text()), one line per action, which a game keeps in its user settings and applies at startup with map:load_text(text):

lights = Hold L | Joy RB
road_lights =

load_text returns the lines it could not apply (an action that no longer exists, a binding that does not read) and applies the rest. From C#, Save() and Load() use a dictionary of string arrays.

docs.title: From C
docs.text:
var map = new InputActionMap();
map.AddAction("lights", ["vehicle"], ["L"]);
var router = new InputActionRouter { Map = map, Contexts = ["vehicle"] };
using var devices = new InputDevices(router) { KeyboardCaptured = () => imgui.WantsKeyboard };   // after PlatformHost.Initialize

// each frame, after PlatformHost.PumpEvents():
router.Update(InputDevices.Now);           // fires ActionFired for holds and taps that came due
// …logic reads router.GetStrength("lights")…
router.EndFrame();

Press, Release, Axis and Poll take explicit times in seconds, for tests and replays. ScriptSession.Progress calls Update itself and EndFrame ends the frame.

docs.title: Not done
docs.text: Gamepad rumble, touch, gamepad hot-plug events for scripts, per-device bindings and chords of several keys (modifiers are the only combination). Steam Input's own action sets are not used (a Steam controller configuration arrives as an SDL gamepad).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Input.Tests covers parsing, key names, the map (clashes, saving), the router (modifiers, hold, double tap, axes, listening) and the SDL devices on the dummy video driver with pushed events. Tests/Luau/input.test.luau runs the same checks, with a catalog of about 45 actions, from a script, in the NativeAOT binary too.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text: Apogee.Platform is the engine's window and event layer over SDL3. It runs on the main thread, as SDL requires.

docs.title: Lifetime and events
docs.text:
PlatformHost.Initialize();                       // SDL video + events + gamepads; PlatformHost.Initialize("dummy") for headless tests
using var window = new Window("My game", 1280, 720, WindowOptions.Resizable | WindowOptions.HighPixelDensity | GraphicsDevice.RequiredWindowOptions());

while (!PlatformHost.QuitRequested && !window.CloseRequested)
{
    PlatformHost.PumpEvents();
    // …update and render…
}
window.Dispose();
PlatformHost.Shutdown();

PumpEvents drains SDL's queue once per frame. A window learns about its own close request, minimize/restore and focus changes; PlatformHost.QuitRequested is set by the platform's quit event. The application decides what a close request means, so CloseRequested stays set until ClearCloseRequest(). PlatformHost.RawEvent is called with every SDL event before the platform handles it: the dev tools' input backend and InputDevices (see Input actions) hook in there.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: PixelSize is the drawable size in pixels, which is what a swapchain is created with; LogicalSize is in points, which is what the window manager and mouse coordinates use. They differ on high-density displays (PixelDensity is the ratio) when the window was created with HighPixelDensity. ConsumeResize() returns true once after the pixel size changed, which is the cue to recreate the swapchain.

docs.title: Windows for a graphics API
docs.text: A window is made for the API it will be drawn with: WindowOptions.Vulkan (loads the Vulkan loader) or WindowOptions.Metal. Ask the graphics layer which: GraphicsDevice.RequiredWindowOptions() (Vulkan for now; Metal on macOS when that backend exists). Apogee.Platform knows no graphics API beyond that flag: the instance extensions and the surface are the graphics backend's business (it uses window.NativeHandle, the SDL_Window*, and window.PixelSize), see Graphics.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: The tests use SDL's dummy video driver, which has windows but no display, and push synthetic events into the queue, so they run on a build server.

docs.title: Runtime and Luau tests
docs.text:
Apogee.Runtime is the game host: one executable, CoreCLR in dev builds and NativeAOT when shipped (./build.sh aot publishes it to Bin/publish/runtime). Its command line is parsed by hand so that it stays AOT-safe.

Apogee.Runtime                                    load the native libraries and run the smoke tests
Apogee.Runtime --luau-test <folder> [--luau-filter <text>]
Apogee.Runtime --run <file.luau> [--frames <n>]   a script with a `world` global, in a window (until it is closed, or n frames)
    --headless                                    no window and no GPU: n frames (default 1)
    --headless --screenshot <file.png>            no window, rendered on the GPU: the last frame as an image
    --size <w>x<h>  --overlay  --gpu <name>       the window or image size (1280x720), the dev overlay in images, which GPU
Apogee.Runtime --game <folder> [--user <folder>]  a game: its packages and mods (see Packages and mods), then the same loops as --run
Apogee.Runtime --workshop-upload <mod folder> ... publish a mod folder as a Steam Workshop item (only describes it without --confirm; see Steam)
Apogee.Runtime --luau-defs <folder>               apogee.d.luau and the engine's Luau modules, for luau-lsp

Exit codes: 0 fine, 1 bad arguments, missing files or failed tests, 2 a script or the engine failed (including Vulkan and window errors), 3 the Vulkan validation layer reported errors.

docs.title: Apogee.Host: what runs a game
docs.text:
Source/Apogee.Host holds what the runtime and the editor share, so that both run a game the same way: ScriptSession (the world, the Luau VM, physics, audio, Steam, the UI, the model library and the hot reloader, made from a script or a game folder), WorldView (the world drawn through its main camera), FrameOverlay (the game's UI and then the dev tools over the picture), GameLibrary (the script table game) and, in Apogee.Host.Editing, the editor's undo and redo: EditHistory and the commands it runs (SetComponentCommand, AddComponentCommand, RemoveComponentCommand, CreateEntityCommand, DestroyEntityCommand, ReparentCommand, RenameCommand, CompositeCommand). Apogee.Runtime is the command line and the three loops over them.

EditHistory.Execute(command) runs a command and records it; Undo and Redo take it back and do it again; the changes of one gesture (a drag of a slider, many small SetComponentCommands on one component) merge into one step until Seal() is called, which the editor does when the mouse is let go. Deleting and creating entities are undone through snapshots, so an entity comes back under the same id and the selection and the other commands in the history still point at it. ReparentCommand keeps the entity where it is in the world (it rewrites its Transform) and refuses a parent that is the entity itself or one of its descendants. A session registers the scene converter for ModelRenderer.Model (the model's path) and leaves physics bodies out of scenes. RenderTarget.Texture(image, bindlessIndex) renders the world into an image that is left ready to be sampled, for the editor's viewport.

docs.title: The frame loop of --run
docs.text:
Each frame steps the world, runs an ImGui frame in which the scripts' devtools.on_gui functions draw, and draws that over a cleared background. There are three loops, which differ only in where the frame goes (RuntimeLoop):

  • A window (the default): an SDL window with a Vulkan swapchain, set up as the viewer sample does it. ImGui gets the window's input, so the panels are live, and the dev overlay is on (F1 toggles it). Esc, closing the window, or --frames ends it. The time step is the real one, capped at a quarter second.
  • --headless --screenshot: no window, an offscreen image of --size, and a fixed 1/60 s step, so that frame n always looks the same. The last frame is written as a PNG. The overlay is left out unless --overlay, because its timings change from run to run. CI renders the fixture game (Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame) this way on lavapipe.
  • --headless: no window and no GPU. The frames run and nothing is shown, but everything a script does with imgui runs. This is what CI runs on machines without Vulkan.

The scripts' imgui calls do nothing outside an ImGui frame, so the same script works in all three.

docs.title: Luau tests
docs.text:
--luau-test runs every *.test.luau under a folder, sorted, skipping folders that start with a dot. Each file gets a VM of its own, so one file's globals, modules and worlds cannot touch another's; the file may require anything under the folder, with the @engine/test library:

local test = require("@engine/test")

test.describe("health", function()
    test.it("drops when hit", function()
        local world = test.world()                      -- this case's own World, destroyed after it
        local Health = world:component("Health", { hp = "i32" })
        local hero = world:create_entity()
        world:set(hero, Health, { hp = 10 })
        world:system("Poison", { Health }, function(_, health) health.hp -= 1 end)

        test.frames(3)                                   -- three frames of that world

        test.expect(world:get(hero, Health).hp).toBe(7)
    end)
end)

A file's describe bodies run as it loads and collect its cases; the cases then run in order, one frame at a time, each in a coroutine. An error in a describe body is reported as a failure named after it. Expectations are toBe, toEqual (deep), toBeNear(n, epsilon), toBeTruthy, toBeFalsy, toBeNil, toThrow(text) and toContainText(text), and .never negates any of them. print goes to the output. --luau-filter text runs the cases whose full name (describe > case) contains it. A case that waits for more than 100 000 frames, or one call that outlives the 10 s time budget, fails the file.

The output, and the same from code (LuauTestRunner.Run):

ok   ecs.test.luau (8 passed)
FAIL bad.test.luau (1 passed, 1 failed)
  - group > fails
    bad.test.luau:5: expected: 1 to be 2

Luau tests: 9 passed, 1 failed, in 2 files (0.02 s).

The engine's own Luau tests are in Tests/Luau. They run in dotnet test (in the JIT build) and in CI against the published NativeAOT binary.

docs.title: Input
docs.text: A game's scripts see the global input, an InputActionRouter whose map they fill with their actions (see Input actions). The windowed loop feeds it from SDL events; ScriptSession.Progress fires what time made due before the systems run, and EndFrame resets the mouse's motion. A headless run has no devices, and scripts can press inputs by hand.

docs.title: Physics
docs.text: A game's scripts see the global physics, the simulation of the session's world (see Physics). ScriptSession.Progress steps it before the world each frame, so that the systems and scripts of the frame see the poses it wrote. It is disposed before the ECS world, which holds its observer.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: The global audio is the session's AudioSystem (see Audio). It plays on the sound device only in a real run: --headless and tests mix into nowhere (OpenAL Soft's loopback device, in the game's time). ScriptSession.Progress updates it after the world has progressed, and it is disposed before the physics world and the ECS world.

docs.title: Steam
docs.text: The global steam is the session's SteamSystem (see Steam), the base game's only. A real (windowed) game connects to Steam; --headless, --run scripts and tests get an inactive one. ScriptSession.Progress updates it first, so that Steam's callbacks are signals before the systems and scripts of the frame run. StartGame also mounts cloud:// and, with Steam running, workshop://.

docs.title: Network
docs.text: The global net is the session's NetSystem (see Network), the base game's only. It is made for every session and opens no socket until a script listens or connects. ScriptSession.Progress updates it after Steam's callbacks and before the input, and it is disposed before Steam.

docs.title: Editor definitions
docs.text: --luau-defs <folder> writes apogee.d.luau, the API from the registry (see Scripting), and engine/<name>.luau, copies of the engine's modules, so that luau-lsp can resolve require("@engine/test"). A project's .luaurc points the engine alias at that folder; at run time the alias is built in.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests (the command line and each command, with their exit codes, and the fixture game run from a folder and from a pack) and, in Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests, the runner itself: discovery order, the report, a file that does not compile, errors outside a case, filters, files that share nothing, and a loop stopped by the time budget.

docs.title: What a game asks of the program
docs.text: The script table game is for a game that runs inside Apogee.Runtime: game.quit() ends the run at the end of the frame (a menu's Quit; a headless run stops too), and game.set_escape_quits(false) stops the Escape key from ending a run in a window, which is the default so that a script or a sample can be closed: a game whose Escape opens its own menu turns it off. See the UI sample.

docs.title: Scripting
docs.text: Apogee.Scripting runs Luau, the only scripting language: the engine is C#, and games and mods are written in Luau and data. It sits on the Luau library and the layer over its C API described in Native libraries.

docs.title: The VM and its owners
docs.text:
using var vm = new LuauVm(new LuauVmOptions { MemoryLimit = 256 << 20, TimeBudgetMilliseconds = 100 });
ScriptOwner mod = vm.CreateOwner("coolmod", isMod: true, memoryLimit: 32 << 20, timeBudgetMilliseconds: 20);

IReadOnlyList<Value> results = vm.Execute(mod, "@/mods/coolmod/main.luau", source);   // what the chunk returns

There is one VM for the game and all its mods. What separates them is the ScriptOwner: the base game's (vm.BaseOwner) or one mod's.

  • Memory: everything an owner's scripts allocate is counted in the owner's memory category (up to 255 owners in a VM). Going over the owner's MemoryLimit is a memory error in that owner's code at its next call or loop iteration; the other owners are not affected. MemoryLimit of the VM is the hard limit for everyone. An owner that is over its limit has its garbage collected before its next call, so one failure does not make the next call fail too.
  • Time: each call gets the owner's TimeBudgetMilliseconds (the VM's default when it has none). Once a call's time is up, every function call and loop iteration raises, so a script's own pcall cannot swallow it. A long native function (string.rep of a gigabyte) is not interrupted.
  • Coroutines belong to the owner of the script that made them, and so do the objects they allocate.
  • A module that a script requires runs as that script's owner, unless LuauVmOptions.OwnerOfModule (the packages) says whose file it is.

A failure is a ScriptException with a Kind (Compile, Runtime, Timeout, Memory) and the script's message; a runtime error has a traceback. An error that crosses coroutine.wrap arrives as a plain runtime error whose message is "not enough memory".

docs.title: The sandbox
docs.text:
Every script runs in a thread of its own with its own globals over the VM's read-only ones (luaL_sandbox, luaL_sandboxthread): a script cannot change string or math, and what it assigns to a global is not seen by the next script. The base library is Luau's, without getfenv, setfenv and loadstring: code comes from require, never from a string. print and warn go to LuauVmOptions.Output (the log by default, with the owner's id), and Vector3(x, y, z) makes a vector (Quat makes rotations: see Math); the compiler turns calls with constant arguments into constants.

Scripts with --!native on their first line are compiled to machine code where the machine supports it (NativeCodeEnabled).

docs.title: require
docs.text:
Require-by-string, as Luau's RFC describes it:

Request Means ./x, ../x relative to the folder of the requiring file @alias/x the alias from the nearest .luaurc ({ "aliases": { "lib": "./libs" } }, comments allowed) in that folder or above it @self/x relative to the folder of an init.luau (an error from any other file) @engine/name a module of the engine, added with AddEmbeddedModule

A module is x.luau or x/init.luau; having both is an error. Paths cannot leave the roots given to AddRoot. A module runs once in a thread of its own and its single result is cached, so a module cannot yield into its requirer, one that returns zero or two values is an error, and a cycle is reported (cyclic require). The requiring file is the nearest Luau function on the stack, so pcall(require, "./x") works from where it was written. A chunk is a file when its name is @path; a =name chunk is not, so it can only require @engine modules.

Scripts are read through IScriptFileSystem: the real file system by default, or VfsScriptFiles for the content file system (res://, mod://<id>/, zips, packs). Add what scripts may load from with AddRoot (a folder, or a prefix such as res://); ./ and ../ never climb out of a scheme, and @alias comes from the nearest .luaurc as usual.

docs.title: Engine objects in scripts
docs.text:
The classes of the registry are what scripts see. A class marked Scriptable = false is not there at all (an object of it is nil).

local actor = Actor.new()                       -- only for Creatable classes
actor.name = "rex"                              -- properties: strings, numbers, vectors, objects, lists, enums
actor.mood = "very_happy"                       -- an enum is the snake_case name of its member
actor.traits = { "fast", "tough_skin" }         -- a [Flags] enum is a list of names
local moved, speed = actor:try_move(Vector3(1, 0, 0), 2)   -- methods take ':'; a tuple gives several results
actor.hurt:connect(function(amount, who) print(amount) end)   -- signals
  • Objects are handles. A script holds an object by its slot and generation (SlotHandle), never by a pointer. == and table keys work, because there is one userdata per live object. A destroyed object, or one whose slot was reused, raises attempt to use a destroyed object.
  • Types are checked. Arguments and values are converted by the declared type, strictly (a number is not a string, a float is not an integer), and a mistake names the member: bad argument #1 (word) to 'speak': expected string, got number.
  • An object a script creates with Class.new() belongs to the script: it is destroyed when the script no longer holds it, unless the engine called Adopt() on it. (The collector only notes it; LuauVm.ProcessPending() destroys, after every Execute and whenever a game loop calls it.) Every other object lives until the engine calls Destroy().
  • Signals: obj.signal:connect(fn) returns a connection with :disconnect() and .connected. A handler that fails is logged with its traceback and the emitter never sees it. A connection stays until it is disconnected or its object is destroyed (ProcessPending lets go of those).
  • Mods: an object of a class with ModsBlocked raises mod "x" can't use Steam: it is the base game's when a mod's script uses it.
  • Static methods are on the class (Actor.make("rex")); a [ScriptLibrary("imgui")] class is a read-only global table.
  • Functions a script passes to the engine come back as ScriptFunctions. Calling one runs it as its owner, on a thread of the owner's, with the owner's time budget.
  • Entities are numbers. A pair (a relationship) does not fit in the 53 bits of a number, so it is a table of two ids: world:add(e, { likes, apple }).
  • vectors have v:length(), v:normalized(), v:dot(w), v:cross(w) and the rest of Luau's vector library as methods.

A host gives scripts its objects with vm.SetGlobal("world", world). The scripts compiled after that read world.x every time (Luau would otherwise resolve global.field once, when a function loads, which is wrong for an object whose members change). Types are registered when their assembly's module initializer runs; make sure the assemblies with described classes are loaded before the VM is made.

docs.title: ECS from scripts
docs.text:
World is a class like the others (world:create_entity("hero"), world:lookup, world:progress(dt), world.frame, world.delta_time) and has the calls that take tables and functions, written by hand and listed in the definitions:

local Position = world:component("Position", { value = "vec3", on = "bool" })    -- or world:component("Health") for one the engine registered
local e = world:create_entity()
world:set(e, Position, { value = Vector3(1, 2, 3) })
local p = world:get(e, Position)                    -- a copy: { value = ..., on = false }

world:each({ Position, { Frozen, "not" } }, function(entity, position)    -- views that write in place
    position.value += Vector3(0, 1, 0)
end)
world:system("Move", { Position, Velocity }, function(entity, pos, vel)
    pos.value += vel.value * world.delta_time
end, "on_update")                                   -- a real Flecs system, in a phase

Field types are bool, i8 … u64, f32, f64, vec3, dvec3 (a world position, narrowed to a vector in scripts), quat and entity. The view a callback gets is the component's memory, not a copy; it is only valid during the call (a component view is only valid during the call it was given to). Writing through a view does not notify observers; world:set does. Structural changes inside each are applied when it ends. An error in each reaches its caller. A system that fails is logged with its traceback and skipped for the rest of that frame, and the other systems still run.

docs.title: Definitions for the editor
docs.text:
DefinitionWriter.Write() writes the API as Luau type definitions (apogee.d.luau) from the registry: classes as declare extern type, enums as unions of strings, signals as Signal<…>, libraries and statics as declare tables, and the hand-written methods with the declarations they were registered with. A host adds the globals it sets (DefinitionOptions.Globals: the runtime declares world) and can leave classes out (HiddenClasses: its smoke-test class). The runtime's --luau-defs <folder> writes the file and the engine's Luau modules (engine/test.luau) to a folder (see Runtime).

To use it in VS Code with the luau-lsp extension: run Apogee.Runtime --luau-defs Bin/defs, add the file to "luau-lsp.types.definitionFiles" ({ "@apogee": "Bin/defs/apogee.d.luau" }), and give each script folder a .luaurc whose engine alias points at Bin/defs/engine, so that require("@engine/test") resolves (at run time the alias is built in; the .luaurc is only for tools). See Samples/Scripting/.luaurc. From a terminal:

luau-lsp analyze --platform=standard --definitions=@apogee=Bin/defs/apogee.d.luau Samples/Scripting Samples/Mods Bin/defs/engine

CI runs exactly that, on Linux, with a pinned luau-lsp (1.70.1), and fails on any error: the engine's own modules type-check against the generated file (the samples are run by hand, not in CI; they are written to type-check too).

Things the definitions cannot say, found by running luau-lsp:

  • Flag lists and field tables that may be omitted are declared ({ Flags } | {})? (and ({ [string]: FieldType } | {})? for world:component). luau-lsp's default solver infers a literal such as { "no_move" } as { string } and refuses it against { Flags }?; the union with an empty table takes the literal, nothing and nil in both solvers, and hover still lists the names.
