The cost is that a misspelled flag in an optional list is not reported. A required list ({ Flags }) is checked.
  • Vector methods (v:length(), v:dot(w), v:cross(w)) are not in the file: vector is a primitive of Luau, which a definitions file cannot extend, so luau-lsp reports them as missing keys. Use them from nonstrict scripts, or --!nolint; the arithmetic operators are fine.
  • type aliases in the file (Entity, the enums) are not visible to scripts, only to the declarations. Scripts name the class types (World, Animal).
  • world:lookup returns 0 for a missing entity, not nil, and 0 is truthy in Luau: compare with == 0.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests (needs the luau native library): values, the sandbox, errors with tracebacks, time and memory limits per owner including coroutines, native code, require with real files, the bridge (properties, methods, enums, lists, identity, lifetimes, signals, libraries, mods), the ECS from scripts, and the definitions (an exact expected block). The runtime's smoke test runs the bridge and the ECS from a script under NativeAOT, which CI runs.

docs.title: Dev tools
docs.text: Apogee.DevTools is Dear ImGui (the docking branch, through cimgui) wired into the engine: an SDL3 input backend and a Vulkan renderer backend written in C#, a thin C# layer over ImGui's C API, and the engine's debug window. The editor and the game's own dev windows use the same pieces.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
using var imgui = new ImGuiHost();
imgui.Attach(window);                                              // input from this window
using var imguiRenderer = new ImGuiRenderer(device);               // draws ImGui's output
var overlay = new DevOverlay();

// each frame
imgui.BeginFrame(deltaSeconds);                                    // display size and scale come from the window
overlay.Draw(new DevOverlayData { GpuName = gpuName, CpuFrameMilliseconds = cpuMs, GpuTimings = loop.Timings,
                                  Plan = renderer.LastPlan, Stats = renderer.LastStats, Settings = settings, Camera = camera });
Ui.Begin("My window"); Ui.Text("anything"); Ui.End();             // any ImGui widgets
imgui.EndFrame();

renderer.Render(frame, scene, camera, target, settings, overlay: imguiRenderer);   // the overlay is the last pass of the frame's graph

imgui.WantsMouse / WantsKeyboard say when ImGui has the pointer over a widget or a text field active: the game should not also react then.

docs.title: Docking
docs.text:
The vendored Dear ImGui is the docking branch (the tag v1.93.0-docking, see ThirdParty/README.md; before 2026-11-05 it was by mistake a master commit without the docking API). Docking is off until a host asks for it, because the dev overlay's windows are meant to float:

imgui.EnableDocking();
// each frame, before the windows that should dock:
uint dockspace = ImGui.DockSpaceOverViewport(0, ImGui.GetMainViewport(), ImGuiDockNodeFlags.PassthruCentralNode, null);

Windows dock inside the one SDL window. ImGui's multi-viewport (windows that leave the main window as OS windows) is not enabled, so there is one swapchain. The editor builds its layout on this.

docs.title: The SDL input backend
docs.text: ImGuiHost.Attach(window) listens to PlatformHost.RawEvent, so ImGui gets its input as the platform pumps events: the pointer and buttons (SDL's left, middle, right are reordered to ImGui's), the wheel, every key (an SDL scancode to an ImGuiKey table: letters, digits, function keys, arrows, the keypad, modifiers), typed text (UTF-8), window focus, and the pointer leaving the window. Each frame it also sets the OS mouse cursor to the one ImGui asks for (arrow, text beam, resize arrows) and starts or stops SDL text input as text fields appear. The clipboard goes through SDL. Events of other windows are ignored; AttachToAllWindows() is for headless use.

docs.title: Text
docs.text: Dear ImGui rasterizes its fonts with FreeType (imgui_freetype.cpp is part of the cimgui library, see Native libraries): text is hinted and anti-aliased by FreeType instead of ImGui's built-in stb_truetype (which is still compiled in, because cimgui calls it, but is not the default). The loader's name (FreeType (2.15.0; 2.15.0), compiled against and linked) is atlas->FontLoader->Name, which TheGlyphsAreRasterizedByFreeType checks. Colour glyphs are off (ImGuiFreeTypeLoaderFlags.LoadColor), so the atlas stays a single-channel coverage image that ImGuiRenderer expands to RGBA8; the flags can be set per font through ImFontConfig.FontLoaderFlags.

docs.title: The Vulkan renderer backend
docs.text: ImGuiRenderer is an IRenderOverlay: it adds one pass to the frame's render graph that draws on the output after tone mapping. It follows Dear ImGui 1.92's texture protocol: ImGui says which textures to create, update and destroy, and the backend answers with an id per texture. The font atlas becomes an RGBA8 image with a bindless slot; an update creates a new image and defers freeing the old one until the GPU has finished the frame that may still sample it. Vertices and indices of every draw list are copied into per-frame-in-flight buffers that grow when needed, and the shader pulls the vertices (imgui.slang, ImGui's 20-byte vertex) with push constants for the projection and the texture. Clip rectangles become scissors, alpha blending is straight alpha, and the output image is the (UNORM) swapchain so the colours ImGui chose reach the screen unchanged.

docs.title: The overlay window
docs.text:
DevOverlay.Draw shows one window with four sections, and above them, in red, the shader errors (DevOverlayData.ShaderErrors, fill it with ShaderLibrary.Errors) while a shader that was edited does not compile: the renderers keep using the shader as it was, and the message, with the file and line, stays until an edit that compiles:

  • Frame: frames per second, average, minimum and maximum frame time, and an ImPlot plot of the last 240 frames, newest on the right (the history keeps filling while the window is hidden, Visible = false).
  • GPU passes: a stacked ImPlot plot of the GPU milliseconds of each top-level render graph pass over the last 240 frames (DevOverlay.GpuHistory; a pass that did not run in a frame has 0 there, and a section inside a pass, Forward/lights, is part of it), and under it the table of every section of the last finished frame, with bars.
  • Render graph: the passes that ran and the ones culled, their type, barriers and what they write, and how many images the graph shares.
  • Lighting: draws, lights, whether the clusters were rebuilt; exposure, the view (final image or the cluster-light heatmap), the camera's field of view and the cluster range, all edited live.

Ui has the ImGui calls the dev tools need with C# strings and ref values (windows, text, sliders, checkboxes, combos, plots, tables, headers); for anything else call ImGui from Apogee.Native.CImGui directly.

docs.title: ImPlot, ImGuizmo and imnodes
docs.text:
Three more libraries sit in the same shared library as Dear ImGui (they use its C++ API and its context, and ImGui's symbols are hidden), each with a small C API of ours over it (see ThirdParty/README.md, and the native libraries):

  • ImPlot (Apogee.Native.ImPlot, class Plot) draws plots. Plots in Apogee.DevTools is the surface the overlay uses, with strings and spans: if (Plots.Begin("id", size)) { Plots.Axes(...); Plots.Limits(...); Plots.Line("label", values, spec); Plots.Shaded(...); Plots.Band(...); Plots.Bars(...); Plots.End(); }.
  • ImGuizmo (Apogee.Native.ImGuizmo, class Gizmo) draws move, rotate and scale gizmos and a view cube over a viewport: Gizmo.BeginFrame(), Gizmo.SetRect(...), then Gizmo.Manipulate(view, projection, operation, mode, matrix, ...) changes the matrix in place while the player drags (the matrices are 16 floats, column-major).
  • imnodes (Apogee.Native.ImNodes, class Nodes) draws node editors: nodes with title bars and pins, links, a minimap, selection and positions.

ImGuiHost makes an ImPlot context and an imnodes context with the ImGui one and makes them current at the start of every frame; they are destroyed with it.

docs.title: Dear ImGui for Luau scripts
docs.text:
ImGuiLibrary ([ScriptLibrary("imgui")]) is the global table imgui, written with the same source generator as everything else, so its declarations in the .d.luau definitions cannot drift from the code. Functions are snake_case; a widget returns changed, value; a window, tree, table, menu, tab or popup that can be open returns whether it is, and every begin_… has its end_… (a script that forgets one, or fails between them, is put right at the end of the frame by ImGui's error recovery). Colors are tables of 3 or 4 numbers from 0 to 1, a combo's index counts from 1, flags and conditions are the names of ImGui's enums ({ "no_title_bar", "no_resize" }, "always"), and ids are the labels, with ImGui's ## and ###.

devtools.on_gui(function()                                 -- called every frame, inside the ImGui frame
    if imgui.begin_window("Spawner", nil, { "always_auto_resize" }) then
        imgui.text("entities: " .. world:count({ Position }))
        local changed, rate = imgui.slider_float("Rate", rate, 0, 10)
        if imgui.button("Spawn") then spawn() end
        devtools.watch("rate", rate)                        -- shown in the engine's debug window
    end
    imgui.end_window()
end)

With no frame open (a headless run, a shipped game that has no overlay) every imgui call does nothing and returns what it was given, so tool code can stay in the game. devtools.frame_open() says which it is. devtools.on_gui(fn) registers a drawing function and returns an id for devtools.remove_gui(id); the host calls ScriptGui.RunGui() once a frame between ImGuiHost.BeginFrame and EndFrame, and a function that raises is logged and removed. devtools.watch(name, value) adds a row to the debug window. The runtime's --run does this every frame, headless. The surface is: windows, text, widgets, layout, ids, trees, tables, menus, tabs, popups, tooltips, style, show_demo_window); ImPlot, ImGuizmo and imnodes are not in the Luau library yet: they are for the dev overlay and the editor, in C#.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The Luau library runs against real ImGui frames with no window and no GPU: widgets return what they were given, draw data is produced, a mouse click on a button reaches the script, a script that forgets an end or fails in the middle does not break later frames, gui functions run and are removed when they fail, and the idle behavior.

ImGuiExtensionTests calls each of the three libraries in a headless frame (a quiet gizmo changes nothing and draws, a plot draws its four kinds of item in float and double, a node editor keeps the positions it was given and draws two nodes and a link) and reads how many vertices the frame produced. The overlay's GPU history (a line per top-level pass, zero where it did not run, the last 240 frames) is tested without a window.

The input translation runs on SDL's dummy video driver with synthetic events: the key table, buttons, the wheel, text, window filtering, display size and who wants the mouse. The renderer tests draw to an offscreen target and check where pixels land (a window and nothing outside it, glyphs from the atlas, clipping at the corners), that the atlas's bindless slot is released with the renderer, that the buffers grow, and that the overlay is the last pass of a real SceneRenderer frame. ImGui keeps a process-wide current context, so these tests run one at a time.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
Very bare-bones for now

The editor is very bare-bones for now: it cannot import 3D models or other assets (it only places and re-imports files already in the game folder), and it has no materials, no animations and no game export. See What is not here.

Source/Apogee.Editor is an ImGui editor for a game folder. It is a CoreCLR program (a tool, never published with NativeAOT) built on Dear ImGui with docking, ImGuizmo, ImPlot and imnodes, Apogee.Host and the scene format.

dotnet run --project Source/Apogee.Editor -- <game folder> [--user <folder>]

The layout (a dock space: hierarchy on the left, inspector on the right, the viewport in the middle, tabs of assets, console, profiler and render graph below) is saved to imgui.ini in ~/.local/share/Apogee/Editor (the platform's local application data folder); the first run, with no file, builds the default one. Quitting with unsaved changes asks first.

docs.title: The panels
docs.text:
• Viewport. The world drawn into an image that ImGui shows as a texture (RenderTarget.Texture; one image per frame in flight, so the GPU never samples what the frame is writing). The editor's camera is not an entity: right mouse button looks around and, with W A S D Q E (Shift is faster), flies; middle button pans; the wheel zooms; F frames the selection. A click that does not drag picks the entity under the pointer: a ray against the models' bounds (measured from the file, so no GPU is needed), and a small sphere for entities that have no model (lights, cameras, empty entities). ImGuizmo moves, rotates and scales the selection (W, E and R choose; local or world axes; optional snapping); a drag is one undo step. The view cube in the corner turns the camera. The helpers drawn as debug lines (a ground grid, the selection's bounds, a mark for each light and camera) can be turned off. Dropping a .glb or .gltf from the assets panel makes an entity at the point of the ground under the pointer.
  • Hierarchy. The scene as a tree: click to select, double click or F2 to rename, Delete, Ctrl+D to duplicate, right click for the menu, and drag an entity onto another to make it a child (onto the empty space below to make it a root). The entity keeps its place in the world when it changes parent, and a name a sibling already has is made unique.
  • Inspector. The components of the selected entity, drawn from the registry's descriptions: a checkbox, drag field, slider (when [Property] gives a Min and a Max), three drag fields for a vector or a double position, three angles for a rotation, a drop target for an entity reference, and for ModelRenderer.Model the model's path (type one, or drop a model file on it). Fields are grouped under their Category, Hidden ones are left out and ReadOnly ones greyed; right click a component to remove it; Add component lists every registered component. See what an inspector shows.
  • Assets. The virtual file system: res:// and, when listed, the packages' mod://id/ folders; each importable file shows whether it is imported, out of date, or not imported yet (AssetImporter.StatusOf), and Re-import imports one file again (Reimport). Double click a .ascene to open it; drag a model into the viewport or the inspector.
  • Console. The log, filtered by level.
  • Profiler. The dev overlay's ImPlot plots: frame times, and the GPU time of every pass stacked over the last 240 frames, with the table.
  • Render graph. The last viewport frame's render graph as a read-only imnodes view: a node for each pass that ran, its inputs and outputs, and a link from the pass that last wrote a resource to the passes that read it.

docs.title: Scenes and undo
docs.text: File creates, opens and saves scenes (.ascene text, see ecs); Save as takes a virtual path (res://scenes/level), and the scenes of the game are listed by Open. Every edit is a command on an EditHistory (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z): component values (a drag is one step), adding and removing components, creating, duplicating and deleting entities (a deleted branch comes back under the same ids), renaming and reparenting. Opening or creating a scene clears the history.

docs.title: Play
docs.text:
Play (F5) runs the game inside the editor. The editor keeps a snapshot of the world, replaces its session with the game's (the same ScriptSession the runtime makes: packages, mods and scripts, physics, audio, the UI) over a copy of the scene, loaded before the scripts run, and shows the game in the viewport through the world's main camera (or the editor's camera when it has none, or when Game camera is off). The game gets the pointer and the input actions while the viewport is hovered or focused; keys and typed text also go to the game's own UI (its text fields) while the viewport has the keyboard; the pointer reaches it through the panel, in the panel's coordinates. Pause and Step freeze and advance the world. Stop makes an editing session again and puts the world back as it was under the same entity ids, so the selection and the undo history still point at the same entities. A game whose scripts fail does not start: the editor says why and stays in editing. Only one session exists at a time (the UI library and others hold process-wide state), which is why Play and Stop replace it. Debug toggles the physics shapes and RmlUi's debugger while playing.

Editing is off while playing: the panels show the game's world, read-only.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: Importing 3D models and other assets from inside the editor (new files go through Apogee.Runtime --import, see Asset import), materials, animations, exporting a game, multiple selection, a scene file dialog beyond a list, material and logic graph editors (imnodes is ready for them), multi-viewport windows, and a physics ray cast for picking (an editing session has no physics bodies). Sound plays in play mode through OpenAL Soft (Audio), which ships beside the editor like any other library.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Editor.Tests: the field codec for every FieldKind (a rotation as angles, integers clamped), the editor camera, picking (rays, boxes, spheres, the ground), the project (creating, naming, reparenting, duplicating and deleting through the history; a scene saved to a file and opened again with the model's path; Play running the game's scripts over the scene and Stop restoring the world under the same ids with the selection and history intact; a failing game), and, on a GPU (skipped without one), a frame of the viewport with no validation errors whose render graph lays out as nodes. Tests/Apogee.Host.Tests covers the history and its commands.

docs.title: User interface
docs.text:
Apogee.UI is the game's UI: RmlUi (HTML and CSS as the game UI world knows them, in RML and RCSS) on the engine's renderer, file system and input, behind the script global ui. A UI is a document (RML text, from a file or built in code) of elements that scripts make, move, style and listen to. Luau-only mods author UI the same way the base game does, with documents that carry their own scripts and data models. The ImGui of the dev tools is a different thing: it is for tools and the editor, this is for players.

local doc = ui:load_document("res://ui/menu.rml")          -- or ui:load_document_text(rml), or ui:create_document() for an empty one
doc:show()
doc:by_id("start"):listen("click", function(event)
    print("clicked", event.target.id, event:get_number("mouse_x"))
end)

local note = doc:create_element("div")                     -- made in code, in no tree yet
note.class_name = "toast"
note:append(note:create_text("Saved"))
doc:append(note)                                           -- the document owns it now

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
• UiSystem (Source/Apogee.UI/UiSystem.cs) starts RmlUi with one context, the screen, and owns what RmlUi asks of its host: files (read through the virtual file system, so res://, mod://<id>/ and user:// paths work in documents' <link>s and srcs, and relative ones resolve against the document), images (decoded by the content loader, premultiplied on loading), the clipboard, the cursor, the clock and the log. There is one at a time, because RmlUi has one state per process. Update(dt) lays out and runs animations; SetSize(width, height, density) follows the window.
  • UiElement is an element as a script holds it: a handle. It names the element without keeping it alive, so one whose element was destroyed (its document was closed, an ancestor destroyed) answers is_alive = false and every call on it does nothing. An element made with create_element or create_text belongs to the object that holds it until append or insert_before puts it in a tree, which owns it from then on; remove(child) gives it back; letting go of an element that no tree ever held destroys it, and destroy_element() destroys one now.
  • UiEvent is what a listener receives: type, target, current, phase, stop_propagation(), and the event's parameters (get_number("mouse_x"), get_string("value"), has(key)). It is good only inside the handler.
  • UiRenderer draws the picture, as a pass of the render graph over the finished image (IRenderOverlay); OverlayChain puts it under the dev tools. UiInput feeds one window's events to the UI.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
RmlUi has no built-in stylesheet: a div is display: inline and takes no width or height, text has no font, body is only as big as its content. ui_base.rcss (Source/Apogee.UI, embedded in the assembly) is added under every document's own rules, so a document, or a mod, overrides anything in it: block elements, box-sizing: border-box for everything, headings, lists, links, a look for form controls and scrollbars, tables, and a body as big as the screen with the default font. The default font is Inter (regular, bold and italic, SIL OFL 1.1; Source/Apogee.UI/Fonts), registered as the family Inter; ui:load_font(path, family, bold, italic, fallback) adds more from any mounted file. Documents loaded from text have [document from memory] as their source unless load_document_text is given a URL.

doc:close() unloads a document with everything in it. A module that is reloaded (--watch) closes the documents it loaded and the listeners it added, and loads them again.

docs.title: Events and input
docs.text:
element:listen(type, handler, capture?) returns a number for ui:unlisten. Events are the DOM's: click, mousedown, mouseup, mouseover, mouseout, mousemove, keydown, keyup, textinput, focus, blur, change, submit, scroll, resize, transitionend, animationend... They go down to the target (capture) and back up (bubble); event:stop_propagation() ends the trip. A handler that throws is logged and the event goes on: nothing may unwind through RmlUi's native frames. Listeners go when their element does (the system forgets their handlers within a couple of seconds).

The host gives the UI the player's input: UiInput turns SDL's events into the UI's (buttons: SDL's left, middle, right are RmlUi's 0, 2, 1; the wheel's y is flipped; keys by USB scancode; typed text; modifiers) and starts SDL's text input when a text field has the focus. Every call says whether the UI used the input, and ui.wants_mouse (the pointer is over an element) and ui.wants_keyboard (a text field is focused) tell the game to leave it alone: the runtime's input actions are not fed while they are true. A host that shows the UI inside something else (the editor shows the game in a panel) sets UiInput.PointerEnabled = false when it feeds the pointer itself, and UiInput.KeyboardEnabled to a function that says whether keys and text may go to the UI now.

docs.title: Scripts in documents
docs.text:
A document can carry its own Luau, the way RmlUi's Lua plugin lets a document carry Lua. The engine implements the same model on Luau (there is no Lua in the engine): <script> tags, on* attributes and data models.

<rml>
<head>
  <link type="text/rcss" href="menu.rcss"/>
  <script src="menu.luau"/>                       <!-- a file next to the document -->
  <script>
    clicks = 0
    function bump(element, event)                  -- a function in the document's globals
      clicks += 1
      element.inner_rml = "Clicked " .. clicks
    end
  </script>
</head>
<body>
  <button id="b" onclick="bump(element, event)">Click</button>
</body>
</rml>
  • Scripts run in the head, when it has been read and before the body is: define functions and open data models there, and do the rest when the document says it has loaded (document:listen("load", function() ... end)).
  • Each document has globals of its own over the ones every script sees. What a <script> defines is there for that document's on* attributes and for nothing else; use require for state that documents share. document is the document's UiElement.
  • An on* attribute is the body of a function with event (the UiEvent) and element (the element the attribute is on, event.current) in scope. It is compiled when its first event comes, because the element is not in its document yet when its attributes are read. A syntax error is logged then.
  • An attribute runs as whoever wrote it. One in the document's own RML runs as the script that loaded the document, with the document's globals. One that another script puts in with inner_rml or set_attribute (a mod adding to the game's HUD) runs as that script, in globals of its own: it has the mod's limits and file rules, and cannot call the game's functions through the document.
  • <script src> is read through the virtual file system with the rules of the script that loaded the document: a mod can read its own files and the ones it depends on, not another mod's (CanAccessFile). require("./helper") in it is relative to the script's file. The path may be relative to the document or a res:// or mod:// one.
  • Scripts run as the script that called ui:load_document: its memory category and its time budget apply, and a mod's UI scripts cannot do what the mod cannot.
  • A script that fails is logged with the document's name and line, and the rest of the document loads.
  • Without a scripting layer (a bare UiSystem in a C# test) scripts and attributes are ignored with a warning; set UiSystem.ScriptEnvironments to give it one.

docs.title: Data models
docs.text:
A data model ties a table of the script to a document: RmlUi's {{value}}, data-if, data-for, data-class-*, data-style-*, data-value and data-event-*. Open the model before the document that uses it loads (a <script> in the document's head can).

-- menu.luau, a <script src> of menu.rml
local game = { volume = 0.8, name = "Ada", items = { { name = "Sword", qty = 1 } }, player = { hp = 100 } }
function game.buy(event, amount) -- data-event-click="buy(3)"
    table.insert(game.items, { name = "Arrow", qty = amount })
    model:dirty("items")
end
model = ui:open_data_model("game", game)

<body data-model="game">
  <p>{{name}} has {{player.hp}} hp</p>
  <div data-for="item : items">{{item.name}} x{{item.qty}}</div>
  <div data-if="player.hp < 20">Low health!</div>
  <input type="range" min="0" max="1" step="0.1" data-value="volume"/>
  <button data-event-click="buy(3)">Buy</button>
</body>
  • The table is read when RmlUi needs a value, so it is the one source of truth. When you change it, say so: model:dirty("items") for one top-level field (a change inside a struct or a list dirties the field that holds it), model:dirty() for everything, or model:set("volume", 0.5) to write a top-level field and dirty it. The elements update at the next ui:update.
  • The top-level fields are bound when the model opens. Each has to exist then (use false, 0, "" or {} for a value that comes later) and keeps its kind: a number stays a number, a list a list, a table with named fields a struct. A table with elements, or an empty one, is a list (counted from 1 in Luau, from 0 in data-for addresses).
  • Functions in the table are events for data-event-*. They get the UiEvent and the arguments of the expression (buy(3, 'sword') calls game.buy(event, 3, "sword")).
  • data-value writes back: typing in a field, or moving a slider, sets the field in the table (text is converted to the field's number or boolean).
  • A model belongs to the script that opened it and is closed when its module reloads; model:close() closes it now (close its documents first). ui:open_data_model returns nil, with a message in the log, when the name is taken.
  • Integers show without a decimal point (5, not 5.0).

docs.title: The Lua manual, in the engine's names
docs.text:
RmlUi's Lua manual describes the plugin; the engine keeps the model and uses its own snake_case names, like every other script API.

RmlUi Lua plugin Here <script>, <script src>, onclick="..." the same; event, element and document are in scope rmlui.contexts["main"] the ui global (one context, the screen) context:LoadDocument(path) ui:load_document(path), ui:load_document_text(rml), ui:create_document() document:Show(), :Hide(), :Close() doc:show(), doc:hide(), doc:close() document:GetElementById(id) doc:by_id(id) element:AppendChild(e), :RemoveChild(e) el:append(e), el:remove(e) element.inner_rml, .class_name, .id the same properties element:SetAttribute(n, v), :GetAttribute(n) el:set_attribute(n, v), el:get_attribute(n) element.style["width"] = "10px" el:set_property("width", "10px") element:AddEventListener(type, fn) el:listen(type, fn) (a number for ui:unlisten) event.parameters.mouse_x, event:StopPropagation() event:get_number("mouse_x"), event:stop_propagation() context:OpenDataModel(name, table) ui:open_data_model(name, table) assigning to a model field model:set(name, value) or change the table and model:dirty(name) Lua 5.x Luau only; its require is Luau's, relative to the file

docs.title: In the runtime
docs.text: --game and --run give every script ui. Each frame the runtime sizes it to the window (in pixels, with the window's pixel density as the dp unit), feeds it input, steps it after the world and the scripts have run, and draws it over the picture (the 3D world if there is a camera, the plain background otherwise) with the dev overlay on top. The UI renderer is made the first frame after a document was loaded, so a script that only has ImGui panels never compiles its shader. ui.debugger = true shows RmlUi's element inspector over the UI.

docs.title: Drawing
docs.text: RmlUi compiles geometry (vertices with positions in pixels, premultiplied-alpha colors and texture coordinates) and asks to render it with a translation, a texture, a scissor rectangle and an optional transform. UiRenderer keeps the compiled vertices and indices in memory and, when a frame's graph is built, packs the geometry that frame draws, once each however often it is drawn, into per-frame upload buffers (as the ImGui backend does), so nothing on the GPU depends on when RmlUi releases a piece of geometry. ui.slang pulls the 20-byte vertices from a buffer, applies the element's CSS transform and the translation, and maps pixels to clip space at the context's size; the pipeline blends premultiplied (source + destination * (1 - source alpha)), the textures are premultiplied when they are made, and colors go to the (UNORM) target as authored, like ImGui's. Textures are bindless images whose index is the handle RmlUi holds (0 is the white texel that untextured geometry samples); a released texture is freed when the frame that last used it is done.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
RmlUi 6 asks the host for more than geometry, and UiRenderer records everything it asks for, in order, then turns the list into passes of the render graph.

RCSS What RmlUi asks What we do overflow: hidden with a border-radius, or a transform a clip mask (EnableClipMask, RenderToClipMask: set, set inverse, intersect) a texture the size of the context whose red channel is the coverage. Every operation draws its shape into a new one (an intersection samples the one before), and ui.slang multiplies what it draws by the mask. This is a coverage texture, not a stencil buffer: it needs nothing from the graphics device's pipelines, and it is the same on every backend. A plain rectangle stays a scissor. filter: opacity() blur() drop-shadow() brightness() contrast() grayscale() hue-rotate() invert() saturate() sepia() layers (PushLayer, PopLayer, CompositeLayers) and filters (CompileFilter) what is inside a filtered element is drawn into a transient RGBA8 layer (an image of the render graph, as large as the context), and the filter chain runs on it as full-screen passes: a 5x4 color matrix for the color filters, a separable Gaussian for blur, shifted and tinted blur under the source for drop-shadow. The result is composited onto the layer below, inside the scissor and the clip mask. box-shadow, mask-image SaveLayerAsTexture, SaveLayerAsMaskImage the box shadow is drawn once into a layer, blurred, and kept as a texture RmlUi gives back to draw; a mask image is drawn into a layer whose alpha multiplies the element when it is composited. decorator: linear-gradient(), radial-gradient(), conic-gradient() (and repeating- forms) shaders (CompileShader, RenderShader) a branch of uiFs: the gradient's stops are in a per-frame storage buffer and the fragment computes its color from its position in the element.

The opacity property is not a layer: RmlUi folds it into the colors of each element, so overlapping children of a half-transparent element show through each other. filter: opacity() is the one that makes a group. Not supported: backdrop-filter (it would sample the frame under the UI, which is not an image the pass can read) and a filter on the root of the context. UiRenderer.LastEffects says how many masks, layers and composites the last frame had; the tests in UiRenderingTests read pixels back for each of the rows above.

docs.title: Animations
docs.text: Animations and transitions run on the sum of the Update steps, so a paused game pauses its UI and a test is deterministic. RmlUi limits one step to a tenth of a second per animation (a long frame does not skip one). Tween names are RmlUi's (linear-in, quadratic-out, cubic-in-out); a transition starts counting at the first update after the change; transition: width 1s linear-in in a rule and a class change is the usual shape.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.UI.Tests runs RmlUi through the whole engine: the base stylesheet under a document's own rules, the default font and its bold face, making and moving and destroying elements from the script surface (and what a handle to a destroyed one does), attributes, inline styles and pseudo-classes, listeners (bubbling, capture, stopping, a handler that throws, pruning), typing into a text field, documents and their stylesheets read through the file system, resizing and density, transitions and the step limit, the debugger, the SDL key and button tables; and on a GPU, pixels read back from the render graph: a box at its place in its color, premultiplied blending over black and white, overflow: hidden clipping, CSS transforms (a translation and a rotation), text from the default font, an image with straight alpha from the file system, the geometry cache across frames, edits showing on the next frame, resizing. RuntimeTests runs a game folder with a document through --headless --screenshot and clicks an element from a Luau system, whose handler writes a file.
